items.title: Young mathematicians are reconsidering their careers: 'None of the individual work will matter'
items.summary: Graduate students studying math are considering leaving their careers because of AI. Malte Mueller/Getty Images As AI remakes the field of math, some students say they feel like giving up. In a survey, nearly 76% of students said they were unlikely to seek careers in math academia. Many respondents also bristled at academic leadership. Frontier AI programs can now do math better than graduate students . Those students, it turns out, aren't taking the news well. In a paper published this week, researchers at MIT found that a vast majority of grad students and postdoctoral scholars they polled see their career prospects rapidly dimming as AI remakes the field. Nearly 76% said they are increasingly unlikely to stay in academic math after earning their degrees. 76% said they feel less motivated to do research "as a result of AI developments ." And in a free-response portion of the survey, grad students laid bare their raw, pent-up feelings about the subject. Perhaps most striking is a red-hot frustration with academic leadership, which respondents described as alternatively wayward, useless, meek, silent, and ineffectual. "It'd be great if institutes gave guidance instead of platitudes on this subject," one respondent wrote. "We are lacking high-level leadership from across the academic community," another said. For the survey, conducted by three MIT-affiliated math students, the researchers polled 268 early-career mathematicians via a Google Form. Questions were multiple-choice and free response. They all centered on AI's ever-expanding ability to do work they've spent years studying. Notably, the response window closed just after OpenAI released hundreds of solutions to long-standing problems on October 6. The authors caveated the survey, saying it represents the vibe at "only a small window of time." "The past couple of months have been exhausting," the researchers wrote. "We're being forced to reckon with existential questions about a field we love, all while incredibly uncertain about our own futures." Since OpenAI first really broke onto the mathematics scene in September, when it published solutions to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize question, the AI-generated solutions have only kept coming. Mathematicians have described going through stages of disbelief, shock, denial, anger, and, for some, acceptance. Though some high-level mathematical councils have convened to issue edicts on how AI should be used, it's not like OpenAI has to listen to them. OpenAI and Anthropic have, however, made some concessions to the math community. Both AI giants pledged a combined $15 million to a foundation to support mathematicians, and OpenAI established an "advisory group" to judge its math operation. If you ask students, though, the concessions haven't changed much for them. "It is difficult to do research and go to seminars when it feels like none of the individual work will matter much in the future," one respondent wrote. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Top-cited scientists in clinical medicine by country: the Stanford–Elsevier top 2% list in R
items.summary_html:
[This article was first published on R Programming – DataScience+, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here) Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

Clinical medicine is by far the largest field in the 2026 Stanford–Elsevier top 2% list: 76,155 of the 249,310 listed authors, 31%, have it as their main field, more than the next three of the 20 fields combined. I wanted to know where those scientists work, and whether the country ranking still looks the same once you ask how many people each country has.

The data is John Ioannidis’s science-wide author database, built with Elsevier from Scopus (Ioannidis, J.P.A. (2026), “August 2026 data-update for ‘Updated science-wide author databases of standardized citation indicators’”, Mendeley Data, v9, doi:10.17632/btchxktzyw.9, licensed CC BY-NC 3.0). An author is listed if they rank in the top 100,000 by a composite citation score or in the top 2% of their main subfield. I use the single-year table, which scores citations received during 2025. Each row carries a main field from the Science-Metrix classification (sm-field) and the country of the author’s most recent institution (cntry).

Find a top-cited scientist or institution: If you would rather skip the tutorial and find your own name or institution, topcitedscientists.com has the whole 2026 list: search for a scientist by name or see institutions ranked by their number of top-cited scientists.

How do I count the Stanford–Elsevier top 2% scientists by country in R?

Download the single-year author table from Mendeley Data, read its Data sheet with readxl, fill the blank countries from the top_cntry_career column, then filter on sm-field and count() the countries. This block runs on its own with readxl 1.5.0 and tidyverse 2.0.0 on R 4.6.1. The file is about 100 MB, so it raises the download timeout first:

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)

url <- "https://data.mendeley.com/public-files/datasets/btchxktzyw/files/a517a94c-3fb0-4cee-b97f-f2d476df66f0/file_downloaded"
file <- "Table_1_Authors_singleyr_2025_pubs_since_1788_wopp_extracted_202608.xlsx"

options(timeout = 600)
if (!file.exists(file)) {
  download.file(url, file, mode = "wb")
}

authors <- read_excel(file, sheet = "Data") |>
  mutate(
    filled = is.na(cntry),
    cntry = coalesce(cntry, str_to_lower(top_cntry_career))
  )

clinical <- authors |>
  filter(`sm-field` == "Clinical Medicine") |>
  count(cntry, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

clinical
## # A tibble: 147 × 3
##    cntry     n  share
##       
##  1 usa   28458 0.374 
##  2 gbr    6303 0.0828
##  3 chn    3924 0.0515
##  4 deu    3770 0.0495
##  5 ita    3710 0.0487
##  6 can    3140 0.0412
##  7 aus    2943 0.0386
##  8 fra    2120 0.0278
##  9 jpn    2074 0.0272
## 10 nld    1955 0.0257
## # ℹ 137 more rows

Three details in that code matter. download.file() gives up after 60 seconds by default, which a slow connection hits long before 100 MB. The workbook’s first sheet is a column key, so read_excel(file) without sheet = quietly returns its 53 rows of definitions instead of the data. And 169 authors have no cntry, 77 of them in clinical medicine, the most of any field; the dataset’s top_cntry_career column (the country that appears most often on their papers) fills them, and the filled column keeps a record of which rows were changed. That moves the US from 28,424 to 28,458.

The United States has 28,458 of the field’s top-cited scientists, 37.4%. The United Kingdom follows with 6,303, then China (3,924), Germany (3,770) and Italy (3,710). Those five hold 61% of the field, and 146 countries have at least one listed author.

Related posts on DataScience+:

  • Machine Learning Results in R: one plot to rule them all! (Part 1 – Classification Models)
  • Visualize your Portfolio’s Performance and Generate a Nice Report with R
  • Creating Slopegraphs with R
Per resident, Switzerland and Denmark lead

A raw count mostly measures how big a country’s research system is. Dividing by population asks a different question: how dense the country’s pool of highly cited clinicians and medical researchers is. I take 2024 population from the World Bank’s API (indicator SP.POP.TOTL, keyless JSON) and keep countries with at least a million residents:

wb <- jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0(
  "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/",
  "SP.POP.TOTL?date=2024&format=json&per_page=400"
))

population <- wb[[2]] |>
  as_tibble() |>
  transmute(
    cntry = str_to_lower(countryiso3code),
    country = country$value,
    pop = value
  ) |>
  filter(cntry != "")

per_million <- clinical |>
  inner_join(population, by = "cntry") |>
  filter(pop >= 1e6) |>
  mutate(per_million = n / pop * 1e6) |>
  arrange(desc(per_million))

per_million |> select(country, n, per_million) |> head(8)
## # A tibble: 8 × 3
##   country            n per_million
##                    
## 1 Switzerland     1345       149. 
## 2 Denmark          820       137. 
## 3 Netherlands     1955       109. 
## 4 Australia       2943       108. 
## 5 Sweden          1028        97.3
## 6 United Kingdom  6303        91.0
## 7 United States  28458        83.7
## 8 Canada          3140        76.1

Switzerland has 149 top-cited clinical medicine scientists per million residents and Denmark 137, against 84 in the United States, which ranks 7th per resident behind the Netherlands, Australia, Sweden and the United Kingdom. China is 2.8 per million and India 0.9. The floor matters: without it, Monaco’s three listed authors would rank it among the leaders. Taiwan (428 authors) drops out of this table because the World Bank does not publish its population.

A country’s count also reflects its field mix

China is second in the whole list, with 37,204 listed authors across all fields, yet only third in clinical medicine. The reason is what its top-cited scientists work on:

field_mix <- authors |>
  summarise(
    listed = n(),
    clinical = mean(`sm-field` == "Clinical Medicine"),
    .by = cntry
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(listed))

field_mix |> head(5)
## # A tibble: 5 × 3
##   cntry listed clinical
##         
## 1 usa    73722    0.386
## 2 chn    37204    0.105
## 3 gbr    18320    0.344
## 4 deu    10942    0.345
## 5 aus     8974    0.328

Clinical medicine is the main field of 39% of listed US authors and 34% of British ones, against 31% across the whole list and 11% in China, where the largest field is Enabling & Strategic Technologies (8,807 authors). So a field-by-country ranking says as much about where a country’s research effort goes as about how strong it is in that field.

Two caveats travel with every number here. The list counts citations, not quality, and the dataset’s authors warn against reading it as absolute evidence of excellence. And cntry is where an author works now, not their nationality or where they trained.

items.title: Prisons Using AI to Predict When Incarcerated People Will Commit Future Crimes
items.summary: Michigan is set to deploy a major new AI system to prisons across the state, meant to classify incarcerated people based on “how dangerous they are.” That’s according to Detroit channel Fox2 , which reports that the Michigan Department of Corrections is plowing ahead with an inmate categorization algorithm that will sort people into various housing levels. In Michigan, incarcerated people are separated into five housing levels according to their security classification. In the past, screenings were performed by a committee of staff appointed by the Warden at each facility. Now, it seems the state wants to outsource that decision — or at least have it be heavily informed by — a non-profit tech company called Recidiviz. Recidiviz began as a data organization project at Google, meant to “uncover how technology could standardize criminal justice data and improve the system nationwide.” Its AI-integrated software platform is said to perform features like identifying individuals eligible for state-offered programs, reclassification, or release, and coordinate access to resources like transitional housing and employment. In a press release , MDOC said the Recidiviz software will be used to “optimize placement of incarcerated individuals” starting with a pilot program in a number of men’s facilities beginning in December. The state agency notes that the AI tool is expected to “improve MDOC’s ability to more accurately predict incarcerated individuals’ risk of future violence by approximately 30 percent,” though how the state arrived at that vague figure is unclear. For incarcerated people, housing designations are extremely consequential, determining which programming and resources an incarcerated person is eligible for, and what kind of population they’ll be housed with for the duration of their sentence. Setting the state’s rationale aside, the MDOC-Recividiz partnership leaves some major questions unanswered. What kind of data will be collected, for example, will matter a great deal with regard to the AI system’s accuracy. As a ProPublica investigation into a similar risk-analysis program in Louisiana found, the kind of data being used to classify incarcerated people contained inherent racial and socioeconomic bias. As a result, Louisiana’s carceral system has become even more cruel and harmful to those earnestly working toward rehabilitation. In one case reported by ProPublica , a blind and wheelchair bound 70-year-old was determined to be a “moderate risk” of reoffending despite having a clean disciplinary record — a classification which results in an automatic loss of eligibility for parole. While Michigan’s system is geared toward housing assignments rather than parole decisions, it seems highly unlikely that software alone will solve the state’s ongoing corrections crisis — and if Louisiana’s embrace of AI is any example, it could very well make matters far, far worse. Michigan Department of Corrections was contacted for comment. More on incarceration: What Are the Ethics of Strapping VR Headsets on Inmates in Solitary Confinement?

items.title: 'SNL' goes after AI, startup culture, and 'predatory tech guys'
items.summary: 'Saturday Night Live' took aim at startup culture and AI across multiple sketches during its Halloween broadcast. : Will Heath/NBC via Getty Images 'SNL' fired shots at startup culture in its latest episode. Comedian Ben Marshall played Pennywise the clown pitching a new AI company to trap kids. In another segment, a Sprite exec admits its new flavor tastes bad because "we used AI to make it." "Saturday Night Live" took aim at startup culture and AI across multiple sketches in its Halloween broadcast, including a spoof of the stereotypical big-talking startup dude, channeled through Stephen King's Pennywise. "We started a company — it's called WeAllFloat.ai," comedian Ben Marshall, playing the malevolent clown, said in the segment. "Instead of trapping one kid with one balloon, what if you had hundreds of AI agents, each with their own digital balloons?" Before Pennywise came on, "Weekend Update" host Michael Che got a joke in about the floundering stock price of Google's parent company, Alphabet. "Today's Google Doodle hung itself," Che said, referring to the animations Google sometimes uses on its homepage. And in another spoof of advertising execs trying to plug a new Sprite flavor on a Latin telenovela, a Sprite rep admits the drink tastes bad because "we used AI to make it." "For the first time in history, AI screwed up," she says sarcastically. Though "SNL" hasn't shied away from lampooning AI and the buzzy startup culture associated with it before, Saturday's broadcast honed in on the Lone Star State as a place where soulless, profit-driven techies are flocking to start new companies. Indeed, since 2020, more than 200 companies have relocated their headquarters to Texas. Many cite comparatively lax regulatory laws and a business-friendly atmosphere. Of course, though, moving down south doesn't guarantee profitability. Pennywise, for instance, might have some trouble getting his AI startup off the ground. "Got a little crew together of cool, like-minded, sober, predatory tech guys," Marshall says in the segment. "I live in a loft in Austin with three other motivated young Christians." items.title: Microsoft Patents an AI That Can Literally Put Words in People’s Mouths in Real Time
items.summary: Microsoft just filed a patent for an AI product that would be able to transform live video in real time to alter speakers’ words and faces. The patent, as first flagged by patent-tracker Patentlyze , is described by its inventors as a “near real-time artificial intelligence (AI) enhancement of video or augmented reality (AR) presentations of live events.” Using AI agents, the system would identify and alter or remove certain words, while editing a speaker’s face and mouth to match. The agents would rely on set parameters or user profiles to make the changes, and would also edit the video and audio just before and after a removed or replaced word to allow for “smooth transitions.” In an era of media and the internet increasingly defined by AI-fueled deepfakes, disinformation, and information-muddling slop, the system described in this patent may represent a new world of filtering tools that subtly alter reality as it takes place, in this case on a highly-personalized level. Viewers, the patent suggests, could consume whatever live event they want to without hearing what they don’t want to hear. The potential use cases floated in the patent vary. One possible application is real-time translation, with the system allowing for broadcasts and other live footage to be both heard and seen in a viewer’s preferred language. The patent also posits that such a tool could be used to remove filler words like “um” or “ah” from live speech, or to erase stutters or speech impediments. Other possible use cases, though, go much further. According to the patent, the system could be used to cut down on “personal words or phrases” like “coined terms,” as well as “colloquial terms” like the term “y’all” or the phrase “bite the bullet.” The patent also claims that the system could eliminate “mumbled words, mispronounced words, misused words, misspoken words, offensive words, insensitive words, or inappropriate words.” Replacement words, it adds, may come from an “internet search.” In other words, live broadcasts may not be so live anymore after all. Microsoft didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Dubbing has existed for ages, and video footage is edited all the time, both for normal and for insidious reasons. Automatically editing live videos in this way with the help of AI agents, however, could change how audiences fundamentally engage with live footage. As it stands, if people don’t like what they hear, they can simply turn something off; the system outlined by Microsoft describes an environment where people can instead adjust someone else’s speech to their personal taste. Language translation aside, does using a tool that eliminates errors, or erases words and phrases associated with a speaker’s local dialect, move us further into personalized bubbles? What’s so bad about hearing someone from the South say “y’all?” To that end, the patent does mention that an event’s original live video and audio may be recorded and stored for the sake of “ground truth,” nodding to potential misuse and confusion that could arise from such a tool. The kinds of live footage that could be transformed by the system include lectures, presentations, a range of television productions — awards ceremonies, game and cooking shows — and live sports, among several others. More on Big Tech patents: Meta Patents Technology to Detect Your Mood by Constantly Analyzing Your Tone of Voice

items.title: New Data Centers in the US Set to Wipe Out 15 Years of Greenhouse Gas Reductions
items.summary: Nearly 15 years worth of hard-won pollution reduction efforts are set to be undone in the United States, as a wave of data centers powered by gas plants enters construction. That’s according to a new analysis by the Sierra Club, first reported by Bloomberg , which notes that the US energy grid is expected to belch out 2.1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by 2030, assuming the country’s currently-planned AI developments enter operation as scheduled. That’s a massive rise compared to even 2025 — itself a near-record year for US carbon emissions. If the AI industry and its data center developers get their way, the analysis found, emissions will likely skyrocket by 42 percent over the five-year period, an expected increase of 618 million tons compared to 2025. “The numbers continue to sort of boggle our minds,” the Sierra Club’s principal advisor for climate and energy Jeremy Fisher told Bloomberg . Due to major bottlenecks in the electrical grid, many data center developers have opted for on- or near-site power plants, which are overwhelmingly fueled by noxious fossil fuels. Projects like Elon Musk’s 1.2 gigawatt data center near Memphis are already choking out residents with fleets of methane generators, which legal experts say flaunt all kinds of local permitting and federal environmental regulations. Still, for anybody banking on having clean air to breathe, there is some hope. The number of data center projects at risk of cancellation is rising precipitously as time goes on — driven by grass roots organizing and increasing financial pressures . So if you’re one of the many activists mounting opposition to data centers in your community, just know that the benefits of a cancelled hyperscale facility extend far beyond your backyard. More on data centers: Thieves Are Making a Fortune Heisting AI Data Center Equipment

items.title: Open-source security in the AI exploit era: Patch without changing a thing
items.summary: Here’s how a vulnerability in a popular open-source library plays out in 2026: A maintainer merges a fix and publishes an advisory. Within hours, someone points a model at the diff between the old and new versions and gets a working exploit back. Your scanner flags the CVE the next morning, a ticket gets filed, and the fix is scheduled into next week’s change window. By then the exploit has been circulating for days. That was a fine enterprise lifestyle choice last year, but it’s considered out of fashion nowadays. And for good reason, as Michael Cembalest goes over in his “ Patchmageddon ” report from July 2026, which includes input from J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s cybersecurity leadership. Models such as Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT–5.5 now find previously unknown vulnerabilities at a scale no human research team can match. Anthropic and its Project Glasswing partners found more than 10,000 new high- and critical-severity zero-days in the first month alone. At the same time, the exploitation clock shrank. The note puts the median time from disclosure to first exploitation at roughly a year in 2021. Now it’s down to one day in 2026, and projected to be one minute by 2027. Almost 80% of exploitations now land on or before their public disclosure. Models can find vulnerabilities, and hackers can exploit them just as fast, if not faster. Open source takes the first hit That pressure lands on open source first, because open source is what modern software is made of and because the source is, well, open for all to see. This is fantastic, and as it should be: it just means it’s the low-hanging fruit for hackers. The people expected to absorb this flood of AI-driven vulnerabilities are mostly volunteers. Of 530 high- and critical-severity findings Anthropic reported to open source maintainers by May 2026, only 75 had been patched. This past summer was filled with open source maintainers closing down bug bounty programs and putting up the gone fishing sign to de-stress. Your new security strategy Like it or not, corporate mindsets about security tend to shift when there’s urgency and a touch of, well, worry. Here’s some more freak-out fuel: More models are getting better – Cembalest’s note expects capabilities now confined to a handful of nation-state units to be reproducible in freely available open-weight models within 12 to 24 months. Here’s how a vulnerability in a popular open-source library plays out in 2026: A maintainer merges a fix and publishes an advisory. Within hours, someone points a model at the diff between the old and new versions and gets a working exploit back. Your scanner flags the CVE the next morning, a ticket gets filed, and the fix is scheduled into next week’s change window. By then the exploit has been circulating for days.

That was a fine enterprise lifestyle choice last year, but it’s considered out of fashion nowadays.

And for good reason, as Michael Cembalest goes over in his “Patchmageddon” report from July 2026, which includes input from J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s cybersecurity leadership. Models such as Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT–5.5 now find previously unknown vulnerabilities at a scale no human research team can match. Anthropic and its Project Glasswing partners found more than 10,000 new high- and critical-severity zero-days in the first month alone.

At the same time, the exploitation clock shrank. The note puts the median time from disclosure to first exploitation at roughly a year in 2021. Now it’s down to one day in 2026, and projected to be one minute by 2027. Almost 80% of exploitations now land on or before their public disclosure. Models can find vulnerabilities, and hackers can exploit them just as fast, if not faster.

Open source takes the first hit

That pressure lands on open source first, because open source is what modern software is made of and because the source is, well, open for all to see. This is fantastic, and as it should be: it just means it’s the low-hanging fruit for hackers.

The people expected to absorb this flood of AI-driven vulnerabilities are mostly volunteers. Of 530 high- and critical-severity findings Anthropic reported to open source maintainers by May 2026, only 75 had been patched. This past summer was filled with open source maintainers closing down bug bounty programs and putting up the gone fishing sign to de-stress.

Like it or not, corporate mindsets about security tend to shift when there’s urgency and a touch of, well, worry. Here’s some more freak-out fuel:

  3. The yardstick has changed – Cembalest is blunt that organizations will have to judge themselves on patching speed, not just accuracy. Programs built around 90-day disclosure windows are now measured against a clock that runs in hours.

If you own a platform, run application security, or sign off on technology risk in a regulated industry, this problem is circling you whether you act or not. Urgency without a plan is like listening to your seatmate on a five-hour-late flight rapidly text back and forth, with that duck quack at max volume for each message they receive. Annoying and a bit of a vibe killer.

To de-quackify, let us share the plan Oren has been sharing with platform and security leaders across financial services.

Not enough people work on open source to patch it fast enough.

Cembalest spends serious time on maintainer concentration. In a Linux Foundation and Harvard study of the top 50 open source projects, 23% had a single developer responsible for more than 80% of lines added, and 94% had fewer than ten developers writing more than 90% of the code. At registry level, Anchore counted more than 18 million npm packages listing a single maintainer.

“Enterprises have enjoyed decades of free beer – open source software – while being told it was sort of irresponsible of them.”

Most communities that write and support open source are doing the best they can, and many have burned out doing even more. But the promise of “free as in beer” was never that they’d keep you perfectly secure and deliver day-zero patches. The promise was, well, free beer. Enterprises have enjoyed decades of free beer – open source software – while being told it was sort of irresponsible of them. Now we’re seeing proof of that, in an entirely self-inflicted way. Morgan’s own technology leadership, summarized in Cembalest’s note, is explicit: run current versions, and move off dependencies where you can’t identify who maintains them, where the maintainer looks like a one-person shop, or where the package appears abandoned. Erik Scales, who leads platform engineering for Tanzu Platform at Charles Schwab, put it bluntly in a VMware Explore talk this year:

  2. Know who maintains your critical dependencies. For each one, write down the organization behind it. Single-maintainer and abandoned packages go on their own list.
  3. Use AI to find and propose fixes, and keep people on the merge. Ideally, those people are the code’s maintainers.

items.title: Proxmox VE 9 high availability: HA rules, fencing and a failover you have actually tested
items.summary: High availability is the feature most people build a Proxmox VE cluster for: a node dies at 3 a.m. and its important guests are running again on another node before anyone wakes up. Proxmox VE does this with two daemons, a watchdog and a set of rules. This post explains how those pieces fit together, adds guests to HA, writes placement rules (which changed in Proxmox VE 9), walks through a node failure step by step, and covers planned shutdowns and maintenance. The trap HA gets switched on for a cluster that is not ready for it: two nodes and no QDevice, or guests whose disks live on local storage with no replica. When a node fails, nothing restarts, or the surviving node fences itself. The second trap is using HA as a substitute for backups. HA restarts the guest. It does not undo whatever was wrong with it. The documented requirements are short: at least three cluster nodes (or two plus a QDevice) for reliable quorum, shared storage for the guests (or replicated storage, with a data-loss window back to the last replica), hardware redundancy, and a watchdog. The HA stack in two daemons Every node runs: pve-ha-lrm , the local resource manager. It starts and stops HA guests on its own node, following the state the CRM requests. pve-ha-crm , the cluster resource manager. One node's CRM is the active master at any time. It tells the LRMs what to run, moves guests when something fails and handles fencing. Both rely on locks in the cluster file system and on a watchdog . While a node is healthy and quorate, its daemons keep resetting the watchdog timer. If the node loses quorum or the HA daemons stop working, the timer runs out and the watchdog resets the node. Why fencing matters Before a guest from a failed node can start somewhere else, the cluster must be certain the failed node is not still running it, perhaps cut off from the network but still writing to shared storage. Starting a second copy would corrupt the disk. Making sure the node is really off is called fencing. Proxmox VE fences with watchdog timers. A node outside the quorate part of the cluster cannot reset its watchdog, so the watchdog resets it. Once the CRM master can take the failed node's lock, it knows the node has fenced itself and can recover its guests. Without a configured hardware watchdog, Proxmox VE uses the Linux kernel's softdog , which the docs describe as reliable but not independent of the server's hardware. Hardware watchdog modules are blocked by default; to use one, name its module and reboot: # /etc/default/pve-ha-manager WATCHDOG_MODULE = iTCO_wdt One warning from the docs worth repeating: never kill pve-ha-crm , pve-ha-lrm or watchdog-mux by hand. They manage the watchdog, and killing them can cause an immediate reset of the node. Adding guests to HA An HA resource is a type and an ID: vm:100 , ct:110 . ha-manager add vm:100 ha-manager add ct:110 --state started --max_restart 1 --max_relocate 1 ha-manager config ha-manager status In the web interface it is Datacenter → HA → Resources → Add , or More → Manage HA on a guest. --state is the requested state: started , stopped , disabled or ignored . Once HA manages a guest, ordinary qm start and qm stop simply change its requested state. max_restart is how often HA retries starting it on the same node after a failed start, and max_relocate how often it tries another node; both default to 1. ha-manager set vm:100 --state stopped # stop and keep stopped ha-manager migrate vm:100 pve2 # live migration ha-manager relocate vm:100 pve2 # stop, move, start ha-manager remove vm:100 # stop managing (does not stop it) Before you add a guest, check it can run on every node HA might pick: disks on shared or replicated storage, bridges with the same names on every node, and no passthrough devices. If a dependency exists on only some nodes, restrict the guest to them with a strict node affinity rule. HA groups became HA rules in Proxmox VE 9 Earlier releases used HA groups to say which nodes a guest prefers. Proxmox VE 9.0 deprecated them in favour of HA rules , stored in /etc/pve/ha/rules.cfg . Existing groups are migrated to node affinity rules automatically once every node runs Proxmox VE 9; if anything looks wrong afterwards, the upgrade guide points to the active CRM's log, journalctl -eu pve-ha-crm . Node affinity: which nodes a guest runs on # Prefer pve1 for the firewall VM; any node is fine if pve1 is down ha-manager rules add node-affinity fw-on-pve1 --resources vm:100 \ --nodes pve1 # Make it a hard requirement instead ha-manager rules set node-affinity fw-on-pve1 --strict 1 # Ordered preference: pve1 first, then pve2 or pve3 equally ha-manager rules add node-affinity ha-core \ --resources vm:101,ct:110 --nodes "pve1:2,pve2:1,pve3:1" # Keep these guests off pve3 (the small node) ha-manager rules add node-affinity not-pve3 --affinity negative \ --resources ct:200,vm:300 --nodes pve3 Node affinity rules are not strict by default : if none of the listed nodes is available, the guest may run elsewhere. With --strict 1 it is restricted to the listed nodes and stopped if none of them is up. Priorities are relative; higher numbers win, and nodes without a number get 0. failback , a per-resource property that defaults to on, moves a guest back to its highest-priority node when that node returns. Resource affinity: guests together or apart # Two DNS servers should never share a node ha-manager rules add resource-affinity dns-apart --affinity negative \ --resources ct:120,ct:121 # An app and its database should stay together ha-manager rules add resource-affinity app-with-db --affinity positive \ --resources vm:130,vm:131 Resource affinity rules are the opposite: strict by default. A negative rule cannot list more resources than there are nodes. Rules are checked for conflicts before they apply. A resource can be in only one node affinity rule, for example, and two resources cannot be kept both together and apart. A conflicting rule is disabled until you resolve it, so run ha-manager rules config after every edit. What happens when a node dies Node pve2 loses power. Corosync on pve1 and pve3 stops hearing from it and forms a new membership without it. Two of three votes: still quorate. The CRM master marks pve2 's HA guests as waiting for fencing (state fence ). If pve2 were still running but cut off, it would be in a minority without quorum and unable to reset its watchdog, and the watchdog (60 seconds, per the docs) would reset it. A node with no power is already fenced in practice. Once the CRM can take pve2 's lock, the node counts as fenced and its guests move to recovery . The CRM picks a node for each guest from the online, quorate nodes, narrowed by the affinity rules, and chooses the one with the lowest load. The guests start there. When pve2 comes back it rejoins the cluster, and guests with failback move back if a rule prefers it. With Ceph or shared storage the guests start with every completed write intact. With ZFS replication they start from the last replica. And every guest that ran on the failed node now runs on fewer nodes, which the docs warn can overload small clusters: size each node so the others can carry its HA guests, or mark only what truly matters as HA. Test it with the power cord Before you trust HA with the firewall, test it with a disposable VM: add it to HA, then pull the power cord (not a clean shutdown) of the node running it. Watch ha-manager status on another node until the VM shows as started on its new home. A clean shutdown tests something else, the shutdown policy. Planned shutdowns: pick a shutdown policy A planned shutdown is not a failure, and HA handles it according to the cluster's shutdown policy, set in Datacenter → Options → HA Settings or in datacenter.cfg : ha: shutdown_policy=migrate conditional (the default): on shutdown, stop the guests and let other nodes take them over; on reboot, freeze them and start them again on the same node. migrate : mark the node unavailable and live-migrate its HA guests away first; they return when it is back. failover : stop the guests and recover them elsewhere if the node is not back soon. freeze : stop and freeze the guests; nothing moves until the node returns. The docs note that conditional is the default for backward compatibility and that some users find migrate behaves more as expected. One catch with migrate : a guest restricted by a strict node affinity rule to unavailable nodes makes the shutdown hang until you step in. Maintenance mode for one node For work on a single node, maintenance mode is the cleanest tool. It migrates the node's HA guests away and brings them back when you disable it: ha-manager crm-command node-maintenance enable pve2 ha-manager status # wait until no HA guests remain on pve2 # ... patch, reboot, replace hardware ... ha-manager crm-command node-maintenance disable pve2 It can run from any node. The LRM shows maintenance as soon as the request is picked up, before every guest has moved, so watch the guest list rather than the status word. Maintenance mode survives a reboot and ends only when you disable it. For work that could briefly break quorum everywhere, such as re-cabling the corosync network, Proxmox VE 9.2 added a cluster-wide switch: ha-manager crm-command disarm-ha freeze , then ha-manager crm-command arm-ha when you are done. While HA is disarmed it protects nothing, so keep the window short. Checklist Quorum survives one node down (three nodes, or two plus a QDevice). Every HA guest's disks are on shared, Ceph or replicated storage. Every rule in ha-manager rules config is enabled (no conflicts). The shutdown policy is a deliberate choice, not the default by accident. A pulled-power failover test of a disposable VM succeeded. Each node can carry the HA guests of any one failed node. This is adapted from my book Cluster Without Fear (Homelab the Right Way, Book 13). The free sample is here and the full book is here . ha-manager rules add node-affinity fw-on-pve1 --resources vm:100 \
  --nodes pve1
# Make it a hard requirement instead
ha-manager rules set node-affinity fw-on-pve1 --strict 1
# Ordered preference: pve1 first, then pve2 or pve3 equally
ha-manager rules add node-affinity ha-core \
  --resources vm:101,ct:110 --nodes "pve1:2,pve2:1,pve3:1"
# Keep these guests off pve3 (the small node)
ha-manager rules add node-affinity not-pve3 --affinity negative \
  --resources ct:200,vm:300 --nodes pve3

Node affinity rules are not strict by default: if none of the listed nodes is available, the guest may run elsewhere. With --strict 1 it is restricted to the listed nodes and stopped if none of them is up. Priorities are relative; higher numbers win, and nodes without a number get 0. failback, a per-resource property that defaults to on, moves a guest back to its highest-priority node when that node returns.

Resource affinity: guests together or apart 
# Two DNS servers should never share a node
ha-manager rules add resource-affinity dns-apart --affinity negative \
  --resources ct:120,ct:121
# An app and its database should stay together
ha-manager rules add resource-affinity app-with-db --affinity positive \
  --resources vm:130,vm:131

Resource affinity rules are the opposite: strict by default. A negative rule cannot list more resources than there are nodes.

Rules are checked for conflicts before they apply. A resource can be in only one node affinity rule, for example, and two resources cannot be kept both together and apart. A conflicting rule is disabled until you resolve it, so run ha-manager rules config after every edit.

What happens when a node dies
  1. Node pve2 loses power. Corosync on pve1 and pve3 stops hearing from it and forms a new membership without it. Two of three votes: still quorate.
  2. The CRM master marks pve2's HA guests as waiting for fencing (state fence).
  3. If pve2 were still running but cut off, it would be in a minority without quorum and unable to reset its watchdog, and the watchdog (60 seconds, per the docs) would reset it. A node with no power is already fenced in practice.
  4. Once the CRM can take pve2's lock, the node counts as fenced and its guests move to recovery.
  5. The CRM picks a node for each guest from the online, quorate nodes, narrowed by the affinity rules, and chooses the one with the lowest load. The guests start there.
  6. When pve2 comes back it rejoins the cluster, and guests with failback move back if a rule prefers it.

With Ceph or shared storage the guests start with every completed write intact. With ZFS replication they start from the last replica. And every guest that ran on the failed node now runs on fewer nodes, which the docs warn can overload small clusters: size each node so the others can carry its HA guests, or mark only what truly matters as HA.

Test it with the power cord

Before you trust HA with the firewall, test it with a disposable VM: add it to HA, then pull the power cord (not a clean shutdown) of the node running it. Watch ha-manager status on another node until the VM shows as started on its new home. A clean shutdown tests something else, the shutdown policy.

Planned shutdowns: pick a shutdown policy

A planned shutdown is not a failure, and HA handles it according to the cluster's shutdown policy, set in Datacenter → Options → HA Settings or in datacenter.cfg:

ha: shutdown_policy=migrate
  • conditional (the default): on shutdown, stop the guests and let other nodes take them over; on reboot, freeze them and start them again on the same node.
  • migrate: mark the node unavailable and live-migrate its HA guests away first; they return when it is back.
  • failover: stop the guests and recover them elsewhere if the node is not back soon.
  • freeze: stop and freeze the guests; nothing moves until the node returns.

The docs note that conditional is the default for backward compatibility and that some users find migrate behaves more as expected. One catch with migrate: a guest restricted by a strict node affinity rule to unavailable nodes makes the shutdown hang until you step in.

Maintenance mode for one node

For work on a single node, maintenance mode is the cleanest tool. It migrates the node's HA guests away and brings them back when you disable it:

ha-manager crm-command node-maintenance enable pve2
ha-manager status          # wait until no HA guests remain on pve2
# ... patch, reboot, replace hardware ...
ha-manager crm-command node-maintenance disable pve2

It can run from any node. The LRM shows maintenance as soon as the request is picked up, before every guest has moved, so watch the guest list rather than the status word. Maintenance mode survives a reboot and ends only when you disable it.

For work that could briefly break quorum everywhere, such as re-cabling the corosync network, Proxmox VE 9.2 added a cluster-wide switch: ha-manager crm-command disarm-ha freeze, then ha-manager crm-command arm-ha when you are done. While HA is disarmed it protects nothing, so keep the window short.

Checklist
  • Quorum survives one node down (three nodes, or two plus a QDevice).
  • Every HA guest's disks are on shared, Ceph or replicated storage.
  • Every rule in ha-manager rules config is enabled (no conflicts).
  • The shutdown policy is a deliberate choice, not the default by accident.
  • A pulled-power failover test of a disposable VM succeeded.
  • Each node can carry the HA guests of any one failed node.

items.title: What Is d3kOS?
items.summary: The Marine Operating System Built for the Future Your phone has an operating system. So does your laptop, your car's infotainment screen and your TV. Boats are the exception. A modern recreational boat can carry a chartplotter, a depth sounder, engine gauges, an AIS receiver, a VHF radio, cameras and a stereo, and almost none of them talk to each other in a way the owner can use. d3kOS was built to change that. It is an open-source marine operating system that runs on a Raspberry Pi at the helm and turns the data already on your boat into one connected, intelligent system. The Problem with Today's Marine Technology Marine electronics have grown one box at a time. Each device solves one problem well, but together they leave the boater with: Fragmented displays. Engine data is on one screen, the chart on another, and cameras somewhere else. Closed ecosystems. Many devices only share data fully with equipment from the same manufacturer. Data with no context. The engine sensor knows the coolant temperature, but nothing on the boat knows whether that temperature is normal for this engine at this RPM . No single place to ask a question. If you want to know what a warning means, you usually have to dig through a paper manual. The data exists. What's missing is a layer that collects it, makes sense of it and presents it in one place. Why Boats Need an Operating System An operating system does three jobs: it manages hardware, runs applications, and gives the user one consistent interface. A vessel operating system does the same for a boat: Manages hardware: GPS receivers, NMEA 2000 adapters, AIS receivers, IP cameras, microphones and speakers. Runs marine applications: charts, engine monitoring, anchor watch, collision advisory, voice assistance and logging. Gives one interface: a single touchscreen dashboard at the helm, plus remote access from a phone. d3kOS ships as a complete image for the SD card. You flash it, boot the Pi, and a setup wizard walks you through configuring the vessel. No programming is needed after installation. What d3kOS Includes Today The current release (v0.9.9.5.1, October 2026) provides these tools on the helm touchscreen: ToolWhat it does* AI Navigation Ask plain-English questions about navigation, regulations or a route Engine Dashboard Live RPM, coolant temperature, oil pressure, battery voltage and fuel level, with alerts Helm Assistant Hands-free voice AI. Say "Helm" and ask a question Anchor Watch Sounds an alarm if the boat drifts beyond a set radius Marine Vision Connects up to 20 IP cameras, with fish detection for fishing boats SafeHelm Collision-avoidance advisory using AIS targets and COLREGs logic Boat Log Automatic trip log of engine starts and stops, position snapshots and voice notes Upload Documents Load your engine manual or checklists so Helm can answer from your own documents Charts and Weather *AvNav chart plotter and a live wind and wave map built into the dashboard d3kOS supports 18 display languages and runs on the Raspberry Pi 3B+, 4B and 5 (4 GB RAM minimum). Signal K Integration: The Data Foundation d3kOS is built on Signal K , the open marine data standard. Signal K takes data from NMEA 0183 and NMEA 2000 devices and turns it into a consistent, web-friendly JSON data model. Every value, whether speed over ground, depth or engine RPM, has a predictable address and consistent units. This is why d3kOS works with existing equipment instead of replacing it. Your chartplotter, depth sounder and engine sensors keep doing their jobs. d3kOS reads what they already broadcast. (See How Signal K and d3kOS Create the Digital Vessel .) AI-Native Architecture Most marine software adds AI as an afterthought. d3kOS was designed around it from the start: Helm voice assistant. On-device speech recognition (Vosk) and speech synthesis (Piper), with the Gemini language model for answers when a connection is available. Retrieval from your own manuals. Upload a PDF and Helm can answer questions from it. Offline fallback. With no internet, Helm still answers from its local knowledge base. That matters on the water, where connectivity is never guaranteed. Computer vision. The Forward Watch plugin uses a custom-trained YOLOv8 model to detect ships, boats, buoys, kayaks, logs and debris from a bow camera. Governed autonomy. Every automated action follows the AAO methodology , a framework that limits what AI is allowed to do, logs every action and guarantees recovery. Built to Stay Current d3kOS updates itself over the air. Updates are signed packages that are checked with an ECDSA signature and a SHA-256 integrity check before they install. If a health check fails afterwards, the update rolls back automatically, and the installer refuses to "update" to an older version. You don't need to swap SD cards or open a terminal. Future Roadmap The d3kOS roadmap is driven by real on-water testing. Areas in active development include: More Forward Watch model training on real-world marine footage Expanded SafeHelm collision-avoidance capability More engine-sensor integration options for boats without NMEA 2000 engine data Research into short-range proximity sensing for small craft Important Safety Note d3kOS is not a certified navigation instrument . It is an aid to awareness and does not replace proper seamanship, certified charts, a proper lookout, or the equipment the law requires. AI answers can be wrong. Never rely on them for safety-critical decisions. Frequently Asked Questions Is d3kOS open source? Yes. d3kOS is released under the GNU GPL v3. A separate commercial licence is available for bundling it with hardware for resale. Does d3kOS replace my chartplotter? No. d3kOS works alongside your existing electronics. It reads their data through Signal K and adds intelligence on top. Does d3kOS need the internet? No. Core functions work offline. An internet connection adds Gemini AI answers, weather maps and remote access. Who supports d3kOS? AtMyBoat.com is the community and support platform for d3kOS. It provides the mobile companion app, the Fix My Pi diagnostics and a community forum.
items.summary_html:
The Marine Operating System Built for the Future

Your phone has an operating system. So does your laptop, your car's infotainment screen and your TV. Boats are the exception. A modern recreational boat can carry a chartplotter, a depth sounder, engine gauges, an AIS receiver, a VHF radio, cameras and a stereo, and almost none of them talk to each other in a way the owner can use.

d3kOS was built to change that. It is an open-source marine operating system that runs on a Raspberry Pi at the helm and turns the data already on your boat into one connected, intelligent system.

The Problem with Today's Marine Technology

Marine electronics have grown one box at a time. Each device solves one problem well, but together they leave the boater with:

  • Fragmented displays. Engine data is on one screen, the chart on another, and cameras somewhere else.

  • Closed ecosystems. Many devices only share data fully with equipment from the same manufacturer.

  • Data with no context. The engine sensor knows the coolant temperature, but nothing on the boat knows whether that temperature is normal for this engine at this RPM.

  • No single place to ask a question. If you want to know what a warning means, you usually have to dig through a paper manual.

The data exists. What's missing is a layer that collects it, makes sense of it and presents it in one place.

Why Boats Need an Operating System

An operating system does three jobs: it manages hardware, runs applications, and gives the user one consistent interface. A vessel operating system does the same for a boat:

  • Manages hardware: GPS receivers, NMEA 2000 adapters, AIS receivers, IP cameras, microphones and speakers.

  • Runs marine applications: charts, engine monitoring, anchor watch, collision advisory, voice assistance and logging.

  • Gives one interface: a single touchscreen dashboard at the helm, plus remote access from a phone.

d3kOS ships as a complete image for the SD card. You flash it, boot the Pi, and a setup wizard walks you through configuring the vessel. No programming is needed after installation.

What d3kOS Includes Today

The current release (v0.9.9.5.1, October 2026) provides these tools on the helm touchscreen:

ToolWhat it does*AI NavigationAsk plain-English questions about navigation, regulations or a routeEngine DashboardLive RPM, coolant temperature, oil pressure, battery voltage and fuel level, with alertsHelm AssistantHands-free voice AI. Say "Helm" and ask a questionAnchor WatchSounds an alarm if the boat drifts beyond a set radiusMarine VisionConnects up to 20 IP cameras, with fish detection for fishing boatsSafeHelmCollision-avoidance advisory using AIS targets and COLREGs logicBoat LogAutomatic trip log of engine starts and stops, position snapshots and voice notesUpload DocumentsLoad your engine manual or checklists so Helm can answer from your own documentsCharts and Weather*AvNav chart plotter and a live wind and wave map built into the dashboard

d3kOS supports 18 display languages and runs on the Raspberry Pi 3B+, 4B and 5 (4 GB RAM minimum).

Signal K Integration: The Data Foundation

d3kOS is built on Signal K, the open marine data standard. Signal K takes data from NMEA 0183 and NMEA 2000 devices and turns it into a consistent, web-friendly JSON data model. Every value, whether speed over ground, depth or engine RPM, has a predictable address and consistent units.

This is why d3kOS works with existing equipment instead of replacing it. Your chartplotter, depth sounder and engine sensors keep doing their jobs. d3kOS reads what they already broadcast. (See How Signal K and d3kOS Create the Digital Vessel.)

AI-Native Architecture

Most marine software adds AI as an afterthought. d3kOS was designed around it from the start:

  • Helm voice assistant. On-device speech recognition (Vosk) and speech synthesis (Piper), with the Gemini language model for answers when a connection is available.

  • Retrieval from your own manuals. Upload a PDF and Helm can answer questions from it.

  • Offline fallback. With no internet, Helm still answers from its local knowledge base. That matters on the water, where connectivity is never guaranteed.

  • Computer vision. The Forward Watch plugin uses a custom-trained YOLOv8 model to detect ships, boats, buoys, kayaks, logs and debris from a bow camera.

  • Governed autonomy. Every automated action follows the AAO methodology, a framework that limits what AI is allowed to do, logs every action and guarantees recovery.

Built to Stay Current

d3kOS updates itself over the air. Updates are signed packages that are checked with an ECDSA signature and a SHA-256 integrity check before they install. If a health check fails afterwards, the update rolls back automatically, and the installer refuses to "update" to an older version. You don't need to swap SD cards or open a terminal.

Future Roadmap

The d3kOS roadmap is driven by real on-water testing. Areas in active development include:

  • More Forward Watch model training on real-world marine footage

  • Expanded SafeHelm collision-avoidance capability

  • More engine-sensor integration options for boats without NMEA 2000 engine data

  • Research into short-range proximity sensing for small craft

Important Safety Note

d3kOS is not a certified navigation instrument. It is an aid to awareness and does not replace proper seamanship, certified charts, a proper lookout, or the equipment the law requires. AI answers can be wrong. Never rely on them for safety-critical decisions.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is d3kOS open source? Yes. d3kOS is released under the GNU GPL v3. A separate commercial licence is available for bundling it with hardware for resale.

Does d3kOS replace my chartplotter? No. d3kOS works alongside your existing electronics. It reads their data through Signal K and adds intelligence on top.

Does d3kOS need the internet? No. Core functions work offline. An internet connection adds Gemini AI answers, weather maps and remote access.

Who supports d3kOS? AtMyBoat.com is the community and support platform for d3kOS. It provides the mobile companion app, the Fix My Pi diagnostics and a community forum.

items.title: Hreflang Routes International URLs, but It Does Not Make Them Rank
items.summary: Hreflang is often treated as an international SEO ranking tactic. Google’s newer framing points to a more useful interpretation: hreflang helps the search engine understand and route between alternate versions of a page, but it does not make those pages rank better on its own. That distinction matters for businesses operating multilingual or multi-market websites. A regional URL can be a valid alternate in a hreflang cluster even when Google has not independently indexed it as the main representative of that cluster. The practical question is no longer simply whether every market has a URL. It is whether each market page gives users, and increasingly AI-driven retrieval systems, a meaningful reason to select it. Hreflang is a relationship signal, not a ranking signal In Bill Hunt’s analysis for Search Engine Journal , hreflang is described through Google’s emerging “alternate names” mental model. The idea is that localized or regional versions are connected representations of substantially the same underlying content. Google can use that relationship to serve the appropriate version to a user based on language, region, device, or other context. This is different from treating each alternate URL as a separately competing ranking asset. Google’s own Alternate URLs help documentation similarly explains that alternate URLs may be served for language or device and can include unmarked duplicates. In this model, an alternate can be useful to serve even when it is not the URL Google has chosen to represent the duplicate cluster in its index. The consequence is straightforward: correctly implemented hreflang can reduce ambiguity about which localized version belongs with which page, but it does not create a direct ranking advantage. It cannot compensate for weak relevance, poor technical accessibility, or near-identical market pages with little user value. Discovery, indexing, and serving are not the same process The key insight in the “alternate names” framing is that discovery, indexing, and serving can be separated. A site may publish many localized URLs and connect them correctly with hreflang. Google can discover those URLs and understand their relationship. It may then cluster them as duplicates or near-duplicates and select one version as the indexed representative. Later, it can still serve a different alternate from the same cluster when that version better matches a searcher’s language or market context. Hunt illustrates the concept with a common international SEO challenge: a company maintains versions of one product page across dozens of markets, while most of the on-page information remains the same. Google does not necessarily need to index every version independently to understand the product and its alternates. It can consolidate similar pages while retaining the ability to route users to an appropriate local URL. This helps explain why an SEO team should not use an individual URL’s apparent indexing status as the only measure of whether hreflang is working. A URL may still have a role in a language or regional cluster. At the same time, being included in a cluster should not be mistaken for evidence that the page has earned visibility for competitive queries. Why distinct market content matters more For international sites, the important strategic shift is from URL coverage to market differentiation. A translated page can be necessary for users, compliance, and local conversion. But translation alone does not automatically establish a separate search value proposition. When pages are substantively equivalent, Google has a rational basis to cluster them. In AI-heavy search experiences and semantic retrieval systems, equivalent meaning can also be recognized across languages more readily than marketers may expect. That raises the standard for localized content. A market page is more likely to offer distinct value when it addresses real local differences, such as: Country-specific regulations, eligibility, or product restrictions. Local prices, currencies, taxes, delivery terms, or availability. Regionally relevant use cases, examples, terminology, and customer concerns. Local support arrangements, contact details, or service coverage. Market-specific product configurations, specifications, or legal information. These differences are not merely SEO embellishments. They can make a page more useful to the intended audience and clarify why it should be treated as more than a duplicate representation of a global template. What this means for AI search visibility Hreflang remains important in an AI-influenced search environment, but its role is foundational rather than promotional. It helps systems interpret which versions are intended alternatives. It does not by itself make a brand more likely to be cited, recommended, or selected in an AI-generated response. For that, the underlying content still needs to be accessible, specific, and relevant to the query. A page describing local eligibility requirements or locally available product options has clearer evidence to contribute than a regional URL that repeats a generic global description. This does not mean every market needs wholly original editorial content. It means teams should be deliberate about where genuine differences exist and represent those differences accurately. Artificially rewriting identical content simply to appear unique can create maintenance burdens without improving usefulness. A practical audit for international websites Start by reviewing market pages in groups , not as isolated URLs. For each product, service, category, or editorial page, ask whether the regional variants genuinely differ in ways that matter to users. Then review the technical implementation . Google’s localized versions guidance remains the reference point for implementing hreflang annotations. Ensure intended alternates are connected consistently and that language and regional targeting reflect the actual page audience. A useful audit should separate three questions: Relationship: Are the alternate URLs correctly declared and mutually connected where appropriate? Accessibility: Can Google discover and crawl the pages without avoidable technical barriers? Differentiation: Does each market page contain accurate local information that justifies its existence for users? The third question is often the most important strategic one. If a market version has no material local distinction, it may still be appropriate as an alternate for users. But teams should not expect hreflang alone to make it independently competitive in search results. If your international pages are largely template-driven, create a GEO Search Leads account to begin assessing where your website’s content may need clearer market-specific signals. A structured review can help identify opportunities to make localized pages more useful for real customer questions while keeping technical relationships and content strategy aligned. Frequently Asked Questions Does hreflang improve rankings? No. Hreflang helps Google understand language and regional alternatives, but it is not a direct ranking signal. Ranking still depends on the relevance, quality, accessibility, and usefulness of the underlying content. Can Google serve a hreflang URL that is not independently indexed? According to the alternate URL model discussed in the source material, Google can cluster similar URLs, index one representative, and serve an appropriate alternate URL for a relevant language or regional context. Should every country have its own page? Not automatically. Separate pages make sense when they serve users in a language or market and accurately reflect local needs. Their value is stronger when they include meaningful differences such as availability, regulations, pricing, or local use cases. Is hreflang still important for AI search? Yes, as a way to clarify the relationship between localized alternatives. However, hreflang does not itself create AI visibility. Market-specific, useful content remains the stronger basis for retrieval, citations, and recommendations. Conclusion Hreflang is best understood as a routing and relationship mechanism, not a shortcut to higher rankings. International SEO teams should maintain accurate alternate annotations, while investing their main effort in content that reflects real differences between markets. That combination gives search systems clearer technical context and gives users a stronger reason to choose the local page.

items.title: MiniMax H3 Action Director: One Graph, Three Modes, Nine LoRA Presets
items.summary: The useful starting point for this action-video workflow is not its most dramatic promotional claim. It is the control panel: which generation mode is selected, which prompt belongs to that mode, and which LoRA coefficients actually reach the model? The supplied MiniMax H3 Action Director export is one workflow with 95 nodes and 160 links . Its nine presets are arithmetic recipes inside that graph, not nine independent workflow files. It supports three intended input routes and an optional latent-refinement path. This walkthrough follows the saved configuration; it does not report a new video render, successful character match, or verified action-contact result. Prepare the exact dependencies Both base-model loaders select minimax_h3_fl2va_pruned_int8_convrot.safetensors . The reference branch adds minimax_h3_ref_lora_layer20-49adaln_proj_rank_256_bf16.safetensors before its action LoRAs. It does not select a separate Ref2VA checkpoint in this export. Other common loader references are: qwen3vl_32b_minimax_h3_nvfp4_awq.safetensors , with encoder type minimax ; minimax_h3_video_vae_int8_convrot.safetensors ; minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32.safetensors . items.summary_html:
The useful starting point for this action-video workflow is not its most dramatic promotional claim. It is the control panel: which generation mode is selected, which prompt belongs to that mode, and which LoRA coefficients actually reach the model?

The supplied MiniMax H3 Action Director export is one workflow with 95 nodes and 160 links. Its nine presets are arithmetic recipes inside that graph, not nine independent workflow files. It supports three intended input routes and an optional latent-refinement path. This walkthrough follows the saved configuration; it does not report a new video render, successful character match, or verified action-contact result.

Prepare the exact dependencies

Both base-model loaders select minimax_h3_fl2va_pruned_int8_convrot.safetensors. The reference branch adds minimax_h3_ref_lora_layer20-49adaln_proj_rank_256_bf16.safetensors before its action LoRAs. It does not select a separate Ref2VA checkpoint in this export.

Other common loader references are:

  • qwen3vl_32b_minimax_h3_nvfp4_awq.safetensors, with encoder type minimax;
  • minimax_h3_video_vae_int8_convrot.safetensors;
  • minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32.safetensors.

The five action-LoRA filenames are H3_Combat_V2.safetensors, Bunny_weapon_combatV1.safetensors, GunFu.safetensors, Motion_Repair_V2.safetensors, and H3_Fight_Flow_V1.safetensors. Optional refinement also references minimax_h3_latent_upscaler_3d_fp16.safetensors through MinimaxH3LatentUpscaler3DRefineHandoff.

These are asset references, not bundled weights or proof of architecture, quantization mechanics, license, or GPU compatibility. Resolve matching implementations and assets before queueing. A zero coefficient does not establish that an unavailable LoRA filename will be accepted by every loader or validation system.

Read the saved defaults before choosing a route

The current export stores main mode ① as true, secondary mode ② as false, refinement ③ as false, preset ④ as 2, duration ⑥ as 10 seconds, and both manual-LoRA switches ⑦/⑧ as false.

The top-level controls route the following inputs:

Main mode ① Secondary mode ② Intended route Inputs to replace False False Text-to-video Prompt node 17 False True First/last-frame video Image nodes 97 and 98; prompt 96 True Either Reference-conditioned video Image nodes 26 and 27; prompt 25

The main mode takes precedence through the model, conditioning, and latent switches. In the saved reference configuration, flipping ② alone does not select the first/last-frame route.

Each route has its own prompt text. The saved first/last-frame prompt, for example, describes a promotional sequence rather than the same action scene as the reference prompt. Replace the prompt associated with the selected route rather than assuming one global prompt controls all modes.

The selected input filenames are not proof that those pictures are included. Supply real, authorized images and inspect which ones reach the active branch.

Follow model routing and step selection

The ordinary model path starts at loader 2 and passes through the five action-LoRA loaders. The reference path starts at loader 22, adds reference adapter 95, and then passes through its five action-LoRA loaders. Switch 29 selects between those paths using main control 35.

Conditioning and latent selectors 30 and 31 follow the same main control. Their ordinary inputs come from the text-versus-first/last selectors 101 and 102; their reference inputs come from node 28.

Step selector 108 receives 20 from node 107 on its false branch and 25 from node 33 on its true branch. Its switch input also comes from main control 35. Both scheduler nodes receive this selected step value through links. Consequently, a scheduler's stored 20 widget is not enough to describe the current reference-mode configuration.

The sampler selector stores res_multistep. The first scheduler stores simple and denoise 1; the refinement scheduler stores simple and denoise 0.3. The latter value does not establish that refinement executes a full additional 20 or 25 iterations. Actual scheduling and node behavior require the matching implementation and a run record.

What the nine automatic presets change

Preset node 39 feeds the coefficient expressions. The first-stage manual switch at node 40 determines whether those expressions use their preset recipe or manual values. The second-stage expressions also receive first-stage manual controls and their own override switch at node 68.

The following table evaluates the saved expressions with both manual switches false. Values are static arithmetic results, not measured image effects. The order is Combat / Weapon / GunFu / Motion / Fight Flow. Refinement coefficients matter only when that stage is used.

Preset label from the source note First-stage coefficients Refinement coefficients A0 Basic action 0.65 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0 0.4 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0 A1 Dynamic-motion repair 1 / 0 / 0 / 0.5 / 0 0.65 / 0 / 0 / 0.2 / 0 A2 Two-character interaction 0.65 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.65 0.4 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.25 A3 Combined action 0.7 / 0 / 0 / 0.5 / 0.65 0.45 / 0 / 0 / 0.2 / 0.25 A4 Weapon choreography 0 / 0.45 / 0 / 0 / 0 0 / 0.25 / 0 / 0 / 0 A5 GunFu 0 / 0 / 0.9 / 0 / 0 0 / 0 / 0.65 / 0 / 0 A6 Sustained action 0 / 0 / 0.9 / 0.5 / 0 0 / 0 / 0.65 / 0.25 / 0 A7 Close-range action 0.5 / 0 / 0.9 / 0.3 / 0 0 / 0 / 0.65 / 0.25 / 0 A8 General motion repair 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.9 / 0 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.3 / 0

The second-stage recipe is not simply a uniform percentage of the first. A7, for example, has a nonzero first-stage Combat coefficient but zero in its automatic refinement recipe. Enabling either manual switch changes the formula inputs, so the table no longer describes every effective coefficient.

Changing the preset number changes these connected coefficient expressions. It does not rewrite the separate prompt strings at nodes 17, 25, or 96. Keep the selected prompt consistent with the fictional scene you intend to generate, and do not assume a preset creates the right action merely because of its label.

Duration is a frame budget, not a rendered result

Duration node 105 supplies this expression at node 106:

max(5, round(a * 24)) + (5 - (max(5, round(a * 24)) % 17)) % 17

Its integer output connects to the length inputs of all three generation-condition nodes. Evaluating the expression gives 124 frames for 5 seconds and 243 frames for 10 seconds, both satisfying the intended 17n+5 form.

At the configured 24 fps, those budgets correspond arithmetically to approximately 5.17 and 10.13 seconds. They are not measurements of produced video files. The condition nodes' stored length defaults are connected over, so quoting their saved 124 value as the current ten-second setting would be incorrect.

Single-stage versus optional refinement

With control 59 false, width and height come from resolution selector 104. It stores 16:9, a 0.98-megapixel target, and alignment 32. Those controls describe the selected configuration, not independently checked dimensions.

With control 59 true, width and height selectors instead receive 896 and 512 from nodes 60 and 61. Refinement node 65 stores a 1344×768 target, and output switch 66 selects its latent result instead of the first sampler's output. Both video decoder 13 and audio decoder 14 consume that selected latent.

The source note warns that the refinement extension may still be required to import or validate the graph even when the refinement switch is off. A disabled route is not a guarantee that missing custom-node classes can be ignored. Use a compatible installation or a separately verified single-stage version; this package does not invent one.

Refinement is not guaranteed to improve a particular scene. Compare actual results before describing it as sharper, more faithful, or more stable.

Audio and output need their own inspection

Reference node 28 has an audio connection from LoadAudio 109, but that loader is saved in mode 4 with a None selection. Verify the installed node's handling of this state instead of assuming that a usable audio reference is present.

The graph decodes audio from the selected latent and connects it, alongside decoded video frames, to CreateVideo and then SaveVideo. That is not a direct source-audio remux or proof of synchronized, preserved audio.

The save prefix still contains the word Veda, while the current notes say the Turbo/Veda acceleration routes were removed. The node list contains no separately named Turbo/Veda acceleration route. A filename prefix is not evidence that acceleration is active, and this export should not be promoted as an eight-step configuration on that basis.

A practical first-run checklist
  1. Resolve the exact assets and node implementations, including the optional refinement node's import requirements.
  2. Confirm the main route and edit its corresponding prompt. Replace only the relevant image inputs with authorized material.
  3. Start with the saved automatic preset controls unless deliberately testing manual weights. Record changes rather than altering several variables at once.
  4. Check duration, the selected resolution route, and any audio-reference state before queueing.
  5. After an actual run, inspect output dimensions, duration, audio, character consistency, continuity, and whether the intended interaction is visually coherent.

No render, compatibility test, performance result, or licensing determination is attached here. The source-provided tutorial offers context; its URL was not live-verified for this package. The local file named as subtitles contains promotional metadata rather than a spoken transcript, so it is not treated as a record of tested behavior. Check workflow, model, LoRA, node, artwork, and input-image rights separately before redistribution or commercial use.
