items.title: Why Sales Reps Forget Most of Their Sales Training, and What Actually Sticks
items.summary: Originally published on the Kulissa blog: Why sales reps forget most of their training, and what actually sticks Sales enablement loves a packed agenda. Product decks. Competitive slides. Role-play that lasts until someone looks at the clock. Then Monday arrives, the calendar fills, and the classroom becomes a blur. ATD's State of Sales Training 2023, citing Gartner, reports that B2B reps forget about 70% of training within a week and 87% within a month unless they use it. First-year sellers still spend more than ten days in formal training. That is a lot of stage time that never makes it into the show. The forgetting curve is not a mystery. Hermann Ebbinghaus mapped it more than a century ago: unused memory decays fast, then slower. What surprises revenue leaders is how often the curriculum assumes the opposite. We treat exposure as competence. We treat a single rehearsal as muscle memory. The call, of course, is the reveal. Without practice under pressure, the wings stay crowded and the performance stays thin. The classroom was never the stage Formal training is useful for shared language. It is a poor substitute for live conversation. A workshop can introduce a discovery framework. It cannot teach a rep what to do when a buyer cuts them off mid-sentence, or when procurement joins on minute twelve with a price objection the playbook never covered in that order. Most programs optimize for coverage. Cover the ICP. Cover the competitors. Cover the objection list. Coverage feels responsible. It also creates a false sense of readiness. The Bridge Group's AE Models, Motions and Metrics 2026 puts average AE ramp at 6.2 months, with only 48% of AEs at quota. If classroom hours alone closed the gap, those numbers would look different. Reps do not forget because they are lazy. They forget because the brain prioritizes what gets retrieved under load. A slide deck is passive. A live buyer is not. Without retrieval practice, the methodology stays in the binder. Three reasons training evaporates 1. Spacing is optional, not designed Enablement often runs as an event. Kickoff week. Quarterly SKO. A two-day bootcamp for new hires. Dense input, thin follow-up. Spaced retrieval is what keeps skills available. Without it, the first week of forgetting does the predictable damage. A practical rule: if a skill matters on the phone, schedule at least three short practice reps across ten days after the workshop. Not another lecture. Practice. 2. Feedback arrives late or not at all Managers coach when they have time. Call recordings help, but they coach after the fact. The rep already shipped the performance. Delayed feedback still helps for pattern recognition. It does less for building automatic responses under interruption. Ericsson's research on deliberate practice is blunt about this. Improvement needs a clear goal, immediate feedback, and repetition at the edge of current ability. Most sales "practice" fails two of the three: goals are vague ("be more consultative"), feedback is sparse, and the difficulty never climbs. 3. The scoreboard rewards activity, not readiness Pipeline reviews count meetings and stage movement. Training completion is a checkbox. Neither tells you whether a rep can hold a value conversation when the buyer is cold. When the org measures attendance, people attend. When it measures live performance against a shared scorecard, people rehearse. What actually sticks Skills stick when three conditions hold. Retrieval under pressure. The rep must produce the behavior without a slide behind them. Voice practice with interruptions beats watching a model call. Evidence-based coaching. Vague praise ("good energy") does not change behavior. Quoted transcript moments do. "You skipped the impact question after they said budget was frozen" is actionable. Playbook-native scenarios. Generic AI buyers teach generic habits. Scenarios built from your own discovery framework, objection tree, and competitive traps teach the show your team actually runs. That is the difference between theatre games and dress rehearsal. If you want a Monday-ready test for any training module, ask: Can the rep demonstrate the skill live in under five minutes? Is there a shared rubric that names pass and fail behaviors? Will they practice again within 72 hours with a harder version? If any answer is no, you bought exposure, not readiness. A simple retention design for enablement Use this as a template for the next cohort, not as a manifesto. 0. Input: 45-minute workshop on one skill; Practice: None; Check: Pre-assessment score 1. Input: Short reminder card; Practice: One 8-minute scenario; Check: Rubric score + one coach note 3. Input: Peer listen-in (optional); Practice: Harder buyer temperature; Check: Rubric delta vs day 1 7. Input: None; Practice: Same skill, new persona; Check: Pass threshold or rematch 14. Input: Manager 1:1 on evidence; Practice: Assignment based on weak dimension; Check: Cohort readiness view Keep the curriculum narrow. One skill per cycle beats five half-learned skills. The sales onboarding plan for the first 30 days expands this into a full ramp calendar. For teams rebuilding from methodology documents, turning a playbook into roleplay scenarios is the conversion step most enablement skips. Where conversation intelligence fits (and where it does not) Gong-style conversation intelligence is excellent for coaching real calls. It is a poor primary practice loop. You cannot schedule enough live buyer meetings to create deliberate practice volume. You also cannot ask a strategic account to be your classroom. Role-play and conversation intelligence are complementary. Practice builds the skill. Recorded calls audit transfer to the field. Treating recordings as the only gym is like only reviewing game film and never running drills. The longer comparison is in role-play vs conversation intelligence . How this works in Kulissa Kulissa is built around rehearsal before the reveal. A rep opens the browser, speaks into the microphone, and faces a live AI buyer who interrupts, objects, and changes temperature. Sessions are transcribed and scored against your methodology, with evidence quoted from the transcript. Scenarios can be generated from your playbooks so practice stays native to how you sell. Managers see readiness by rep and cohort, not just completion. That matters if your goal is retention of skill, not attendance. Product detail lives on kulissa.com/product . If ramp and onboarding are the pain, start with kulissa.com/use-cases/sales-onboarding . Maya on kulissa.com/maya is the public gatekeeper demo: convince her your team deserves access, and you can win promotional credits for a workspace. It is a rehearsal of the product idea itself. The uncomfortable conclusion If 87% of unused training fades within a month, the expensive part of enablement is not the facilitator. It is the false confidence. Teams that treat practice as a first-class operating system reduce that waste. Teams that keep buying more slides keep buying forgetting. The stage does not care how many workshops you attended. It cares whether the line lands when someone talks over you. What enablement leaders should stop funding Before you renew another content library, ask whether last year's modules produced measurable retrieval. If the only dashboard is completion percentage, you are funding forgetting with better production value. Stop funding: One-time certifications with no rematch window Manager "coaching" that is really forecast interrogation Competitive battle cards that are never practiced aloud Kickoff theatre that crowds out the first two weeks of spaced practice Start funding: Scenario libraries tied to loss reasons Manager calibration time on shared scorecards Protected practice blocks on the AE calendar Rematch capacity when someone fails a gate This is capital allocation, not pedagogy fashion. The forgetting curve does not care about your brand fonts. A worked example: discovery that does not stick Imagine a two-day onboarding that covers discovery thoroughly. Reps can recite the question list. On day ten, a buyer asks for pricing in minute two. Most reps pitch. The discovery list was never retrieved under interruption, so it never became available. Now change the design. After the workshop, every rep runs three scenarios: friendly discovery, price-interrupt discovery, and dual-stakeholder discovery. Failures rematch within forty-eight hours. Managers quote transcript lines in 1:1s. By day fourteen, the question list is no longer a list. It is a reflex with judgment. Same content hours. Different retention. The difference is deliberate retrieval, which is also why deliberate practice for sales teams belongs next to this article on your enablement reading list. Measuring retention without fake precision You do not need a neuroscience lab. You need three operational signals: Scenario rematch rate falling over a cohort's first month Dimension stability when the same skill is tested ten days later with a new persona Live transfer on conversation intelligence reviews using the same rubric language If signal one improves while signal three stays flat, your scenarios are too polite. If signal two collapses, you never had learning; you had short-term performance. If all three move, congratulations: you built a practice system instead of a content museum. Sources ATD, State of Sales Training 2023 (citing Gartner on training forgetting rates and first-year formal training days) The Bridge Group, AE Models, Motions and Metrics 2026 (AE ramp and quota attainment) Ericsson, K. Anders et al., research on deliberate practice and expert performance Ebbinghaus, Hermann, work on the forgetting curve (classic memory research) FAQ Why do sales reps forget training so quickly? Because unused memory decays fast, and most programs deliver dense input without scheduled retrieval under pressure. ATD citing Gartner puts forgetting near 70% within a week and 87% within a month unless the material is used. Classroom coverage without live practice accelerates that curve. How many practice sessions does it take for a skill to stick? There is no universal magic number, but spaced practice with feedback beats one marathon. A workable pattern is three to five short scenarios across two weeks for a single skill, each scored against a shared rubric, with difficulty rising as the rep clears the bar. Does conversation intelligence replace practice? No. Conversation intelligence coaches real calls after they happen. Deliberate practice needs volume, controlled difficulty, and immediate feedback. Recordings and role-play work best together: drills for building skill, film for transferring it to live deals. What should managers measure instead of training completion? Measure demonstrated readiness: rubric scores on live practice, weak dimensions by cohort, and rematch rates after a failed scenario. Completion proves attendance. Scored rehearsal proves whether the skill is available on stage. See how it works at kulissa.com .

Ericsson's research on deliberate practice is blunt about this. Improvement needs a clear goal, immediate feedback, and repetition at the edge of current ability. Most sales "practice" fails two of the three: goals are vague ("be more consultative"), feedback is sparse, and the difficulty never climbs.

3. The scoreboard rewards activity, not readiness

Pipeline reviews count meetings and stage movement. Training completion is a checkbox. Neither tells you whether a rep can hold a value conversation when the buyer is cold. When the org measures attendance, people attend. When it measures live performance against a shared scorecard, people rehearse.

What actually sticks

Skills stick when three conditions hold.

Retrieval under pressure. The rep must produce the behavior without a slide behind them. Voice practice with interruptions beats watching a model call.

Evidence-based coaching. Vague praise ("good energy") does not change behavior. Quoted transcript moments do. "You skipped the impact question after they said budget was frozen" is actionable.

Playbook-native scenarios. Generic AI buyers teach generic habits. Scenarios built from your own discovery framework, objection tree, and competitive traps teach the show your team actually runs. That is the difference between theatre games and dress rehearsal.

If you want a Monday-ready test for any training module, ask:

  1. Can the rep demonstrate the skill live in under five minutes?
  2. Is there a shared rubric that names pass and fail behaviors?
  3. Will they practice again within 72 hours with a harder version?

If any answer is no, you bought exposure, not readiness.

A simple retention design for enablement

Use this as a template for the next cohort, not as a manifesto.

  • 0. Input: 45-minute workshop on one skill; Practice: None; Check: Pre-assessment score
  • 1. Input: Short reminder card; Practice: One 8-minute scenario; Check: Rubric score + one coach note
  • 3. Input: Peer listen-in (optional); Practice: Harder buyer temperature; Check: Rubric delta vs day 1
  • 7. Input: None; Practice: Same skill, new persona; Check: Pass threshold or rematch
  • 14. Input: Manager 1:1 on evidence; Practice: Assignment based on weak dimension; Check: Cohort readiness view

Keep the curriculum narrow. One skill per cycle beats five half-learned skills. The sales onboarding plan for the first 30 days expands this into a full ramp calendar. For teams rebuilding from methodology documents, turning a playbook into roleplay scenarios is the conversion step most enablement skips.

Where conversation intelligence fits (and where it does not)

Gong-style conversation intelligence is excellent for coaching real calls. It is a poor primary practice loop. You cannot schedule enough live buyer meetings to create deliberate practice volume. You also cannot ask a strategic account to be your classroom.

Role-play and conversation intelligence are complementary. Practice builds the skill. Recorded calls audit transfer to the field. Treating recordings as the only gym is like only reviewing game film and never running drills. The longer comparison is in role-play vs conversation intelligence.

How this works in Kulissa

Kulissa is built around rehearsal before the reveal. A rep opens the browser, speaks into the microphone, and faces a live AI buyer who interrupts, objects, and changes temperature. Sessions are transcribed and scored against your methodology, with evidence quoted from the transcript. Scenarios can be generated from your playbooks so practice stays native to how you sell.

Managers see readiness by rep and cohort, not just completion. That matters if your goal is retention of skill, not attendance. Product detail lives on kulissa.com/product. If ramp and onboarding are the pain, start with kulissa.com/use-cases/sales-onboarding.

Maya on kulissa.com/maya is the public gatekeeper demo: convince her your team deserves access, and you can win promotional credits for a workspace. It is a rehearsal of the product idea itself.

The uncomfortable conclusion

If 87% of unused training fades within a month, the expensive part of enablement is not the facilitator. It is the false confidence. Teams that treat practice as a first-class operating system reduce that waste. Teams that keep buying more slides keep buying forgetting.

The stage does not care how many workshops you attended. It cares whether the line lands when someone talks over you.

What enablement leaders should stop funding

Before you renew another content library, ask whether last year's modules produced measurable retrieval. If the only dashboard is completion percentage, you are funding forgetting with better production value.

Stop funding:

  • One-time certifications with no rematch window
  • Manager "coaching" that is really forecast interrogation
  • Competitive battle cards that are never practiced aloud
  • Kickoff theatre that crowds out the first two weeks of spaced practice

Start funding:

  • Scenario libraries tied to loss reasons
  • Manager calibration time on shared scorecards
  • Protected practice blocks on the AE calendar
  • Rematch capacity when someone fails a gate

This is capital allocation, not pedagogy fashion. The forgetting curve does not care about your brand fonts.

A worked example: discovery that does not stick

Imagine a two-day onboarding that covers discovery thoroughly. Reps can recite the question list. On day ten, a buyer asks for pricing in minute two. Most reps pitch. The discovery list was never retrieved under interruption, so it never became available.

Now change the design. After the workshop, every rep runs three scenarios: friendly discovery, price-interrupt discovery, and dual-stakeholder discovery. Failures rematch within forty-eight hours. Managers quote transcript lines in 1:1s. By day fourteen, the question list is no longer a list. It is a reflex with judgment.

Same content hours. Different retention. The difference is deliberate retrieval, which is also why deliberate practice for sales teams belongs next to this article on your enablement reading list.

Measuring retention without fake precision

You do not need a neuroscience lab. You need three operational signals:

  1. Scenario rematch rate falling over a cohort's first month
  2. Dimension stability when the same skill is tested ten days later with a new persona
  3. Live transfer on conversation intelligence reviews using the same rubric language

If signal one improves while signal three stays flat, your scenarios are too polite. If signal two collapses, you never had learning; you had short-term performance. If all three move, congratulations: you built a practice system instead of a content museum.

Sources
  • ATD, State of Sales Training 2023 (citing Gartner on training forgetting rates and first-year formal training days)
  • The Bridge Group, AE Models, Motions and Metrics 2026 (AE ramp and quota attainment)
  • Ericsson, K. Anders et al., research on deliberate practice and expert performance
  • Ebbinghaus, Hermann, work on the forgetting curve (classic memory research)
FAQ Why do sales reps forget training so quickly?

Because unused memory decays fast, and most programs deliver dense input without scheduled retrieval under pressure. ATD citing Gartner puts forgetting near 70% within a week and 87% within a month unless the material is used. Classroom coverage without live practice accelerates that curve.

How many practice sessions does it take for a skill to stick?

There is no universal magic number, but spaced practice with feedback beats one marathon. A workable pattern is three to five short scenarios across two weeks for a single skill, each scored against a shared rubric, with difficulty rising as the rep clears the bar.

Does conversation intelligence replace practice?

No. Conversation intelligence coaches real calls after they happen. Deliberate practice needs volume, controlled difficulty, and immediate feedback. Recordings and role-play work best together: drills for building skill, film for transferring it to live deals.

What should managers measure instead of training completion?

Measure demonstrated readiness: rubric scores on live practice, weak dimensions by cohort, and rematch rates after a failed scenario. Completion proves attendance. Scored rehearsal proves whether the skill is available on stage.

items.title: Anthropic's internal AI use, valued at retail prices, now exceeds its employee pay
items.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images A version of this story originally appeared in the AI Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly AI Insider newsletter here . Here's a remarkable milestone in the AI revolution: Anthropic now spends more on internal AI usage than it does paying employees. The company revealed this in its IPO filing . In April, the value of Claude AI used internally, calculated at prices Anthropic charges customers, exceeded its monthly employee compensation costs, excluding stock awards. By September, that internal AI usage had surged more than 250-fold since January. There's an important distinction here. Anthropic isn't actually spending more cash on AI than salaries. It's valuing its internal AI consumption at retail prices. Still, this feels like a watershed moment for the tech industry. In March, I wrote about a new trend : Tech companies are starting to treat AI tokens (the main way to measure usage) as a fourth component of employee compensation, alongside salary, bonuses, and stock awards. Anthropic's numbers show why. More than 90% of the code added to its software in September was written by Claude. Meanwhile, revenue has grown vastly faster than headcount. For decades, talented humans were the most valuable resource in Silicon Valley. Now AI is challenging that assumption. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: A step-by-step guide for how to kill the line-by-line code review
items.summary: Agents verify; people decide. Most teams running AI code review today have it the other way around. They point a model at the diff, ask it whether the change is good, and leave a human to skim the result and click approve. The model reads every line, never gets tired, and holds the same standard on every PR. What it doesn’t have is your codebase’s standards. It doesn’t know them, and no matter how well you instruct it, it doesn’t always follow the ones you write down. “Judgment needs intent, and accountability needs a person.” It never saw what was decided, has no context for previous decisions, can’t tell you not to build the thing, and can’t be held accountable. A diff can’t give it any of that. Judgment needs intent, and accountability needs a person. So what does a code review look like when verification goes to agents and judgment stays with people? At Aviator, we’ve been building that review into Aviator Verify . Below are its seven parts, in order. The anatomy of an intent-driven review Click to enlarge image. Every change gets checked against two layers . Acceptance criteria describe what this change should do. Invariants are the codified rules of your engineering org or team: the standards that are always true, whatever the change. Criteria without invariants leave your standards to memory. Every engineer has to remember every standard, or someone has to catch the obvious agent mistakes in code review. Invariants without criteria give you code that follows the rules but doesn’t consider what the result should be, so the agent strays, overengineers, or solves the wrong problem. The seven parts build both layers, verify the change against them, and hand the decision to a person: Invariants (defined before any change): the team’s standing rules, drawn from its own code reviews. Intent and acceptance criteria (captured from the coding session): why the change exists and how it should behave. Core decisions (captured from the coding session): the choices made along the way, and who made them. A test plan (built at submit): the criteria plus the invariants that apply, turned into scenarios. Evidence (gathered at submit): proof from a running environment behind every verdict. A review (decided by a person): intent, decisions, and evidence, approved or pushed back on. Not code. Invariants refreshed (updated after merge): waivers and recurring comments that sharpen the invariants. 1. Invariants Every review checks a change against something. In most teams, that something lives in senior engineers’ heads and comes out as review comments. Use the Money type for anything with a currency. No direct writes to the users table. Every error path emits a counter. Each of those has been typed more than once, and coding agents keep making the same mistakes because the rule was never written down anywhere an agent or a verifier could use it. An invariant is that rule, written once and checked on every matching change. Together, your invariants become an AI slop registry , the running list of patterns your team keeps correcting. Agent instruction files like CLAUDE.md help, but they’re an input to generation. The same non-deterministic agent that wrote the code is asked to follow them, and nothing proves it did. Invariants sit on the verification side, checked by a deterministic script or at least a different agent that returns a verdict for each rule. Your PR history already holds most of them. Verify reads the comments your team posts in GitHub and drafts invariants from the patterns it finds. It also drafts them from CONTRIBUTING.md and agent instruction files or on the spot when someone tags @aviator invariant in a PR comment or a Slack thread. Generate your team’s invariants with the Aviator Verify free account and keep them even if you decide not to continue with Verify. Three things determine whether an invariant helps or becomes noise. Ownership. Every draft goes to the team it belongs to, with the reason it was proposed, and goes live only once that team approves it. Nothing AI-drafted becomes a standing check without a human saying yes. Wording. Assert the outcome and leave the implementation open, so the rule survives renames and file moves. Scope. A rule should only run where it can break. A frontend invariant has no business checking database migrations. 2. Intent and acceptance criteria The obvious way to give a reviewer intent is to write a spec up front or capture as a detailed JIRA ticket. Specs take time, get written before the work teaches anyone anything, and drift the moment implementation starts. The most accurate intent already exists in the coding session. Every time the agent stops to ask a question and the engineer makes a call, acceptance criteria get defined in real time. There is no reason to throw all of that away when the session ends! The intent says why the change was made. The acceptance criteria say how it should behave. Verify captures both from the session the engineer already had. An agent skill and a hook run verify submit before the agent opens a pull request. The agent extracts the intent and the criteria from everything it saw in the session, and the engineer reviews and corrects them before anything is submitted. Click to enlarge image. 3. Core decisions A decision is any point where the change could have gone another way. Where state lives, what happens when a dependency fails, whether to reuse an existing helper or write a new one. An AI-written PR is full of calls like these, and almost none of them show up in the diff. “An AI-written PR is full of calls like these, and almost none of them show up in the diff.” Verify records the decisions next to the intent, with humans and agents labeled separately, so the reviewer knows who made which call and can argue with it. I wrote more about why decisions are the thing people should review in How to review AI code without reading the code . 4. A test plan When a change is submitted, Verify reads the intent and the criteria and uses the diff to identify the invariants to apply. Both layers merge into one list of scenarios: the steps an agent takes to validate behavior, derived from the requirements rather than the code. That’s where the two layers pay off. The engineer stays focused on the change, and the registry covers the standards. 5. Evidence When the same model writes and reviews the code, they share the same blind spots. Verification must be structurally separate from generation, and it must produce more than an opinion. “When the same model writes and reviews the code, they share the same blind spots.” Verify spins up a preview environment and dispatches verifier agents to run the scenarios. They capture screenshots, database state, server logs, and console logs, and every verdict, for a criterion or an invariant, points at that evidence. For a UI change, the verifier actually clicks through the interface and confirms the result. You don’t need a preview on day one. Code scans handle structural checks straight from the diff, with no infrastructure, and many invariants are converted to deterministic scripts. A preview earns its place once your criteria start asking about behavior the diff can’t show. 6. A review This is where people come back in, and the work looks different. As a reviewer, you’re looking at evidence rather than reading code line by line. You read the intent, look at the hot spots where the core changes are, go through the decisions and the verdict on each criterion and invariant, and open the live preview if you want to see the change for yourself. Click to enlarge image. The pull request workflow barely changes. Verify adds a link to the review, the diff stays where it was, and the results are reported as a status check similar to the CI behavior. The reviewer answers one question: does the evidence match what the team agreed to build? They approve, push back on a decision, ask for another scenario, or waive a failed invariant with a reason. That’s judgment, and someone owns it. 7. Invariants refreshed Most reviews end at merge, and everything they learned leaves with them. The next PR makes the same mistake, and the same comment shows up again. Invariants keep what each review learned. When an invariant fails on a PR, the author can waive it with a reason: maybe it doesn’t apply, maybe the invariant is incorrect, or maybe it gets fixed separately. The team that owns the Invariants sees every waiver. Click to enlarge image. Insights show which invariants apply most, how often each one fails, and why people waive them. An invariant that keeps getting waived is wrong, so the team rewrites or narrows it. A comment reviewers keep typing becomes the next draft. That way invariants become a set of rules that are continuously maintained over time and guard every code change. Where to start Don’t switch it all on at once. Start with the invariants, because they’re the cheapest part and your PR history already holds them. Month one will feel like double work, with the team still reviewing code while the registry fills up. In month two, invariants catch enough that reviews shrink. By month three, reviewers read intent, decisions, and evidence, and open the diff only when something doesn’t add up. The review your team already does is full of rules waiting to be written down. Aviator Verify turns them into invariants, verifies every change against them, and leaves the decisions to people. items.summary: Adobe Research and UC San Diego built EditAgent, an AI system that edits images more like a Photoshop pro. items.title: Trump Living in Alternate World of AI Slop, Insiders Say
items.summary: President Donald Trump’s obsession with AI is even grimmer than we believed. The commander-in-chief has hardly hidden his enchantment with AI slop, regularly posting bizarre AI videos glorifying himself, denigrating his foes, and at times, attempting to rewrite reality . But a behind-the-scenes look suggests that Trump is now completely lost in an AI alternate reality of his own making. While Republicans scramble and prepare for what could be a disastrous midterm election season for their party, sources told the New York Times that Trump is cloistering himself in a world made of sycophantic press coverage, disparaging clips about his foes, and, not least of all, “AI slop,” in the words of one White House official. One person keeping him hooked on the stuff is Bill Pulte, a top federal housing official. According to the reporting, Pulte regularly joins Trump in his cabin on Air Force One and shows him memes — some of which are almost certainly AI-generated — posters, and documents related to the mortgage industry. One administration official even described Pulte as a “court jester.” Trump is now so isolated from critical coverage that his indignation and incredulity when encountering it can be petulant and extreme. When comedian Bill Maher — who you wouldn’t describe as particularly left wing — joked about Trump’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein and his affinity for Russia, Trump’s response was absurdly disproportionate: a maniacal 1,300 word rant raging against Maher that he posted on his website Truth Social, which breaking news accounts on social media struggled to capture in one screenshot . The signs of his AI infirmity have long been apparent. But some worry that AI is playing a direct role in the president’s decision-making, too. President Donald Trump’s obsession with AI is even grimmer than we believed.

The commander-in-chief has hardly hidden his enchantment with AI slop, regularly posting bizarre AI videos glorifying himself, denigrating his foes, and at times, attempting to rewrite reality. 

But a behind-the-scenes look suggests that Trump is now completely lost in an AI alternate reality of his own making.

While Republicans scramble and prepare for what could be a disastrous midterm election season for their party, sources told the New York Times that Trump is cloistering himself in a world made of sycophantic press coverage, disparaging clips about his foes, and, not least of all, “AI slop,” in the words of one White House official.

One person keeping him hooked on the stuff is Bill Pulte, a top federal housing official. According to the reporting, Pulte regularly joins Trump in his cabin on Air Force One and shows him memes — some of which are almost certainly AI-generated — posters, and documents related to the mortgage industry. One administration official even described Pulte as a “court jester.”

Trump is now so isolated from critical coverage that his indignation and incredulity when encountering it can be petulant and extreme. When comedian Bill Maher — who you wouldn’t describe as particularly left wing — joked about Trump’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein and his affinity for Russia, Trump’s response was absurdly disproportionate: a maniacal 1,300 word rant raging against Maher that he posted on his website Truth Social, which breaking news accounts on social media struggled to capture in one screenshot.

Top Democrats are now demanding to see those Grok conversations and others.

items.title: Guarding the Gates of Knowledge
items.summary: A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion. Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must. Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “ I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper ,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses. “He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.” Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it. Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions , Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools. “Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.” If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty . Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity. Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

items.title: Cisco Gives a Former Startup Founder an AI Budget With No Ceiling
items.summary: Cisco’s Unlimited-Token Refactor Shifts the Bottleneck From Writing Code to Proving It Cisco president Jeetu Patel has given one engineer unlimited AI tokens and 24 months to refactor 98% of the company’s legacy code. The cost ceiling that normally stops a project of this size is gone, which leaves a harder question: how Cisco will prove the refactored code still behaves like the original. A Four-Week Proof of Concept Comes First Patel described the plan to Fortune at a small roundtable dinner, and the outlet published the account on October 30, 2026. The engineer is Padmanabhan “Paddy” Krishnamurthy, 27, who cofounded the real-time translation startup EzDubs in 2023 and joined Cisco when it acquired the company in 2025. Patel told Fortune he found Krishnamurthy five levels below him in the organization, working on something Patel called unstrategic. Krishnamurthy told Patel he could rewrite Cisco’s legacy code with a team of two, and Patel said even the most AI-forward people on his own team were not thinking that way. A four-week proof of concept comes first, with the 98% target due within 24 months. On tokens, Patel’s instruction was to “go nuts.” Fortune’s report does not say which products or how many lines of code count as legacy, and it carries no results from the proof of concept. The coverage uses “refactor” and “rewrite” interchangeably, and they are not the same job. Refactoring restructures code while keeping its behavior identical; a rewrite can change what the software does. Patel’s own word was refactor, which sets the stricter standard: whatever the AI produces has to act exactly like what it replaced. Generation Gets Cheap, Verification Does Not Earlier large migrations show where the effort goes once generation costs little. Airbnb moved nearly 3,500 React test files from Enzyme to React Testing Library in about six weeks, against a manual estimate of 1.5 years. Its pipeline ran each file through automated Jest, lint and TypeScript checks and retried failures up to a set limit. A first bulk run reached 75% of files in four hours, and four days of prompt and script refinement lifted completion to 97%. Engineers fixed the remaining 100 or so files by hand, which took about another week. Google reported a similar pattern in a paper on its internal migrations. In an int32-to-int64 ID change across the Google Ads codebase, which spans more than 500 million lines, AI wrote 80% of the code modifications in landed changes, and engineers estimated a 50% cut in total time. The authors also reported that in most cases the engineer had to revert at least some of the model’s changes, and they named the speed of human review as the bottleneck. GitHub’s numbers show where that load lands. The platform recorded 7.38 billion commits in September 2026, more than five times the figure a year earlier, and GitHub Actions, its workflow automation service, ran 3.26 billion times, more than four times as often as a year before. The implication is that every company letting agents write code at that pace inherits the same multiplier on its own build and test systems. Cisco Has Already Named the Standard In an interview with SDxCentral, Patel said organizations should prepare for a world in which humans cannot review all the code AI writes, and that teams must “automate the test beds and harnesses” that measure outputs. He added that whoever evaluates those outputs should answer for the code, and that every piece of it should trace back to a human. In the same interview he said Cisco’s AI Defense product was built entirely with AI, and he set targets of about half a dozen fully AI-written products by the end of 2026 and roughly 70% of the portfolio by the end of 2027. Those are targets, not results. One way to read the legacy refactor is as the older-code counterpart to that strategy, facing the same test. The implication is that Cisco’s test coverage, more than its token spend, will decide whether the 98% figure holds. Fortune’s report does not say how Cisco will measure it, and the four-week proof of concept is the first chance to show a method exists. What to Have in Place Before You Try This Fortune’s report does not describe Cisco’s method, so what follows is advice drawn from the Airbnb and Google cases and from Patel’s stated standard, not a description of what Cisco does. If you plan a large AI-driven refactor, settle three things before you spend the first token. Test coverage that can fail the code. Airbnb’s pipeline worked because every migrated file faced an automatic judge: it passed the Jest, lint and TypeScript checks or it went back for another attempt. Production code needs the same kind of referee. Map which of the modules you plan to change have tests that would catch a behavior change, and write tests that record what the code does today for the ones that do not. Do that before the model touches them, because a test written against the model’s output can only confirm what the model already did. A named owner for every change. Patel’s stated standard is that whoever evaluates AI output should answer for the code, and that every piece of it should trace to a human. Google’s paper found that engineers reverted at least some of the model’s changes in most cases, so someone has to read each diff and sign for it. Assign owners by module before the run starts. Then budget their review hours as a line item, since Google named the speed of human review as the bottleneck. A pass-rate threshold fixed in advance. Decide before the first run what share of changes must pass your checks unchanged for the project to continue, and what happens to the rest. Airbnb’s first bulk run cleared 75% of files in four hours, four days of tuning lifted completion to 97%, and the final 100 or so files took about another week by hand. The long tail is where the schedule goes, so staff for it. The right number depends on what a failure costs in that system: a test-file migration can tolerate more misses than a payments service. Cisco’s four-week proof of concept is where these three items will show up first. If Cisco discloses how much of the refactored code passed its existing tests unchanged and how many reviewer hours the rest consumed, the industry gets rare evidence from a company that builds networking infrastructure. Without those numbers, the 98% target stays an ambition with an open-ended token allowance behind it.

items.title: A 'humbling' career move led to Catherine Zeta-Jones' big break
items.summary: Catherine Zeta-Jones currently stars in "Killing Jackie." Getty; TriStar Pictures; USA Films; BI Catherine Zeta-Jones' arrival in Hollywood in the mid-1990s was an ego check. The Welsh actor, then in her 20s, had starred for years on the popular early-'90s British series "The Darling Buds of May," and was already a sensation in the UK. But when she touched down in California, she went from being recognized on the street to having casting agents ask her in auditions if she had any acting experience. That wasn't all. "I couldn't get cable TV," Zeta-Jones told Business Insider with a laugh. "I had been working since I was 9, but I couldn't buy anything in the States because I didn't have a credit card yet. I had to start from scratch." Starting over turned out to be worth it for Zeta-Jones. After taking a role in the CBS miniseries "Titanic," she caught the attention of Steven Spielberg , who recommended her for "The Mask of Zorro." The role would make her a star Stateside and lead to an illustrious three-decade career in Hollywood. Business Insider's " Role Play " series features interviews where acting legends revisit their most memorable roles. See more here . Zeta-Jones is now known on both sides of the pond for memorable roles ranging from the pregnant wife of a Mexican drug lord in "Traffic" to her Oscar-winning turn as the iconic Velma Kelly in "Chicago" to Morticia Addams in Netflix's " Wednesday. " But despite her long list of credits, there's one thing she still hadn't done for a role until now: use her native Welsh accent. Catherine Zeta-Jones in "Killing Jackie." AMC+ Her latest project, the AMC+ series "Killing Jackie," marks Zeta-Jones' long-awaited return to her Welsh roots. After decades of having her brain work overtime doing English, American, and Scottish accents — and many more — the opportunity to speak in her native accent was grounding. "It was liberating and cathartic," Zeta-Jones said. So, too, was the subject matter. Based on the 2018 novel "The Price You Pay" by Nick Harkaway (using the pseudonym Aidan Truhen), the revenge thriller stars Zeta-Jones as the titular Jackie Price, a Welsh high-end art dealer with a shady past in the drug trade who discovers a hit has been put out on her. With a deadly team of assassins known as The Seven Demons on her tail, Jackie goes to great lengths to stay alive — at one point even biting off a man's ear. Navigating the series' ultra-violent scenes was a blast for Zeta-Jones, who relished the chance to go off the rails. "I love this character," Zeta-Jones said. "I wanted the audience to come along on this ride with me and root for her. In all the craziness." In the latest edition of Business Insider's Role Play series , Zeta-Jones reflects on her instant bond with Sean Connery, helping her husband Michael Douglas get a part in "Traffic," and the leading man she was most intimidated to work across from. Zeta-Jones in 1997. Frank Trapper/Corbis/Getty Images On being discovered by Steven Spielberg and golfing with Sean Connery Business Insider: Let's go back to your 20s. You're in London, where you can't walk down the street without paparazzi all over you thanks to "The Darling Buds of May." Then you go to LA, where nobody knows you. What was that like? Catherine Zeta-Jones: I had six months on a visa, so I could go and give the States a shot for six months. I would have hated myself if I decided the American thing wasn't for me. I would have always thought, What if I had given it a shot ? It was good for me once I got over my ego being knocked a bit. I'd been in this business since I was 9 years old, professionally in theater and in television, and a few films in Britain at that point. But I'd go into casting agents, and they'd be asking me what I had done. I took a job that was not a huge career leap for me — the CBS show, "Titanic," the TV series after the blockbuster movie came out. I kept reminding myself that I came to give America a shot. Steven Spielberg, on a Sunday night, was watching this CBS "Titanic" series when he saw me. As the producer of "The Mask of Zorro," he suggested that I screen test. Literally, within a week of it coming on TV, I was shipped down to Mexico to screen test with Antonio Banderas. Five days later, they called my agent and said I got the job, and three days after that, I was down there starting my sword-fighting lessons. After that, you worked across from Sean Connery in "Entrapment," which cemented your stardom. Is it true you got that role because you told Connery you play golf? [ Laughs .] He used to say that tongue-in-cheek. You know, Sean Connery was a dear, dear force of nature. Would you guys play golf? Yeah. Did you ever beat him? No. And even if I could, I would never tell. I beat Michael Douglas. Any day of the week. But not Sean Connery. You can't beat 007. No way. Even if he cheated, I would just turn my head. Zeta-Jones and Michael Douglas in 1999. Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection/Getty Images On working with her husband on 'Traffic' and tap dancing with Christopher Walken Speaking of your husband, is it true that Michael finally signed on to "Traffic" because he kept looking over your shoulder, looking at the drafts you were getting for the role you took in that movie? There is a lot of truth in that. I was pregnant, and no one knew. And Steven Soderbergh asked me to do "Traffic." And I kept saying, "Oh my gosh, there's no way I can do this. Steven Soderbergh wants me in his movie, and I'm having a baby!" I was happy to be having a baby, but I so wanted to do this movie. So I called Steven and said, "I love the script, um, I think she would be even better if she was pregnant." And he said, "When are you due?" I went, "August," and he said, "We'll make it work." Michael never reads my scripts. I never read Michael's scripts. It's the one thing we kind of do on our own; we don't really talk shop at home. We just don't. But he knew how great that script was, and so Soderbergh called him and asked him if he had a chance to read my script. [ Laughs .] And he said, "Kinda, but she's been telling me." So that's when he came on board. What I loved about that movie was not just the stellar performances, but I love that I can say I've been in a movie with Michael Douglas. Because if he wasn't my husband, I so would want to work with him. So even though we didn't have any scenes together, it was phenomenal. You starred in the rom-com "America's Sweethearts." The movie ends with Christopher Walken showing up to the junket to show footage of the movie he made with your character. It turns out to be all behind-the-scenes footage of the movie, which seems to be a musical, and we see you tap dancing with Walken. Is it true that subplot is in "America's Sweethearts" because you specifically wanted to tap dance with Christopher Walken? Absolutely. I wanted to tap dance with Christopher Walken! I'm a big tap dancer. There are not many actors of my generation or Michael's generation, yes, [Michael Douglas' father] Kirk's generation, that can tap dance. So when I had the chance to do that, I was like, "Guys, we can't miss this chance." It was totally, selfishly, for myself. Zeta-Jones and Tom Hanks in "The Terminal." DreamWorks We touched on a few leading men you have worked with over your career. Looking back, is there one who made you stay on your game the most? Someone who you knew you had to bring your A-game to every time you walked on set? I have to say Sean, but it wasn't that I had to be on my A-game. I just never wanted to stop acting with him, because we were such good buddies. He was so incredibly protective of me, like a daughter he never had, and he said that to me. And I loved his wife. I can't really say family, because he's not family, but I never wanted to act with anyone else after Sean Connery. I just didn't. It was fun. But I will say when I did "The Terminal" with Steven Spielberg at the helm and working so closely with Tom Hanks, I did go to work on the first day and go, "Mommy, I want to go home and cuddle." items.summary_html:
Catherine Zeta-Jones currently stars in "Killing Jackie."

Getty; TriStar Pictures; USA Films; BI

Catherine Zeta-Jones' arrival in Hollywood in the mid-1990s was an ego check.

The Welsh actor, then in her 20s, had starred for years on the popular early-'90s British series "The Darling Buds of May," and was already a sensation in the UK. But when she touched down in California, she went from being recognized on the street to having casting agents ask her in auditions if she had any acting experience.

That wasn't all.

"I couldn't get cable TV," Zeta-Jones told Business Insider with a laugh. "I had been working since I was 9, but I couldn't buy anything in the States because I didn't have a credit card yet. I had to start from scratch."

Starting over turned out to be worth it for Zeta-Jones. After taking a role in the CBS miniseries "Titanic," she caught the attention of Steven Spielberg, who recommended her for "The Mask of Zorro." The role would make her a star Stateside and lead to an illustrious three-decade career in Hollywood.

Business Insider's "Role Play" series features interviews where acting legends revisit their most memorable roles. See more here.

Zeta-Jones is now known on both sides of the pond for memorable roles ranging from the pregnant wife of a Mexican drug lord in "Traffic" to her Oscar-winning turn as the iconic Velma Kelly in "Chicago" to Morticia Addams in Netflix's "Wednesday."

But despite her long list of credits, there's one thing she still hadn't done for a role until now: use her native Welsh accent.

Catherine Zeta-Jones in "Killing Jackie."

AMC+

Her latest project, the AMC+ series "Killing Jackie," marks Zeta-Jones' long-awaited return to her Welsh roots. After decades of having her brain work overtime doing English, American, and Scottish accents — and many more — the opportunity to speak in her native accent was grounding. "It was liberating and cathartic," Zeta-Jones said.

So, too, was the subject matter. Based on the 2018 novel "The Price You Pay" by Nick Harkaway (using the pseudonym Aidan Truhen), the revenge thriller stars Zeta-Jones as the titular Jackie Price, a Welsh high-end art dealer with a shady past in the drug trade who discovers a hit has been put out on her. With a deadly team of assassins known as The Seven Demons on her tail, Jackie goes to great lengths to stay alive — at one point even biting off a man's ear.

Navigating the series' ultra-violent scenes was a blast for Zeta-Jones, who relished the chance to go off the rails.

"I love this character," Zeta-Jones said. "I wanted the audience to come along on this ride with me and root for her. In all the craziness."

In the latest edition of Business Insider's Role Play series, Zeta-Jones reflects on her instant bond with Sean Connery, helping her husband Michael Douglas get a part in "Traffic," and the leading man she was most intimidated to work across from.

Zeta-Jones in 1997.

Frank Trapper/Corbis/Getty Images

On being discovered by Steven Spielberg and golfing with Sean Connery

Business Insider: Let's go back to your 20s. You're in London, where you can't walk down the street without paparazzi all over you thanks to "The Darling Buds of May." Then you go to LA, where nobody knows you. What was that like?

Catherine Zeta-Jones: I had six months on a visa, so I could go and give the States a shot for six months. I would have hated myself if I decided the American thing wasn't for me. I would have always thought, What if I had given it a shot?

It was good for me once I got over my ego being knocked a bit. I'd been in this business since I was 9 years old, professionally in theater and in television, and a few films in Britain at that point. But I'd go into casting agents, and they'd be asking me what I had done.

I took a job that was not a huge career leap for me — the CBS show, "Titanic," the TV series after the blockbuster movie came out. I kept reminding myself that I came to give America a shot.

Steven Spielberg, on a Sunday night, was watching this CBS "Titanic" series when he saw me. As the producer of "The Mask of Zorro," he suggested that I screen test. Literally, within a week of it coming on TV, I was shipped down to Mexico to screen test with Antonio Banderas. Five days later, they called my agent and said I got the job, and three days after that, I was down there starting my sword-fighting lessons. 

After that, you worked across from Sean Connery in "Entrapment," which cemented your stardom. Is it true you got that role because you told Connery you play golf?

[Laughs.] He used to say that tongue-in-cheek. You know, Sean Connery was a dear, dear force of nature. 

Would you guys play golf?

Yeah. 

Did you ever beat him?

No. And even if I could, I would never tell. I beat Michael Douglas. Any day of the week. But not Sean Connery.

You can't beat 007. 

No way. Even if he cheated, I would just turn my head. 

Zeta-Jones and Michael Douglas in 1999.

Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection/Getty Images

On working with her husband on 'Traffic' and tap dancing with Christopher Walken

Speaking of your husband, is it true that Michael finally signed on to "Traffic" because he kept looking over your shoulder, looking at the drafts you were getting for the role you took in that movie?

There is a lot of truth in that. I was pregnant, and no one knew. And Steven Soderbergh asked me to do "Traffic." And I kept saying, "Oh my gosh, there's no way I can do this. Steven Soderbergh wants me in his movie, and I'm having a baby!" I was happy to be having a baby, but I so wanted to do this movie. So I called Steven and said, "I love the script, um, I think she would be even better if she was pregnant." And he said, "When are you due?" I went, "August," and he said, "We'll make it work." 

Michael never reads my scripts. I never read Michael's scripts. It's the one thing we kind of do on our own; we don't really talk shop at home. We just don't. But he knew how great that script was, and so Soderbergh called him and asked him if he had a chance to read my script. [Laughs.] And he said, "Kinda, but she's been telling me." So that's when he came on board. 

What I loved about that movie was not just the stellar performances, but I love that I can say I've been in a movie with Michael Douglas. Because if he wasn't my husband, I so would want to work with him. So even though we didn't have any scenes together, it was phenomenal. 

You starred in the rom-com "America's Sweethearts." The movie ends with Christopher Walken showing up to the junket to show footage of the movie he made with your character. It turns out to be all behind-the-scenes footage of the movie, which seems to be a musical, and we see you tap dancing with Walken. Is it true that subplot is in "America's Sweethearts" because you specifically wanted to tap dance with Christopher Walken?

Absolutely. I wanted to tap dance with Christopher Walken! I'm a big tap dancer. There are not many actors of my generation or Michael's generation, yes, [Michael Douglas' father] Kirk's generation, that can tap dance. So when I had the chance to do that, I was like, "Guys, we can't miss this chance." It was totally, selfishly, for myself. 

Zeta-Jones and Tom Hanks in "The Terminal."

DreamWorks

We touched on a few leading men you have worked with over your career. Looking back, is there one who made you stay on your game the most? Someone who you knew you had to bring your A-game to every time you walked on set?

I have to say Sean, but it wasn't that I had to be on my A-game. I just never wanted to stop acting with him, because we were such good buddies. He was so incredibly protective of me, like a daughter he never had, and he said that to me. And I loved his wife. I can't really say family, because he's not family, but I never wanted to act with anyone else after Sean Connery. I just didn't. It was fun. 

But I will say when I did "The Terminal" with Steven Spielberg at the helm and working so closely with Tom Hanks, I did go to work on the first day and go, "Mommy, I want to go home and cuddle." I got a little intimidated. Then — and I say this all the time — I learned the better they are, the nicer they are.

Now I've worked for so long, I've worked with some actors and gone, "Ugh, you just burst my bubble; I so wanted to work with you." Very rarely, but it has happened.

But working with all those guys on the "Oceans" movies: Matt [Damon], Brad [Pitt], George [Clooney]… I did a movie with George with the Coen brothers, and that was exceptional. So it's not so much bringing your A-game, because I want to do that with everyone I work across from.

Even on the movies where you realize, I don't think this is going to work, how do you get through it and feel positive and 100% committed? It's usually that the actors you're working with are so amazing. 

This interview has been condensed and edited for length and clarity.

New episodes of "Kill Jackie" drop Fridays on AMC+.

items.title: Innocent People Are Being Accused of Shoplifting by Faulty AI-Facial Recognition Systems at an Alarming Rate
items.summary: From New York City to the streets of Tokyo , creepy AI-facial recognition security systems are quickly becoming a common sight across the world. Unfortunately for many, the tech is nowhere near ready for the responsibility of live use as the troubling rise of false-positive matches makes clear. In the United Kingdom, AI surveillance systems in retail stores have led to a surge in customers being wrongly accused of shoplifting. TechRadar highlighted a number of recent cases throughout the country, where shoppers say false accusations have left them shaken, with a feeling that their privacy had been horribly violated. As one woman identified as Mary told the publication, her husband has been socially “isolated” after a quick jaunt into a Home Bargains store for vitamins went awry. When the stores’ system flagged the anonymous man as a shoplifter, the couple was forced to leave by management, seemingly without any chance to refute the accusation. “I was scared to go into a shop,” the man told TechRadar . Another man was said to be “shaking from head to toe” following his wife’s removal from a Budgens chain store for the crime of stealing “loads of meat” days before — an accusation complicated by the fact that they hadn’t set foot in the store for months. In these and other cases, the publication reports a dizzying labyrinth of corporate bureaucracy and vague insinuations that leave innocent people unable to access their local businesses, and with little recourse to clear their name. In the UK, individuals can file Subject Access Requests, or SARs, which are like US-Freedom of Information Act requests but for private companies. Though the avenue technically exists for those wrongly accused of shoplifting, it’s a massive undertaking just for the hope of clearing your name — and requires handing over even more private information to private companies. As head of advocacy at civil liberty group Big Brother Watch Jack Coulson told TechRadar , it’s “the stuff of Kafkaesque nightmares to be trapped in a maze of bureaucracy and forced to hand over even more personal data just to be told the accusation.” More on facial recognition: Innocent Man Freed After Spending Over 50 Days in Jail Due to Horribly Inaccurate AI Facial Recognition Tech

items.summary_html:

Learn the R skills needed to analyse data confidently, build powerful statistical models, create publication-quality figures, and answer complex research questions with the Centre for Biodiversity and Conservation Science (CBCS) 2027 Summer R Workshops @ UQ.

These hands-on workshops are designed for both beginners and researchers looking to strengthen their analytical skills. You’ll learn how to wrangle data efficiently, develop reproducible workflows, apply appropriate statistical methods, and avoid common analytical pitfalls. By the end of the workshop, you’ll have practical skills that can be immediately applied to your own research projects. Although most of our example datasets are ecological in nature, the approaches and skills are equally applicable in many other research contexts.

Why learn to code in the age of AI?

AI can generate code in seconds, but it cannot tell you whether the analysis is appropriate, the assumptions are valid, or the conclusions are scientifically defensible. Learning the fundamentals of R gives you the skills to critically evaluate code and identify errors, ensuring you remain the expert in the AI loop.

Each day is self-contained so you can attend the workshops you want to.

  • Day 1 (Monday 8th February) Introduction to R and data wrangling in the tidyverse
  • Day 2 (Tuesday 9th February) Introduction to visualisation and linear modelling
  • Day 3 (Wednesday 10th February) Generalised linear modelling
  • Day 4 (Thursday 11th February) Mixed modelling
  • Day 5 (Friday 12th February) Spatial modelling with temporal and spatial autocorrelation

Registration for the 2027 Summer R Workshops @ UQ in February is OPEN.

We are passionate users of R and want to share our experience. Our workshops are accessible, interactive, informative and fun. They are run in-person only (no online option) to provide a tailored student experience and we provide all the code and learning materials. For more information on the topics covered and to view testimonials, see our website https://mathmarecol.github.io/RWorkshop/summer.html and the attached flyer.

These workshops are brought to you by the Centre for Biodiversity and Conservation Science (CBCS). For any questions about registration, email cbcs-workshops@uq.edu.au.

We look forward to seeing you there.

The R Workshops @ UQ team (Anthony, Dave, Jason, and Tin)

items.title: Fox News Takes Massive Ratings Hit As It Triples Down on Pro-Data Center Coverage
items.summary: It’s obvious by now that data centers are political kryptonite. Across the US, bipartisan backlash to data center projects has upended city councils , while billionaire developers and industry-aligned political candidates are being routed by grassroots opposition. But beyond those running for or occupying political office, the backlash is also taking a toll on news networks viewed as pushing pro-data center propaganda. Case-in-point is Fox News , which has tailed president Donald Trump in embracing the AI industry’s narrative on data centers — an editorial decision which happens to coincides with viewers fleeing the network in droves. According to a new analysis by Media Matters for America, coverage spinning data centers in a positive light shot up by a staggering 420 percent across Fox News over the past two months. On August 18, a memo issued by the National Republican Senatorial Committee went out to party insiders and top corporate executives, warning that opposition to data centers presented a major challenge to the party’s victory in the upcoming US midterm elections. As Media Matters notes, Fox News quickly fell in line, increasing the total number of pro-data center claims to 203 between August 19 and September 2, compared to just 39 from August 5 through August 18. Bizarre claims of “far-left activists” and Chinese government propaganda likewise proliferated, teeing up Republican faithfuls to blame a boogeyman for the rise in anti-data center rhetoric. Surprisingly, the tactic appears to have backfired, as even the network’s most devoted acolytes reacted with disgust. “Just in case there were any dummies who thought Fox News cares what voters want,” one disaffected viewer wrote in the YouTube comments under an extremely sunny Fox and Friends segment on data centers. “They’ll always protect corporate interests over conservative interests and (perhaps) even over protecting Trump in certain cases.” “For the first time I’m going to say, FOX is GREEDY,” another angry viewer commented. “For people who like to say they believe in God, [they] sure are failing on following his word.” Recent reporting by Status found that viewership of Fox News is in freefall following the shift — plummeting down 27 percent across the month of October to an average of 1.1 million total viewers. That data comes from media tracking company Nielsen, which also noted that viewership across the months of July, August, and September shriveled by 16 percent compared to the previous three months. Viewers in the 24 to 54 age range — a crucial demographic — tumbled 24 percent over the period. While there are likely a litany of other reasons for the shift, it’s nonetheless a striking correlation that coincides with a broader falling out with Trump as president. American voters overwhelmingly disprove of his handling of the economy, not to mention the extremely costly war on Iran. With a crucial midterm election coming up, it remains to be seen how the backlash against the right’s embrace of third rail issues like data centers will cost Republicans at the polls. More on media: You Know Those Three Brothers Who Buy Struggling News Sites and Turn Them Into AI-Powered Content Farms? It Turns Out One of Them Has Extensive Connections to Ghislaine Maxwell

items.title: Anthropic says helping others is core to its mission. 3 philanthropy gurus say they'll believe it when they see it.
items.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg/Getty Images Anthropic outlined several ways it plans to give back in its IPO filing this week. They include reserved shares, cofounder pledges, donation matching, and stock incentives. Philanthropy gurus said it's partly "reputation management," and how the money is used will be key. Anthropic's IPO filing this week contained myriad revelations about the state of the AI firm's finances, as well as an eye-opening series of claims about its commitment to helping others. We asked three experts in the world of philanthropy what they thought of these giving pledges. Their verdict: we'll see. A culture of giving? The company behind the AI chatbot Claude, which filed this week to go public in what could be the biggest IPO in history, laid out how it plans to give back and encourage its employees to do the same. Anthropic's seven cofounders said they've pledged 80% of their personal stock in the startup to charitable causes, gifts that could together be worth $80 billion. They also said they've earmarked 5% of Anthropic's equity for a "fund devoted to the public good," and plan to set aside another 2% for every sustained 50% rise in the company's stock price, with its IPO price as the base. Moreover, they said that new employees are offered a donation match, meaning that for every share they pledge to give away to good causes, Anthropic creates an additional share and matches the donation. Anthropic said that just over half of its employees have pledged at least some of their equity, including 70% of employees hired before May 2024, and nearly 50% of those hired after that date. The company noted that 25% of the former group, who were offered up to a 50% match, pledged the full amount. That figure was nearly 30% for the latter group, who were offered a 25% match. Anthropic also said it plans to issue Class E shares — which carry limited voting rights but have no economic value — to reward tenure and charity. Employees stand to receive one share for every six months they stay at the company, and one Class E share for every normal share they pledge to donate, Anthropic said. Anthropic didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. 'Judge us on this' Three philanthropy experts told Business Insider via email this week that Anthropic's giving plan is promising but represents only a first step. "It's admirable, and it's well-designed," said Dr. Vandana Arcot, the founder and CEO of Komselj, a philanthropic strategy firm. She noted that "building it into the compensation structure makes generosity the default, not the exception." Arcot said Anthropic's giving seemed to be grounded in an "ethic of accountability, not abundance." She pointed to CEO Dario Amodei's January essay in which he said that people who get rich from AI have a responsibility to address its economic fallout. Arcot also cited Anthropic's $200 million commitment this summer to fund research on preparing people for AI's economic impacts. She said that valuing generosity "tends to help companies attract mission-driven talent and keep it, which is a business case on top of the moral one." She added that "defining your giving in advance is a way of saying: judge us on this." But Arcot said her full evaluation of Anthropic's efforts will depend on "who sits on the decision-making body, how recipients are chosen, and what gets reported." Bella DeVaan, the director of the Charity Reform Initiative and deputy director of the Program on Inequality and the Common Good at the Institute for Policy Studies, said there's such "dire" wealth inequality in the US that "any efforts to center the public benefit are commendable." However, she said they're "no substitute for structural reform," and "giving to the public benefit shouldn't be voluntary, but should be guaranteed by our tax system." DeVaan also noted the charitable pledges by Anthropic's cofounders aren't legally binding and can be revoked. She said it was "concerning" to see that personal interest could trump public benefit, and added that it's "exactly why voluntary efforts alone won't be sufficient to rely on." Hans Peter Schmitz, a professor of nonprofit leadership at North Carolina State University, said he applauded Anthropic for promoting generosity from the top down, but it struck him as "part of an intentional effort in managing public opinion ." He said that any positive publicity around Anthropic's giving could help differentiate it from competitors and counter bad news about AI. The nascent technology has proven contentious due to concerns about job losses, environmental damage, cybersecurity threats, and even danger to humans. Schmitz said Anthropic appeared to be engaging in "reputational management," as "pledges are a relatively cheap 'signal' to be viewed in a positive light."
