Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.

Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg/Getty Images

  • Anthropic outlined several ways it plans to give back in its IPO filing this week.
  • They include reserved shares, cofounder pledges, donation matching, and stock incentives.
  • Philanthropy gurus said it's partly "reputation management," and how the money is used will be key.

Anthropic's IPO filing this week contained myriad revelations about the state of the AI firm's finances, as well as an eye-opening series of claims about its commitment to helping others.

We asked three experts in the world of philanthropy what they thought of these giving pledges. Their verdict: we'll see.

A culture of giving?

The company behind the AI chatbot Claude, which filed this week to go public in what could be the biggest IPO in history, laid out how it plans to give back and encourage its employees to do the same.

Anthropic's seven cofounders said they've pledged 80% of their personal stock in the startup to charitable causes, gifts that could together be worth $80 billion.

They also said they've earmarked 5% of Anthropic's equity for a "fund devoted to the public good," and plan to set aside another 2% for every sustained 50% rise in the company's stock price, with its IPO price as the base.

Moreover, they said that new employees are offered a donation match, meaning that for every share they pledge to give away to good causes, Anthropic creates an additional share and matches the donation.

Anthropic said that just over half of its employees have pledged at least some of their equity, including 70% of employees hired before May 2024, and nearly 50% of those hired after that date.

The company noted that 25% of the former group, who were offered up to a 50% match, pledged the full amount. That figure was nearly 30% for the latter group, who were offered a 25% match.

Anthropic also said it plans to issue Class E shares — which carry limited voting rights but have no economic value — to reward tenure and charity.

Employees stand to receive one share for every six months they stay at the company, and one Class E share for every normal share they pledge to donate, Anthropic said.

Anthropic didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

'Judge us on this'

Three philanthropy experts told Business Insider via email this week that Anthropic's giving plan is promising but represents only a first step.

"It's admirable, and it's well-designed," said Dr. Vandana Arcot, the founder and CEO of Komselj, a philanthropic strategy firm. She noted that "building it into the compensation structure makes generosity the default, not the exception."

Arcot said Anthropic's giving seemed to be grounded in an "ethic of accountability, not abundance."

She pointed to CEO Dario Amodei's January essay in which he said that people who get rich from AI have a responsibility to address its economic fallout.

Arcot also cited Anthropic's $200 million commitment this summer to fund research on preparing people for AI's economic impacts.

She said that valuing generosity "tends to help companies attract mission-driven talent and keep it, which is a business case on top of the moral one."

She added that "defining your giving in advance is a way of saying: judge us on this."

But Arcot said her full evaluation of Anthropic's efforts will depend on "who sits on the decision-making body, how recipients are chosen, and what gets reported."

Bella DeVaan, the director of the Charity Reform Initiative and deputy director of the Program on Inequality and the Common Good at the Institute for Policy Studies, said there's such "dire" wealth inequality in the US that "any efforts to center the public benefit are commendable."

However, she said they're "no substitute for structural reform," and "giving to the public benefit shouldn't be voluntary, but should be guaranteed by our tax system."

DeVaan also noted the charitable pledges by Anthropic's cofounders aren't legally binding and can be revoked. She said it was "concerning" to see that personal interest could trump public benefit, and added that it's "exactly why voluntary efforts alone won't be sufficient to rely on."

Hans Peter Schmitz, a professor of nonprofit leadership at North Carolina State University, said he applauded Anthropic for promoting generosity from the top down, but it struck him as "part of an intentional effort in managing public opinion."

He said that any positive publicity around Anthropic's giving could help differentiate it from competitors and counter bad news about AI. The nascent technology has proven contentious due to concerns about job losses, environmental damage, cybersecurity threats, and even danger to humans.

Schmitz said Anthropic appeared to be engaging in "reputational management," as "pledges are a relatively cheap 'signal' to be viewed in a positive light."

"Like many pledges in the past, there is also a high likelihood that it may never happen and/or a lot of the funding is channeled into a narrow set of issues, like AI safety," he said.

items.title: Canceled port calls and cash appeals: Inside the final months of the Villa Vie Odyssey's doomed round-the-world cruise
items.summary: The Villa Vie Odyssey was bogged down by financial trouble in its final months at sea. Suy SE/AFP/Getty Images Villa Vie Residences promised residents the world. The company's cruise ship, the Odyssey, kept circling one corner of it while finances worsened, services deteriorated, and cash calls mounted. "We were going in a smaller and smaller circle," said Claude Sadovsky, who joined the Odyssey when it first set sail from Belfast in September 2024. "I signed up for a world cruise, and I was in purgatory." By early October, Sadovsky was frustrated enough with the itinerary changes that he left the ship and returned to his home in Maui. For Starr Davis, who also joined in Belfast in 2024, it was the constant appeals for fuel money that got her to jump ship in late September. "I got so sick of all the cash calls," she said. For those aboard the Odyssey in its final months, the crisis grew so acute that some passengers began fundraising for crew members, residents told Business Insider. The financial distress culminated in the ship's abrupt halt in Cambodia on Tuesday, when passengers were given eight hours to pack up their belongings and leave. While the speed of the end came as a shock to some, residents said signs of trouble had been growing. "The ship was just a pressure cooker," Davis said. "You know, 'Are we going to exist?'" In an interview with Business Insider on Friday, Villa Vie Residences cofounder and executive chairman Mikael Petterson confirmed the company had made cost-cutting changes. "There were itinerary changes," he said. "Of course there were." He said the changes aboard the Odyssey — home to a "never-ending" cruise for permanent residents who bought cabins for $119,999 to $439,999 — were driven by rising fuel costs and logistical challenges. "When you're the first one doing something, of course you're going to make a ton of mistakes," he said. Petterson said roughly 88% of Villa Vie is owned by residents; the rest is owned by the founders, management team, and him. A drawback of that structure is that residents were the ones turned to when money got tight, he said: "When there's money needed, residents are naturally called upon because there's no private equity. There's no big owner." "When things didn't go as planned, it was a double whammy," he added. "That is what made Villa Vie Residences so strong, yet so weak." Villa Vie Residences CEO Kathy Villalba did not respond to multiple requests for comment from Business Insider. In a now-deleted apology to residents, Villalba said Villa Vie was still speaking to potential investors and "holding onto whatever hope remains." Columbia Cruise Services, Villa Vie's operational partner, did not reply to several requests for comment. The round-the-world route started shrinking Villa Vie had marketed the three-and-a-half-year voyage as a circumnavigation with more than 425 port calls across 147 countries. For the period between October 2024 and October 2026, its initial itinerary listed 275 ports in 69 countries and territories, or 54 sovereign nations. As fuel costs rose after the onset of the war with Iran and Villa Vie's financial pressures worsened, the company increasingly pared down its route: It canceled stops, slowed the ship at sea, extended stays in ports, and revisited destinations to conserve fuel and reduce operating costs. To see how plans changed, Business Insider compared itineraries the ship issued at four different times: its initial itinerary from October 2024; its November 2025 itinerary, which showed where it went in 2024 and 2025; one from January 2026 showing changes before the war; and an October 2026 itinerary showing this year's stops. We also reviewed messages Villalba and Petterson sent to ship residents at various points over the past three months. Villa Vie Odyssey passengers in Cambodia after the voyage abruptly ended. TANG CHHIN Sothy / AFP via Getty Images We found that while the ship visited 54 nations between October 2024 and October 2026, it missed some territories and called at only 198 ports — 28% fewer than originally planned. Across the two years, our comparison of the itineraries showed the ship spent nearly two fewer months at sea than initially scheduled. Petterson blamed the skyrocketing price of fuel : "We had no choice," he said. Business Insider's analysis shows the Odyssey also made itinerary changes before fuel prices rose , including in Australia and New Zealand. Residents said those appeared to be for reasons other than fuel costs. Planning around an ever-changing itinerary For some residents, the route changes turned an around-the-world voyage into one long bout of déjà vu. "We have revisited some of the same ports countless times in the last several months," Angela Nuran Gokturk, 65, said. Messages from Petterson and Villalba to residents demonstrated how fuel, financing, and operating costs directly shaped the ship's route. In a message to residents on the ship's internal messaging platform on August 1, Villalba said they would cancel a stop in Brunei and sail directly from Singapore to Nha Trang in southern Vietnam "to conserve fuel and reduce operating costs." On August 7, Petterson said in a memo that the ship had "aggressively reduced costs" and "redesigned itineraries to spend more time in port and consume less fuel." In a message on September 6, Villalba said the Odyssey would extend its stay in Ha Long, Vietnam, by one or two days, depending on "fuel availability and funding." What was meant to be a three-night stay became a 10-night layover, the revised itinerary shows. Residents said the route changes made it difficult to plan flights and excursions in advance. "People stopped trying to make plans because things could change literally within a few days," said Sally Stunkel, 75, who joined the ship in February. During the stay in Ha Long , Stunkel joined an eight-person excursion to China, but the group had already booked flights to one of the Vietnamese stops that was later cut from the itinerary. They had to buy new tickets to rejoin the ship at its revised next port. "We spent more money trying to chase the ship, basically, to the next port so we could then board again," she said. The Villa Vie Odyssey had frequent itinerary changes. Suy Se / AFP via Getty Images Singapore became a repeat stop: The ship stopped there three times between May and July, spending 16 days there in total, according to the October 20 itinerary. Stunkel said the one change that frustrated her most was the removal of Japan and South Korea from the itinerary. In March, the ship's public itinerary showed it was supposed to visit 19 ports in Japan and South Korea, between June 26 and August 19. In April, the itinerary was updated to instead show stops in Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, and Brunei during that period. Stunkel said she had bought a cabin on the cruise in part because it was scheduled to visit Japan over the summer. She said she was "extremely disappointed" by the change, adding, "Japan is my No. 1 bucket list destination." Onboard services like dining and internet were hit Some onboard services were also disrupted. In a memo to residents on September 10, Villalba said that because the ship had fewer residents on board and fewer staff available, dining service would be consolidated. An on-board restaurant, The Palms, would temporarily close, while breakfast and lunch would be served buffet-style. Dinner would be a combination of à la carte and buffet. Davis said residents would joke when they went to dinner that it was "slim pickings." Starr Davis said the final months on the ship were like a "pressure cooker." Starr Davis Internet and TV services also suffered. Two residents said the internet had become spotty and unreliable. In a September 7 memo, Villalba said she had paid an outstanding balance and that internet service was being restored. Paul Montoya, 68, said the internet issues especially affected digital nomads living and working on the ship. Some would have to get off at port to find a nearby hotel with internet access, he said. Davis said air conditioning on the ship was throttled up or down pending fuel needs, adding, "Everything was about saving fuel." Petterson, who did not live on the ship and said he was not closely involved in its daily operations, said the company took measures to save money that went beyond conserving fuel. "We were cutting back where the residents would feel it the least, and that balance sometimes was difficult," he said. Residents were repeatedly asked to help keep the ship moving Management made repeated requests for residents to help cover Villa Vie's costs. In April, Villa Vie offered residents an "Emergency Loan Investment Opportunity," asking them to lend tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars to the company at interest rates of 12% to 24%, according to a letter viewed by Business Insider. Petterson said the request netted around $2 million that helped the ship survive for a few months. Aerial view of the Odyssey's pool deck. Villa Vie Odyssey From April onwards, Gokturk said it was "cash call after cash call." Gokturk and her husband did not participate in the loan program, she said, but they contributed to later appeals, including a voluntary fuel surcharge. "It became exhausting because it was constantly, 'Hey, we need more money. We need more money. If we don't get the money, then we're not going to be able to sail,'" Gokturk said. The uncertainty affected the mood aboard the ship . "It became very, very difficult," she said. Stunkel said the cash calls felt "incessant." She continued, "We felt like they were just leaching us out of whatever we had to keep the ship moving until the last possible moment." Four residents said that when they heard that staff had gone unpaid, they organized a fundraiser for the crew. Montoya said residents collected about $12,000 in cash outside the ship's café and distributed it to workers in $100 bills. There were several times in the last couple of months when payment owed to the crew was delayed, Petterson said, including by three weeks this month. He said as of around Wednesday, the crew had been paid. An employee in the Florida office said staff had received a partial payment, and that commissions hadn't been paid in months. Petterson said the company had been doing everything it could to keep the ship afloat. The company had tried to make the fuel surcharge mandatory but realized the residents' contracts didn't allow for it, so it became voluntary. Some residents contributed to the surcharge, while others bought additional discounted cabins through the VIP program. He said he had spent July looking for outside investment. By August, the situation was dire. A potential deal with Oneil Khosa, the former CEO of Margaritaville's cruise line, fell through last week. They were out of time. Business Insider was unable to reach Khosa for comment. In the days since the Odyssey's journey came to a halt in Cambodia, passengers have expressed a range of emotions. Some are heartbroken that their dream retirement came crashing to an end; others are hopeful the ship will sail again. One passenger said a group of fellow passengers is working on a "Hail Mary" attempt at buying the ship. Petterson said the focus is on a recapitalization, adding, "Preferably we need an operational partner that can come in with a stronger hand and a bigger pocket." Several residents said that despite how it ended, they don't regret the experience. But Sadovsky, who left before the Odyssey came to a halt, said the voyage he thought he had bought had become unrecognizable by the time he disembarked. "There was no reason for me to stay because I wasn't being exposed to new places anymore," he said. "I was revisiting the same old places, and I'd rather be home." Additional reporting by Amanda Goh. items.title: I'm running the NYC marathon along with four of my BI colleagues. These are our best tips for runners and spectators alike.
items.summary: BI's 2026 NYC marathon runners (left to right): Noah Sheidlower, Anthony DeMaio, Zak Jason, Kathleen Elkins, and Steve Russolillo BI This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Welcome to Marathon Sunday! Yours truly will be among nearly 60,000 runners taking on the five boroughs today. I've spent months training for this one — with a little help from Muse, Meta's AI agent. Several weeks ago, I wrote about how I had become addicted to Muse . Since then, Muse has become part of my marathon training, helping me map out long runs and shape an overall race plan. After the Staten Island half marathon last month, it even asked me, unprompted, "how'd the half go?" The other day, I gave Muse my bib number and asked it to track my run. I'm hoping for real-time feedback and analysis, delivered straight through my AirPods, on how my race is unfolding and how I can stay on pace to achieve my goals. But no AI agent can replicate the wisdom from real people. At Business Insider, five of us are running the NYC marathon this year. We range from a first-time marathoner (Discourse editor Zak Jason) to a true veteran in Anthony DeMaio on the sales team, who will be running his 23rd NYC marathon (and roughly his 40th overall marathon; he says he's lost count!) I asked them to share their best marathon advice for runners, spectators, or if you're simply trying to understand why someone would pay $330 to run 26.2 miles . Here's what they had to say: Noah Sheidlower , senior economy reporter: Live in the moment and acknowledge the spectators who came out to support. My race time last year was disappointing, but I had an absolute blast because I was high-fiving everyone and making people's days. Tap the "power up" marathon sign that little kids are holding, give a fist pump to strangers, and laugh when you see a funny sign that someone put a lot of effort into. The marathon shouldn't just be a celebration of your individual work but a community celebration honoring the greatest city on earth. Oh also, buy merch and don't feel guilty about it ! I bit the bullet and got the blue jacket, and it looks so good. Kathleen Elkins , investing correspondent : Soak it all in! Write your name on your shirt, absorb all of the hearty cheers, give the high-fives and the smiles! When you give New Yorkers energy, they'll give it right back. Zak Jason , Discourse executive editor: As a first-time marathoner, I'm in no position to advise on anything — other than to trust the advice of people who have done hard things before you, because they want you to be awake to the gift of being alive. (Then again, someone also told me it's OK to pee yourself during the race.) Anthony DeMaio , global head of sales : Can't wait to run my 23rd NYC Marathon. The marathon is a celebration of preparation. Every early morning and every tough summer long run builds the confidence to stand on the starting line. The days you don't want to run are often the ones that matter most, discipline is choosing what you want most over what you want right now. Embrace the hard moments; they prepare you for the miles when things get tough. And remember, running is a team sport. Let people support you, and support them in return. To all my fellow runners: May the wind be at your back, the sun on your shoulders, and the crowds carry you all the way to the finish. And for me, my standard advice is that the first five miles can make or break a marathon. Go slower than your expected pace at the beginning. If you think you're going too slow at the onset, go even slower. You'll thank yourself later! Read the original article on Business Insider

Noah Sheidlower, senior economy reporter: Live in the moment and acknowledge the spectators who came out to support. My race time last year was disappointing, but I had an absolute blast because I was high-fiving everyone and making people's days. Tap the "power up" marathon sign that little kids are holding, give a fist pump to strangers, and laugh when you see a funny sign that someone put a lot of effort into. The marathon shouldn't just be a celebration of your individual work but a community celebration honoring the greatest city on earth. Oh also, buy merch and don't feel guilty about it! I bit the bullet and got the blue jacket, and it looks so good.

Kathleen Elkins, investing correspondent: Soak it all in! Write your name on your shirt, absorb all of the hearty cheers, give the high-fives and the smiles! When you give New Yorkers energy, they'll give it right back.

Zak Jason, Discourse executive editor: As a first-time marathoner, I'm in no position to advise on anything — other than to trust the advice of people who have done hard things before you, because they want you to be awake to the gift of being alive. (Then again, someone also told me it's OK to pee yourself during the race.)

Anthony DeMaio, global head of sales: Can't wait to run my 23rd NYC Marathon. The marathon is a celebration of preparation. Every early morning and every tough summer long run builds the confidence to stand on the starting line. The days you don't want to run are often the ones that matter most, discipline is choosing what you want most over what you want right now. Embrace the hard moments; they prepare you for the miles when things get tough. And remember, running is a team sport. Let people support you, and support them in return. To all my fellow runners: May the wind be at your back, the sun on your shoulders, and the crowds carry you all the way to the finish.

And for me, my standard advice is that the first five miles can make or break a marathon. Go slower than your expected pace at the beginning. If you think you're going too slow at the onset, go even slower.

You'll thank yourself later!

items.title: I run an 8-person startup that uses AI agents. We don't let our agents run on vibes — here's the playbook system we created
items.summary: Rachel Woods created playbooks full of AI agents to replace additional hires at her company. Courtesy of Rachel Woods Rachel Woods taught herself AI while studying business in college, later landing a role at Facebook. She left to start her own business, which helps people integrate AI into their everyday workflows. She said the company has saved itself at least 4 new hires by using AI agents and playbooks. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rachel Woods, CEO and cofounder of AMP. The following has been edited for length and clarity. My first official role in AI was at Facebook. I started as an intern and then joined full-time in 2018. I worked on AI research and development for the ads system that's powered by AI. I don't have an engineering degree or background; I studied management information systems at The University of Texas at Austin. Part of why I think I got my role at Facebook was because I spent time building my own side projects and teaching myself how to train AI models and do data analysis. I left Facebook in 2020 to start my own business in the wine industry, and after that company sold, I founded an AI company. I would need to double the number of people on my team if we didn't use AI playbooks. If you're being thoughtful about setting up your AI operations, it's no different than building a team that you can trust. That's something a lot of people are missing: how to actually make these systems things you can take your eyes off and not keep yourself up at night in the process. Business Insider wants to talk to founders of AI-powered companies with fewer than 10 workers, and employees working alongside AI agents and bots, to understand what the "Tiny Teams" era really feels like — the wins, the fears, and the human skills that stand out. Share your story by filling out this quick form . I've been an entrepreneur since the age of 15 My first business was a photography business, and I was too young to even drive to meet my clients. I would always catch rides with people, and my parents hated this. I got into tech because in college, I was exposed to colleagues doing data analytics and working with coding and AI at summer internships. That led me to look online and try to take related classes, and I started to see that if you break a business problem into small enough pieces, you can get AI to handle parts of it: predicting, sorting, generating. Later, when I was applying to Facebook , I used AI and data analysis to build a report of coffee shops in Austin that were less likely to be too busy for me to study at. I think that project helped me land my role. After I left Facebook , I started a wine business called Vinebase in 2020; we built a tech platform that used AI to help winemakers sell their wine online and manage the digital side of their business. Because this was before AI became more mainstream, we didn't market it as AI. We called it our "auto magic" system. I think that if we had said it was AI, it could've been a turnoff for our customers. Vinebase was acquired by Corksy in fall 2022. I use my playbooks and AI agents to replace additional staff My sister and I started AMP, originally called The AI Exchange, before ChatGPT was released in November 2022, because I was using AI in Vinebase and saw how the technology was progressing. ChatGPT came out about a month later and started really accelerating the AI timeline, so we went all in. We have four full-time employees and four part-time contractors right now, but we'd need double if we weren't running as much as we are on AI. Given the company's current size, we'd need at least four to five additional people, including a sales and marketing manager, customer support specialist, executive assistant , and operations coordinator. The way we structure these systems is based on something we call playbooking. Every department in the company has its own system. Each system is a collection of playbooks with AI agents that can run independently or together. How we build our AI playbooks To build an AI playbook, pick one piece of work you do over and over, and write down what starts it, what goes into the task, and what should come out at the end. Next, write the steps the way you'd train a new hire: each step, the decisions in it, and what "good" looks like. Start running it with AI, and while you watch, compare the result to how you would've done it. Then, fix the playbook, not the output, until you trust it to run without you. I always think through how I want a playbook to work and outline it by hand. Whenever you're making an AI playbook, you want to own the thinking and the logic. Otherwise, you can fall into the trap of including something that you don't really understand, and then you're not going to be able to trust that system anyway. We have an AI agent running our sales playbook to review customer calls and ensure they meet our standards, rather than having a sales manager review them manually. Also, instead of sales team members needing to ask their manager questions, they just ask the playbook, which then pulls the answers from our guide for that team. There are two types of AI costs we have in the business. The first is the subscriptions to Claude and ChatGPT for every person on the team. The other is because the majority of our operations are these AI playbooks that are running in the background without us being the ones starting or triggering it. In September, we spent $8,510 on Claude Code to run our playbooks in the background, which is billed by usage and is separate from the team's monthly Claude and ChatGPT subscription costs. Own the playbook, rent the tech We say "own the playbook, rent the tech," which means that if you are creating really good playbooks for your AI to follow, it actually doesn't matter which tool you're running it in. Right now, we have a setup that's running with Claude Code in the background. But I could run all of these playbooks in ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, or Microsoft Copilot . We try to avoid a lot of the risks that people are concerned about with AI going rogue by creating these detailed outlines. We don't just want the agents to run on vibes. There still needs to be a person to decide and design how the work gets done; AI just speeds up everything else. That's the job security we have in this AI era. Start small, and get everyone involved A few of us on the team who are more advanced with AI own the bigger, team-wide playbooks that the business depends on, but everyone playbooks their own personal workflow, and then we use that as the testing ground to graduate things into becoming more part of official systems. My advice would be to just start with something small and really easy, because once you get your first win and see how AI can do that repetitive work for you, it's kind of like a snowball. items.title: Apollo is sharing its private-equity  playbook with nonprofits
items.summary: The Apollo Global Management LLC office. Bloomberg/Getty Images Apollo Global Management gives portfolio companies operational guidance and leadership training. It also provides funding and operational support to 28 nonprofits, including a biennial training summit. The summit included discussions about the labor market and advice on making high-stakes decisions. Keeping up with AI and an uneven labor market is challenging enough for corporate leaders. For nonprofit executives working with tighter budgets and leaner teams, it can be extra daunting. "It's tricky for everyone right now, but for those guys, it's actually very tricky," Scott Kleinman, co-president of Apollo Asset Management and chair of the Apollo Opportunity Foundation Board. The foundation is addressing the challenges nonprofits face by providing 28 organizations with a version of the playbook Apollo uses with its over 190 portfolio companies, which include Yahoo Inc. and Shutterfly. That includes access to experts, leadership training , and a built-in network. The foundation also provides funding based on factors such as the organization's budget size and impact metrics. Apollo has so far provided over $13 million to grantees and committed to $100 million in funding over the next decade. The foundation, which launched in 2022, offered Business Insider an exclusive look at its biennial summit in October, where grantee leaders mingled with Apollo executives and sat in on panels led by subject-matter experts. Applying its portfolio playbook Kleinman said the foundation provides the same type of support it provides its portfolio companies, including operational guidance, data and digital transformation, talent management, and recruitment. "That is the crux of our foundation. Of course, it involves capital." Kleinman said, adding that the "real-value add" is the deal team. Each nonprofit is paired with a deal team of five to 10 employees from Apollo or Athene , which merged with Apollo and provides retirement services. Employees build relationships with the grantees to perform pro-bono projects, source board opportunities, and provide strategic advice. The foundation also holds monthly virtual training sessions to discuss topics like AI, leadership transitions, culture, real estate, fundraising, and succession planning. Beyond the funding At the October leadership summit, Apollo's chief economist Torsten Sløk discussed the labor market and how organizations can adapt to it, while the firm's chief financial officer talked about the factors nonprofits should consider when growing their organizations. The summit also included working sessions for grantees and their Apollo deal teams. The support Apollo offers grantees can be anything from fundraising skill-building to succession planning, said Lauren Coape-Arnold, Apollo Global Management's global head of citizenship and executive director of the Apollo Opportunity Foundation. She said the partnership starts with reorganizing boards to ensure strong governance, because an organization's success ultimately comes down to strong leadership. That may include sourcing candidates to consider for the board of directors or advisory board members. "Who is the leader? Do you believe in the leader? Are they someone inspiring the team to move forward?" Coape-Arnold said. What nonprofits need Jane Veron, cofounder and CEO of Acceleration Project, a nonprofit that helps small business owners said that support included identifying 35 processes the organization could eliminate or modify, from onboarding and technology to client data capture. For example, instead of having her team read through notes on a client's business challenges, Apollo is helping build an AI tool to do that work. It's also building asynchronous training tools to streamline consultant onboarding. "Apollo helped us identify priorities," Veron said, adding that the list includes "very micro and tactical" fixes. Reuben Ogbonna II, the cofounder and executive director of The Marcy Lab School, a one-year program that is an alternative to four-year college, said that meant revamping his school's curriculum to reflect the shifting roles of software engineers. He said Apollo's deal team helped them recognize that technologists need to work more closely with business leaders and integrated more business and industry context into the curriculum. The program also included additional cloud fundamentals and foundational DevOps knowledge, based on the team's input, he said. That sort of hands-on support is the goal, said Kleinman. "Not just to write some checks and get some photo ops, but to really make this a two-way street with our employees." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Why pay $330 to run a marathon? Let me try to explain.
items.summary: The author during the 2021 NYC Marathon. Veranika Li This summer, I spent $333.11 to register for the 2026 New York City Marathon. Between race registration fees and travel, I spend thousands of dollars a year on endurance events. It's money spent in alignment with my values, which experts say is the way to spend. You know the type of person who does run club? The one who wakes up before the sun on a Sunday to stack miles and finishes the run at a coffee shop, still sweating as they're waiting in line captioning their Strava post? That's me. I'm that person. I'm also among the group of people who spend a lot of money to safety-pin a number to their shirt and run from a start line to a finish line in exchange for a generic tech tee, a medal, and a banana. This summer, I spent $333.11 to register for the 2026 New York City Marathon. I didn't bat an eye at checkout — not because I'm rich and the purchase wasn't significant. I'm not, and it was. But, to borrow one of Ramit Sethi's spending concepts , registration fees for endurance events would be one of my top " Money Dials ," which are essentially spending categories that you can either turn up or down. It's how I like to spend my discretionary income, and since I cut back in other areas, I can do so guilt-free, no matter how egregious the registration fee . I came up with the idea to write this particular story on a run. It was a Tuesday in June. I know the date because I left myself an eight-second voice memo recording the idea: "Why pay $300 for a marathon — to run 26.2 miles? Let me try to explain," I say, slightly out of breath. Why do I pay a lot of money to run marathons? And why the marathon — the 26.2-mile event? Why do I invest not only so much money but also so much time in training and racing? I'm not a professional, and never will be. My time is precious, but my chip time doesn't matter to anyone but me. For the past four months, I've pondered those questions — casually at first, and more urgently as the race (and the deadline for this article) approached. My first thought was to distinguish between running and racing. I picked up long-distance running in my early 20s, after more than a decade of junior tennis and four years of collegiate tennis had left me burned out on the sport. I was living in New York City, where finicky weather, high court fees, and complicated logistics make it difficult to hit a tennis ball, even if I wanted to. Looking for an affordable and efficient way to stay in shape, I turned to running. It was perfect for me: a minimalist who doesn't like stuff or clutter. I already had everything I needed: a pair of Nikes and easy access to a smooth running path. As an introvert, running suited me, giving me the time and space to think, plan, ideate, or simply check out of life's stressors. And the more I ran, the better I got at it. My marathon times started to suggest that I was decent at the distance — qualifying for the Boston Marathon is considered the pinnacle for amateur marathoners, a feat I've accomplished a few times — so maybe that's part of the reason I kept running, even if getting better made the activity a little more expensive. We all tend to gravitate toward the things we're good at, don't we? If running is meditative, rhythmic, and solitary, racing is exhilarating, hectic, and communal. It's a shared experience. You toe the line with thousands — sometimes tens of thousands — of other runners. But unless you're vying for the podium, you're not competing against them. You're racing the clock and your past self — alongside, not against, thousands of others. Preparing for a marathon is challenging. It requires time, patience, and work — stacking miles and workouts for months. It's also incredibly satisfying. By the time race day rolls around, the hard part is done. When the gun goes off, the fun begins. NYRR If running is simple, efficient, and cheap, racing is coordinated, time-consuming, and expensive. That $333 entry fee was just the beginning of my expenses for this experience. I bought round-trip flights from Los Angeles and a really expensive pair of "super shoes" for race day. When I'm racing in a city where I don't have friends or family, hotels add up quickly. But back to Sethi and his "Money Dials," how you choose to spend your money matters. In fact, studies show that how you spend is oftentimes more important than how much you spend. Sethi's point is that, no matter your Money Dial — fitness, travel, experiences, or relationships — you can build a life that allows you to "spend extravagantly and unapologetically on the things that truly matter," while cutting costs "mercilessly" on the things that don't matter to you. Simply put: Spend on things that make you happy; don't spend on things that aren't important to you. The 2026 New York City Marathon will be my 21st marathon. I keep track in the Notes app on my phone, recording my times, what I ate the night before, how many gels I consumed, and other random tidbits from the training block or race day. What you get out of the race is entirely up to you. Your goal can be to run the fastest you ever have — a personal record, or "PR" — or it can be to simply cross the line with a smile on your face. Of all the races I've done, the New York City Marathon is my favorite by far. Nearly 60,000 runners gather in Staten Island on the first Sunday of November to run through the city's five boroughs, absorbing high fives and hearty cheers from the millions of New Yorkers lining streets. Anything can happen over the course of 26.2 miles, another component of the marathon's charm. You could cramp up and blow up. You could get an assist from a tailwind and negative split. It's nearly impossible to have a perfect day, but sometimes race day magic strikes. See you out there. Let's dial it up. Read the original article on Business Insider

Why do I pay a lot of money to run marathons? And why the marathon — the 26.2-mile event? Why do I invest not only so much money but also so much time in training and racing? I'm not a professional, and never will be. My time is precious, but my chip time doesn't matter to anyone but me.

For the past four months, I've pondered those questions — casually at first, and more urgently as the race (and the deadline for this article) approached.

My first thought was to distinguish between running and racing.

I picked up long-distance running in my early 20s, after more than a decade of junior tennis and four years of collegiate tennis had left me burned out on the sport. I was living in New York City, where finicky weather, high court fees, and complicated logistics make it difficult to hit a tennis ball, even if I wanted to. Looking for an affordable and efficient way to stay in shape, I turned to running. It was perfect for me: a minimalist who doesn't like stuff or clutter. I already had everything I needed: a pair of Nikes and easy access to a smooth running path.

As an introvert, running suited me, giving me the time and space to think, plan, ideate, or simply check out of life's stressors. And the more I ran, the better I got at it. My marathon times started to suggest that I was decent at the distance — qualifying for the Boston Marathon is considered the pinnacle for amateur marathoners, a feat I've accomplished a few times — so maybe that's part of the reason I kept running, even if getting better made the activity a little more expensive. We all tend to gravitate toward the things we're good at, don't we?

If running is meditative, rhythmic, and solitary, racing is exhilarating, hectic, and communal. It's a shared experience. You toe the line with thousands — sometimes tens of thousands — of other runners. But unless you're vying for the podium, you're not competing against them. You're racing the clock and your past self — alongside, not against, thousands of others.

Preparing for a marathon is challenging. It requires time, patience, and work — stacking miles and workouts for months. It's also incredibly satisfying. By the time race day rolls around, the hard part is done.

When the gun goes off, the fun begins.

NYRR

If running is simple, efficient, and cheap, racing is coordinated, time-consuming, and expensive.

That $333 entry fee was just the beginning of my expenses for this experience. I bought round-trip flights from Los Angeles and a really expensive pair of "super shoes" for race day. When I'm racing in a city where I don't have friends or family, hotels add up quickly.

But back to Sethi and his "Money Dials," how you choose to spend your money matters. In fact, studies show that how you spend is oftentimes more important than how much you spend.

Sethi's point is that, no matter your Money Dial — fitness, travel, experiences, or relationships — you can build a life that allows you to "spend extravagantly and unapologetically on the things that truly matter," while cutting costs "mercilessly" on the things that don't matter to you.

Simply put: Spend on things that make you happy; don't spend on things that aren't important to you.

The 2026 New York City Marathon will be my 21st marathon. I keep track in the Notes app on my phone, recording my times, what I ate the night before, how many gels I consumed, and other random tidbits from the training block or race day.

What you get out of the race is entirely up to you. Your goal can be to run the fastest you ever have — a personal record, or "PR" — or it can be to simply cross the line with a smile on your face.

Of all the races I've done, the New York City Marathon is my favorite by far. Nearly 60,000 runners gather in Staten Island on the first Sunday of November to run through the city's five boroughs, absorbing high fives and hearty cheers from the millions of New Yorkers lining streets.

Anything can happen over the course of 26.2 miles, another component of the marathon's charm. You could cramp up and blow up. You could get an assist from a tailwind and negative split.

It's nearly impossible to have a perfect day, but sometimes race day magic strikes.

See you out there. Let's dial it up.

items.title: This new indie film about an AI startup founder and his family feels less like sci-fi by the day
items.summary: "Anna by the Window" is a film co-directed by filmmakers Myles Flusser and James Hyland. BaggySuit "Anna by the Window" is a coming-of-age film by filmmakers Myles Flusser and James Hyland. The film explores grief and human connection in the age of generative AI. Flusser said the film was at first a "speculative sci-fi" about AI, but then fiction became reality. From tech behemoths scrambling to replicate OpenAI's success with ChatGPT to Twitter rebranding to X under Elon Musk , Silicon Valley was undergoing an undeniable transformation in 2023. Nearly 3,000 miles away in New York, two skeptical 20-somethings were trying to make sense of it all. So, they made a film. "It was very personal," James Hyland, 25, told Business Insider. "We wanted to put something together that spoke to the things we were going through and what the world was like. That ended up being artificial intelligence and technological alienation." Hyland and Myles Flusser created "Anna by the Window," a coming-of-age film exploring grief and how technology can stifle human connection in the era of generative AI. The independent filmmakers wrote, directed, and produced the film in 2023 alongside their friends under their production company, Baggysuit. "Anna by the Window" is a coming-of-age film exploring grief and human connection in the digital era. Baggysuit "Particularly, it feels like the people running these platforms — YouTube, Instagram, et cetera — seem more contented than ever in letting it become a total slop apocalypse full of AI bots and non-human content," Flusser, 26, said. "That intrigues me in a way and scares me, obviously." Zoomers like Flusser and Hyland grew up inundated with smartphones, social media, and all the risks that come along with them. A year after they filmed "Anna by the Window," the US Surgeon General said social media should have a warning label because of its impact on mental health. Earlier this year, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by a coalition of states accusing it of designing platforms to addict children . The din of constant digital exposure has led some young folks to join the neo-Luddite movement , which takes a stand against overreliance on modern technology by emphasizing IRL human connection . Hyland is an organizer for a Luddite group called The Lamp Club . While the film was not made because of the Luddite movement, it shares many of its themes. "I think that it speaks to the synergy of our separate film project and this larger organizing project that's materializing all over the country, where people are fed up with these kinds of technological systems," Hyland said. When fiction becomes reality The "Anna by the Window" crew began screening the film in July. Baggysuit "Anna by the Window" is a glimpse inside the world of Ryan, a teenage boy who travels to New York City to reconnect with his older brother, James, the founder of an AI startup. The film's crew shot across New York State and used a variety of tools to bring the project to life, including ElevenLabs AI audio software to create the voice of Ryan and James' father throughout the film. The pair also pushed a real ChatGPT chatbot toward hallucination and included that audio in the film. "There's an AI chatbot that goes off the rails, you could say. We really cranked up all the dials," Hyland said. "It started saying 'error.' It started speaking different languages." Flusser said they wanted to portray the eerie nature of AI just right. They're not eager to use AI products in future projects, though. The majority of the film relies on traditional tools like a Sony camera, written outlines, and improv. "There's a strangeness and alienation that come up when we interact with chatbots and AI. We were trying to capture that feeling as purely as possible, so it felt totally necessary to use AI to do that," Flusser said. James Hyland and Myles Flusser used Eleven Labs and ChatGPT to create parts of the film. Baggysuit While aspects of the film are fictional, others pull directly from the directors' lives. "My brother had recently died. There's a lot of stuff in there that has to do with that," Flusser said. "There is a climactic moment between the two brothers in this movie that is actually surgically removed from my own life and recreated on screen." However, the way the filmmakers chose to characterize James in the film — delusional, stunted, running from reality — is distinct from Flusser's real brother. In the film, James is portrayed by Hyland, who said his version of an AI startup founder isn't based on a specific person. "My character was in a state of denial. Using this technology to be the thing that could deliver him closure or be the thing that he could connect with," Hyland said. "It makes him, in a way, kind of a sympathetic character." 'Anna by the Window' on the silver screen Hollywood is fixated on the real lives of tech founders . Production companies have backed films about SpaceX founder Elon Musk, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, and former Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes . Even "Toy Story 5" tackled tech by introducing a smart tablet as the story's antagonist. "Anna by the Window" now joins the list of films putting the tech industry under a harsh microscope. "When we first started filming this, we were more mystified by AI, but toward the end our relationship with AI felt very cynical," Flusser said. "Anna by the Window" will become available to stream on Dolph on December 15. Baggysuit Watching AI evolve while creating a film about the technology was surreal, Hyland and Flusser said. "It was strange. When we were making it, we saw this movie as a speculative sci-fi about artificial intelligence," Flusser said. "Now, it's like nothing really is sci-fi about it anymore." The "Anna by the Window" crew began screening the film this summer in New York City and the Hudson Valley. There are upcoming screenings in Los Angeles this November. The film becomes available on Dolph, a streaming platform, beginning December 15. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Vibe coding is old news. People are 'vibe manufacturing' now.
items.summary: David Plakon prototyped an answering box for his kids with GPT-6 Astra. David Plakon These techies are using AI to prototype answering machines, toys, and jewelry. They call it "vibe manufacturing," a play on the term vibe coding. The vibe manufacturers are bullish on its potential. "AI literally does replace CAD engineering completely," one said. Jeff Deehan is a real estate developer by day and a "hobby guy" by night. The 42-year-old has a workshop in his East Lansing house. One project remained elusive: a small piece of steel to secure a camper to his truck. While Deehan was toying with OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra in voice mode, he described the piece he needed and the angle at which it would sit. Five minutes later, the chatbot had prototyped it. GPT-6 Astra designed a steel part to secure a camper to Jeff Deehan's truck. Jeff Deehan Deehan told GPT-6 that he knew of a company called SendCutSend that does custom sheet-metal fabrication. The chatbot downloaded its design as a DXF file, opened SendCutSend's website, filled in the form, and paid the $156 with the payment information he'd stored. Ten days later, it was on his doorstep. "In about 10 minutes, I spoke a part out of my mind into existence, without touching my phone," he said. Deehan is part of a growing class of enthusiasts who are building physical gizmos with AI's help. They use chatbots to build prototypes, then send the AI-generated files to manufacturers, boutique fabricators, and their home 3D printers . Jeff Deehan ordered the truck piece from SendCutSend. It shipped in 10 days. Jeff Deehan Modeling physical items with AI has its risks. Deehan was sure his prototype would be a millimeter off here or there, though it ended up being right on. Other vibe manufacturers said that their products took multiple iterations, burning through their budgets. Normies have long used AI to write software, now dubbed " vibe coding ." These builders say AI is coming for hardware creation, too — and they're calling it "vibe manufacturing." A growing CADtastrophe Amy Zhou and Jake Fitzgerald are building an open-source tool for vibe manufacturing. They call it "text-to-CAD" — and it already tops 23,000 stars on GitHub. Zhou previously worked on the iPhone cases team at Apple and is now a design engineer at the AI rendering startup Vizcom. Fitzgerald wanted to get back into robotics after pivoting to crypto. They text new ideas back and forth between San Francisco and New York. The duo hopes to upend CAD, or computer-aided design . CAD engineers use software to design and optimize 3D models. It takes training and skill. The vibe manufacturers say you can do it easily with a large language model. Zhou makes jewelry with AI. The 25-year-old's previous startup turned pictures users uploaded into 3D models of charms, then cast the models in wax. It made a necklace for Cluely's CEO , Roy Lee, before Zhou left the business. She still occasionally makes AI-rendered charms for friends when they want necklaces of their pets. Amy Zhou turns photos into wax-cast jewelry with AI's help. Amy Zhou Fitzgerald is more interested in making robot arms. Using the text-to-CAD tool, the 31-year-old designed the arm in sheet metal and paid about $200 to have it built by SendCutSend. It has 0.6 meters of reach, with a motor and a camera, and he considers it an "edutainment" product to learn about robotics before the industry booms . A few months ago, Fitzgerald saw "compounding failures" when the AI would build bad designs on top of bad designs. The screw holes came in loose, for example. He spent about $2,000 repeatedly ordering pieces. With GPT-6 Astra, he said that's no longer a problem. Jake Fitzgerald prototyped a robot arm with his text-to-CAD AI tool. Jake Fitzgerald Sourish Sharma has watched AI change CAD. The 20-year-old from London got an MRI scan for a research study three years ago and asked for his data. He got a 3D printer and used an open-source tool to turn the data file into something printable. The tool didn't work very well, so he had to edit it by hand. "Some of the folds of the brain were not very foldy," he said. Now, Sharma has a much bigger printer — and AI. With one prompt, GPT-6 Astra blew the open-source tool out of the water, converting the data and making what he considers a more accurate brain. He's printed out a life-size one, as well as a handful of miniatures that he gives to friends. Sourish Sharma used AI to turn data from his MRI into a 3D-printed brain. Sourish Sharma "AI literally does replace CAD engineering completely," Sharma said. "It's kind of unfortunate if you're a CAD engineer. Fortunately, I'm not." The first audience: kids The more complex a product is, the more difficult it is to vibe manufacture. You won't be able to make a car at home with ChatGPT anytime soon. There's one population whose products are often simple and accessible: kids. Arthur Prince, a 34-year-old IT worker from outside Paris, said the children's toy he modeled in a week with AI would've taken him months with his CAD knowledge alone. Prince's toy creates stories and images with AI based on a kid's voice prompt. He developed everything, from the casing to the internal wiring, with GPT-6 Astra, then asked Claude to criticize its work. Once the two chatbots reached a consensus, he ordered 10 of the toys from the Chinese manufacturer JLCPCB for about 500 euros, fretting that he'd wasted his money on something that wouldn't work. Arthur Prince prototyped a toy for his daughter with GPT-6 Astra. Arthur Prince Luckily, they did. Prince's first tester, his daughter, loves it. "She's very proud to see that I can make something like this," he said. The benefit of vibe manufacturing kids' toys is their simplicity. Many parents don't want their children surfing the web , so AI prototypers don't have to worry about those pesky questions of cell service and web browsers. David Plakon wanted his kids to leave messages for their grandparents in Florida — but didn't want them on the internet. The 39-year-old from Austin is a longtime "tinkerer." He's had a 3D printer since 2015, and was printing his kid a " KPop Demon Hunters " sword while we spoke. So, he and his wife, Lara, figured they could build their own answering machine in the style of the Tin Can phone . David Plakon has printed the case for his answering box about 15 times. David Plakon Plakon gave GPT-6 Astra some design inspiration and instructions to build a prototype. All of the parts had to be purchasable or buildable with his 3D printer, he told the chatbot. It easily put together a model, instructing him to buy a potentiometer, a speaker, and an ESP32 chip, and guided him through the assembly. He's now printed the design some 15 times, improving it on each go. Initially, some of the pieces didn't fit together. "AI's good but not perfect," he said. David Plakon is still iterating on his voicebox, though the tech officially works. David Plakon But the box does work, and he hopes to sell it one day. He's keeping it small-scale for now, aiming to get the answering box in the grandparents' home for Christmas. "I don't have any delusion that I could send this to a factory, and they would be able to make it," Plakon said. "For now, it's very fun to prototype." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: DoorDash's CEO: Don't be 'delusional' after just a few hundred AI agent orders
items.summary: Some third-party AI agents have generated "several hundred" DoorDash orders, CEO Tony Xu said. David Zalubowski/AP DoorDash isn't seeing many orders through AI agents like Muse yet, its CEO said. Third-party agents have generated "several hundred orders in total," Tony Xu said this week. Even so, DoorDash is moving ahead with its own AI ordering tools. The age of AI agents ordering your meals isn't here yet, according to DoorDash. The food delivery service has received "several hundred orders in total" from agents such as Meta's Muse, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said during the company's earnings call on Thursday. By comparison, DoorDash delivered 3.2 billion orders worldwide in 2025. Instead, customers are still using DoorDash's app and website to place orders, Xu said. "For the everyday ordering, what we see is people come to DoorDash, and they come back to DoorDash," he said. Xu's comments suggest that buzzy AI agents like Muse and Instinct have far to go before they become a big part of how users buy things. The agents can be useful for tracking the prices of holiday gifts or airline tickets, users told Business Insider earlier this month. Many are hesitant to let agents make the purchases themselves. They also use more secure payment options, such as single-use credit cards, in case the agents make a mistake. Despite the low order volume through third-party agents, DoorDash is making changes to its own AI tools. The company said in September that it was testing a text-to-order feature with an interface reminiscent of Instinct. Another ordering option, a chatbot called Ask DoorDash, creates an order from a recipe or shopping list and can adjust the contents to match customers' preferences. Those AI tools could eventually generate new orders on DoorDash, Xu said. "My take on all things technology is you never want to fight gravity," he said. "But, at the same time, you do not want to be delusional," he added, referring to the low number of agent-placed orders. Do you have a story idea about DoorDash? items.title: Nace AI Open-Sources Drex Max v1: A 27B Decision Model That Runs Locally on Apple Silicon
items.summary: Nace AI has released Drex Max v1 as open weights . Drex Max is its most capable decision model, and it now runs on your own hardware. The release ships bf16 weights, a Q8_0 GGUF , an affine Q4 checkpoint and forks of llama.cpp and Ollama . For developers, Drex Max open weights mean routing, classification and policy checks can stay on a local machine. TL;DR Size: Dense 27B parameters, 262,144-token window (16,384 by default), up to 255 options per question. Runs on: NVIDIA GPU with Python (H100 bf16, or L40S 48 GB in 8-bit). Apple Silicon Macs with 24 GB+ (affine Q4) or 48 GB (Q8_0 GGUF). CPU via llama.cpp and Ollama. Performance: 67.52 on the public Decision Index 0.4, 6.27 points ahead of Drex v2.0 (self-reported). Best: 97.3 skill on InfographicVQA. Tools area reaches 81.9. A top-tier decision model you can now run offline on a Mac. What is Drex Max? Drex Max is a decision model from Nace.AI that answers typed questions about a given context. You pass a state (text, JSON or images) plus named questions. The model returns a probability for every option in one forward pass. Nothing is generated . Questions come in 3 types: choice among named options, yes/no, and an ordinal score. That makes it a fit for agent routing, ticket triage and guardrail checks. The hosted version is presented at routing, classification and policy checks. How does Drex Max work? The model card describes a dense 27B backbone with 64 layers. 48 are Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers that run left to right. The other 16 are full-attention layers, placed every fourth layer, and they are non-causal. Every token can attend to the whole sequence. Images pass through a native vision tower and are visible to every question in a request. A 255-way readout head then turns the last hidden state into option probabilities. The config lists a qwen3_5 model type with a 262,144-position window. &&& How does Drex Max perform on benchmarks? All figures below are self-reported by Nace AI, Decision Index 0.4 (public text): 67.52. Drex v2.0 scores 61.25 and Jev 1.13.0 scores 57.96. Area skill: Tools 81.9, Language 72.2, Retrieval 68.8, Knowledge and Reasoning 57.1, Arts 53.4. Public vision index: 73.92 across 11 benchmarks and 12,210 rows. Artificial Analysis Decision Index: 64, which Nace says ranks 4th of 18. JevBench: 92.2% (213/231). Decision Bench v4: 94.30% (1010/1071). The results dataset covers 140,620 requests. Unanswered requests count as wrong. How do you run Drex Max locally? Nace documents 5 runtimes. All of them serve the same POST /v1/systemone API. Runtime Hardware Checkpoint Images Python NVIDIA GPU bf16 (~49 GB) or 8-bit (~26 GB) Yes llama.cpp fork Apple Metal, CPU Q8_0 GGUF (27.25 GB) No Ollama fork Apple Metal, CPU Q8_0 GGUF No Kapitsa v0.2.25+ Apple Silicon Q8_0 GGUF or affine Q4 No MLX Apple Silicon affine Q4 (14.45 GB) No The affine Q4 checkpoint targets Macs with 24 GB or more. The Q8_0 GGUF needs 48 GB. On a 48 GB Mac, Nace recommends –context 2048 for Kapitsa. Ollama users set num_gpu 40 to offload 40 layers to Metal. Setting num_gpu 0 runs it on the CPU. The Ollama fork needs a CAPABILITY decision line in the Modelfile. Quantization holds up in Nace’s tests. On a 48 GB Apple M5 Pro, the Q8_0 GGUF matched H100 bf16 within 0.02 per probability. The affine Q4 stayed within 0.0329 of Q8_0, with no choice flips. items.summary_html:
Nace AI has released Drex Max v1 as open weights. Drex Max is its most capable decision model, and it now runs on your own hardware. The release ships bf16 weights, a Q8_0 GGUF, an affine Q4 checkpoint and forks of llama.cpp and Ollama. For developers, Drex Max open weights mean routing, classification and policy checks can stay on a local machine.

TL;DR
  • Size: Dense 27B parameters, 262,144-token window (16,384 by default), up to 255 options per question.
  • Runs on: NVIDIA GPU with Python (H100 bf16, or L40S 48 GB in 8-bit). Apple Silicon Macs with 24 GB+ (affine Q4) or 48 GB (Q8_0 GGUF). CPU via llama.cpp and Ollama.
  • Performance: 67.52 on the public Decision Index 0.4, 6.27 points ahead of Drex v2.0 (self-reported).
  • Best: 97.3 skill on InfographicVQA. Tools area reaches 81.9. A top-tier decision model you can now run offline on a Mac.
What is Drex Max?

Drex Max is a decision model from Nace.AI that answers typed questions about a given context. You pass a state (text, JSON or images) plus named questions. The model returns a probability for every option in one forward pass. Nothing is generated.

Questions come in 3 types: choice among named options, yes/no, and an ordinal score. That makes it a fit for agent routing, ticket triage and guardrail checks. The hosted version is presented at routing, classification and policy checks.

How does Drex Max work?

The model card describes a dense 27B backbone with 64 layers. 48 are Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers that run left to right. The other 16 are full-attention layers, placed every fourth layer, and they are non-causal. Every token can attend to the whole sequence.

Images pass through a native vision tower and are visible to every question in a request. A 255-way readout head then turns the last hidden state into option probabilities. The config lists a qwen3_5 model type with a 262,144-position window.

&&&

How does Drex Max perform on benchmarks?

All figures below are self-reported by Nace AI,

  • Decision Index 0.4 (public text): 67.52. Drex v2.0 scores 61.25 and Jev 1.13.0 scores 57.96.
  • Area skill: Tools 81.9, Language 72.2, Retrieval 68.8, Knowledge and Reasoning 57.1, Arts 53.4.
  • Public vision index: 73.92 across 11 benchmarks and 12,210 rows.
  • Artificial Analysis Decision Index: 64, which Nace says ranks 4th of 18.
  • JevBench: 92.2% (213/231). Decision Bench v4: 94.30% (1010/1071).

The results dataset covers 140,620 requests. Unanswered requests count as wrong.

How do you run Drex Max locally?

Nace documents 5 runtimes. All of them serve the same POST /v1/systemone API.

RuntimeHardwareCheckpointImagesPythonNVIDIA GPUbf16 (~49 GB) or 8-bit (~26 GB)Yesllama.cpp forkApple Metal, CPUQ8_0 GGUF (27.25 GB)NoOllama forkApple Metal, CPUQ8_0 GGUFNoKapitsa v0.2.25+Apple SiliconQ8_0 GGUF or affine Q4NoMLXApple Siliconaffine Q4 (14.45 GB)No

The affine Q4 checkpoint targets Macs with 24 GB or more. The Q8_0 GGUF needs 48 GB. On a 48 GB Mac, Nace recommends –context 2048 for Kapitsa.

Ollama users set num_gpu 40 to offload 40 layers to Metal. Setting num_gpu 0 runs it on the CPU. The Ollama fork needs a CAPABILITY decision line in the Modelfile.

Quantization holds up in Nace’s tests. On a 48 GB Apple M5 Pro, the Q8_0 GGUF matched H100 bf16 within 0.02 per probability. The affine Q4 stayed within 0.0329 of Q8_0, with no choice flips.

Nace AI team states that Decision Index 0.4 uses the same public suite as 0.3.1. 

Key Takeaways
  • Drex Max v1 weights are now public under Nace.AI Open RAIL-M.
  • It scores 67.52 on Decision Index 0.4, above Drex v2.0 (61.25).
  • A 4-bit build runs on 24 GB Apple Silicon Macs via Kapitsa or MLX.
  • Q8_0 on an M5 Pro matched H100 bf16 within 0.02.
  • Local Mac and CPU paths are text only for now.

Check out the model weights, Q8_0 GGUF, code and docs, Tweet and cloud console.

items.title: DeepSeek Open-Sources dsh-superagent, a Router-Worker Coding Agent
items.summary: The DeepSeek Harness team just released dsh-superagent , an MIT-licensed research prototype. DeepSeek dsh-superagent is a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository. It is packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness . It listens to GitHub and, optionally, Feishu. It turns allowed requests into parallel work items, each in its own agent session. The release shipped alongside a design post, Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System . TL;DaR What is it?: A TypeScript bundle, v0.1.0, released as 1 commit under MIT. It uses whatever model the Harness profile is set to. Runs on: Your own machine, as a dedicated DeepSeek Harness profile. Needs Node.js 22.19+ or 24+, git 2.32+, Python 3.8+, tmux and GitHub CLI 2.48+. Performance: In DeepSeek’s simulation, it finished tasks far faster under a noisy message stream than a single-session agent. Best: p95 task completion of 15.7 minutes vs 29.5 minutes for the single-session baseline (about 1.9x faster). Worst: Tested only on synthetic messages and simulated tools. Real coding quality was not measured. What is DeepSeek dsh-superagent? It is a GitHub agent that waits to be asked. When an allowed person addresses it, it opens a work item, called a Ticket. Each Ticket runs in its own session and directory. Results return to the original conversation, often as a pull request. A local web panel lists only what needs a person. The README page states the core rule plainly: take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible. The philosophy doc applies it to behavior. The agent confirms once, stays quiet while working, and writes again only with a result, a question or a failure. Why did DeepSeek build a Super-agent? DeepSeek team argues that mainstream agents treat 1 session as the basic unit. According to the report, as reported by ifeng , a person can actively follow only 3 to 5 sessions at once. Human attention, not model capability, becomes the bottleneck for multitasking. How does the Router-Worker architecture work? The research team describes 2 layers. A long-running Router handles interaction and dispatch. Isolated Worker sessions do the actual work. In the prototype, that flow is concrete, per the domain model : Source → Trigger: GitHub or Feishu produces events. Eval: decides whether a batch of Triggers asks for new work. Ticket: a unit of authorized work, with an immutable Mandate stating why it may proceed. Subscription: later comments on a pull request reach the right Worker without a fresh mention. The main session runs the dsh-superagent-router preset with a smaller tool set. Each Worker runs dsh-superagent-worker . Shell commands move to the background after 5 seconds, so Workers keep receiving messages, per the execution doc . Proactive work is gated. The authorization doc defines 3 accept modes: off , observe (default) and auto . In observe , the agent only records what it would have accepted. The research team also lists ideas beyond the prototype: an external Watchdog, storage and compute separation, and an asynchronous ReAct loop. && How does it perform? DeepSeek tested with simulated group chat and GitHub CI streams. Each run had about 300 messages, of which about 20 were real work requests. Each scheme ran 5 times, per ifeng’s account of the report . Super-agent: p50 of 12.4 minutes, p95 of 15.7 minutes. Single session plus subagents, neutral prompt: p95 of 29.5 minutes. No p50 was given. Why: under the neutral prompt, the baseline called a subagent 0 times in 5 runs . Router load: as arrivals rose from about 1 to 40 per minute, batch size grew from 1.0 to 2.8. Per-request latency rose from 2.5 to 3.9 seconds. An ablation removed direct event pass-through. Router decisions rose about 30%, and cache-read tokens rose about 37%, from 23.23M to 31.77M . All figures are self-reported and come from secondary reports of the report. How does dsh-superagent compare with other GitHub coding agents? Feature DeepSeek dsh-superagent GitHub Copilot cloud agent Claude Code Action OpenAI Codex Trigger Mention by allowed person; written rules Issue assignment, chat, API, Slack and more @claude mention, issue assignment, workflow prompt @Codex in Slack; cloud tasks Unasked (proactive) work Yes, rule-gated; observe by default Yes, via automations Yes, via workflow events Not disclosed Parallel isolated sessions Yes, 1 per Ticket Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Where it runs Your machine (Harness profile) GitHub, in the background Your GitHub Actions runner Codex cloud Chat source Feishu (optional) Slack, Teams Not disclosed Slack License MIT Not disclosed MIT CLI agent open source Availability Research prototype All paid Copilot plans Your API key or cloud provider ChatGPT Plus and above Key Takeaways DeepSeek released dsh-superagent, an MIT-licensed proactive coding agent prototype. A Router dispatches work; isolated Worker sessions execute each Ticket. Simulated p95 task time: 15.7 minutes vs 29.5 minutes for a single session. Proactive work stays in observe mode until a team switches it on. It runs with full OS-user access, so isolate it before use. Check out the GitHub repo , the setup guide and the design docs . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. items.summary_html:
The DeepSeek Harness team just released dsh-superagent, an MIT-licensed research prototype. DeepSeek dsh-superagent is a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository. It is packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness. It listens to GitHub and, optionally, Feishu. It turns allowed requests into parallel work items, each in its own agent session. The release shipped alongside a design post, Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System.

TL;DaR
  • What is it?: A TypeScript bundle, v0.1.0, released as 1 commit under MIT. It uses whatever model the Harness profile is set to.
  • Runs on: Your own machine, as a dedicated DeepSeek Harness profile. Needs Node.js 22.19+ or 24+, git 2.32+, Python 3.8+, tmux and GitHub CLI 2.48+.
  • Performance: In DeepSeek’s simulation, it finished tasks far faster under a noisy message stream than a single-session agent.
  • Best: p95 task completion of 15.7 minutes vs 29.5 minutes for the single-session baseline (about 1.9x faster).
  • Worst: Tested only on synthetic messages and simulated tools. Real coding quality was not measured.
What is DeepSeek dsh-superagent?

It is a GitHub agent that waits to be asked. When an allowed person addresses it, it opens a work item, called a Ticket. Each Ticket runs in its own session and directory. Results return to the original conversation, often as a pull request. A local web panel lists only what needs a person.

The README page states the core rule plainly: take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible. The philosophy doc applies it to behavior. The agent confirms once, stays quiet while working, and writes again only with a result, a question or a failure.

Why did DeepSeek build a Super-agent?

DeepSeek team argues that mainstream agents treat 1 session as the basic unit. According to the report, as reported by ifeng, a person can actively follow only 3 to 5 sessions at once. Human attention, not model capability, becomes the bottleneck for multitasking.

How does the Router-Worker architecture work?

The research team describes 2 layers. A long-running Router handles interaction and dispatch. Isolated Worker sessions do the actual work.

In the prototype, that flow is concrete, per the domain model:

  • Source → Trigger: GitHub or Feishu produces events.
  • Eval: decides whether a batch of Triggers asks for new work.
  • Ticket: a unit of authorized work, with an immutable Mandate stating why it may proceed.
  • Subscription: later comments on a pull request reach the right Worker without a fresh mention.

The main session runs the dsh-superagent-router preset with a smaller tool set. Each Worker runs dsh-superagent-worker. Shell commands move to the background after 5 seconds, so Workers keep receiving messages, per the execution doc.

Proactive work is gated. The authorization doc defines 3 accept modes: off, observe (default) and auto. In observe, the agent only records what it would have accepted.

The research team also lists ideas beyond the prototype: an external Watchdog, storage and compute separation, and an asynchronous ReAct loop.

&&

How does it perform?

DeepSeek tested with simulated group chat and GitHub CI streams. Each run had about 300 messages, of which about 20 were real work requests. Each scheme ran 5 times, per ifeng’s account of the report.

  • Super-agent: p50 of 12.4 minutes, p95 of 15.7 minutes.
  • Single session plus subagents, neutral prompt: p95 of 29.5 minutes. No p50 was given.
  • Why: under the neutral prompt, the baseline called a subagent 0 times in 5 runs.
  • Router load: as arrivals rose from about 1 to 40 per minute, batch size grew from 1.0 to 2.8. Per-request latency rose from 2.5 to 3.9 seconds.

An ablation removed direct event pass-through. Router decisions rose about 30%, and cache-read tokens rose about 37%, from 23.23M to 31.77M. All figures are self-reported and come from secondary reports of the report.

How does dsh-superagent compare with other GitHub coding agents? FeatureDeepSeek dsh-superagentGitHub Copilot cloud agentClaude Code ActionOpenAI CodexTriggerMention by allowed person; written rulesIssue assignment, chat, API, Slack and more@claude mention, issue assignment, workflow prompt@Codex in Slack; cloud tasksUnasked (proactive) workYes, rule-gated; observe by defaultYes, via automationsYes, via workflow eventsNot disclosedParallel isolated sessionsYes, 1 per TicketNot disclosedNot disclosedNot disclosedWhere it runsYour machine (Harness profile)GitHub, in the backgroundYour GitHub Actions runnerCodex cloudChat sourceFeishu (optional)Slack, TeamsNot disclosedSlackLicenseMITNot disclosedMITCLI agent open sourceAvailabilityResearch prototypeAll paid Copilot plansYour API key or cloud providerChatGPT Plus and above Key Takeaways
  • DeepSeek released dsh-superagent, an MIT-licensed proactive coding agent prototype.
  • A Router dispatches work; isolated Worker sessions execute each Ticket.
  • Simulated p95 task time: 15.7 minutes vs 29.5 minutes for a single session.
  • Proactive work stays in observe mode until a team switches it on.
  • It runs with full OS-user access, so isolate it before use.

Check out the GitHub repo, the setup guide and the design docs. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter. Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well.
