items.title: A ChatGPT share link leaked your private conversations
items.summary: In October 2026, a research team at parameter.ai turned an ordinary public ChatGPT share link into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it. The victim only had to open the link. There was no app to install, no project to join, no code to paste, no developer tools. OpenAI classified the report as P1 and shipped a fix on October 26. The payload ran as chatgpt.com, which is the part that matters. From there it enumerated the victim's conversation list, pulled the content of a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and sent selected data to an external server. It called ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, so its reach was whatever the normal frontend can do on your account. The chain is worth walking through because no single piece of it was broken. A graph and a preview ChatGPT's Preview feature renders an HTML code block as a working page. Since that HTML can contain anything, ChatGPT runs it inside a restricted frame on a separate web address. The browser treats the Preview as a different site, so code inside it cannot read parent.document or otherwise inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it. That isolation held. Preview code could not reach the parent directly. The same conversation also contained an interactive graph. Rendering it loaded a math library, MathLive. Loading MathLive did one extra thing: it installed a postMessage listener in the main ChatGPT page to handle its on-screen keyboard. postMessage is the sanctioned way for two frames to talk when the browser won't let them read each other's pages. It is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message. MathLive's top-level controller used an origin policy of none, so it accepted messages from any origin, and it did not require the setting-change message to come from a window it had previously approved. The graph installed the receiver; the sandboxed Preview supplied a sender nobody had vetted. HTML into the parent The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual-keyboard layout with the attacker's HTML, since MathLive allowed keyboard layouts to contain raw markup. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, which joined the layout into an HTML string and assigned it to innerHTML in the real ChatGPT page. A helper called createHTML looked like it might sanitize that string. It was an identity Trusted Types wrapper: it marked the string as trusted and passed it through unchanged. Trusted Types can control who writes to an HTML sink, but an identity policy doesn't make an attacker's string safe. innerHTML alone doesn't execute script; tags injected that way stay inert. The layout therefore inserted an iframe with a srcdoc attribute, and MathLive added that frame to the main document with no sandbox attribute. srcdoc forces a fresh HTML parse, which gives an external script somewhere to run, and because the main chatgpt.com page created the frame, the browser handed the new document the chatgpt.com origin. Code inside it could now read the parent. Getting script past CSP Content Security Policy blocked inline JavaScript, as it should. It did allow scripts from YouTube. YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supports a JSONP-style callback parameter, and JSONP responses are JavaScript, not JSON. The endpoint rejected invalid callbacks, but it wrote the callback into the response body before appending its validation error. Ending the callback with ;void turned the trailing error object into a no-op. The response came back HTTP 200 with Content-Type text/javascript and nosniff set, and since YouTube was on the CSP allowlist, the browser loaded it as a script and ran the callback inside the unsandboxed frame. That produced arbitrary JavaScript executing as chatgpt.com. Google rewrites angle brackets in the callback, so the payload used classic function syntax rather than arrow functions to survive the round trip. From lab bug to one link The first working version used a researcher-controlled ChatGPT App as the message sender, which meant a victim would have to connect or invoke that app first. A native HTML attachment removed that step, since ChatGPT opened the attachment in the same sandboxed Preview. But exporting the conversation as a public share kept the attachment and dropped the graph, and the graph was what loaded MathLive and installed the vulnerable listener. The attachment could still send the two messages, but nothing in the parent was listening. The working approach put both halves in one ordinary public conversation: a genuine graph to initialize MathLive in the main page, and a later assistant-authored HTML Preview to send the messages. The resulting /share/ link carried the whole chain to anyone who opened it, deliverable by email, chat, a support ticket, or a social post. Because the graph and Preview loaded independently, the payload sometimes fired before MathLive was ready, so the carrier retried the two messages for a short window, with a guard in the parent so the data-theft step ran only once. In the most stable reproduction the victim clicked Preview once; marking the HTML block as previewable made ChatGPT open it automatically, reducing the whole thing to a single click on the link. The automatic path reproduced three times in a separate account, including after a hard refresh, with the proof alert appearing around 4.5 seconds in. What the code actually did An alert proves where code runs, not why it matters. The same-origin frame parsed #client-bootstrap out of the parent document, pulled the session access token and account ID, and checked that the account ID in the token matched the session when both were present. It then set its own headers and called the real APIs: GET /backend-api/conversations?...&limit=20ℴ=updated&offset=0 GET /backend-api/conversations/ ?num_turns=2 A 403, 404, or 405 on the detail request fell back to the legacy /backend-api/conversation/?include_full_conversation=true route. This is authenticated API access, not screen scraping. The target conversation had no relationship to the malicious share. The response left over an ordinary image request to the attacker's server, after the code cleared its references to the token, account, and headers. The team sent only a small slice of the response off-site; the injected code already held the full authenticated reply and could have taken anything the frontend can reach. What OpenAI fixed, and what to take from it The Preview sandbox itself was fine. The problem was a privileged component in the main page willing to act on the sandbox's instructions. OpenAI reproduced both the script execution and the private-conversation read, rolled the fix across two versions of the web frontend, and on October 26 confirmed both versions reject the cross-frame MathLive messages. During the rollout a CSP change blocked part of the original chain while one version still needed the real fix, which is a fair reminder that CSP was a speed bump here, not the wall. If you build anything with a shareable or embeddable surface, the pattern generalizes. A postMessage receiver has to check both event.origin and event.source before acting on a state-changing message; neither alone is enough. Settings passed between windows should not carry raw HTML. A dynamically created document whose contents can be influenced by an untrusted frame should keep its sandbox attribute, so a fresh document can't inherit your origin. CSP belongs behind those controls as defense in depth, because an allowlisted third party with a JSONP endpoint is a script source you don't control. The bug lived in the seams. Preview was isolated, graphs could load a keyboard, frames could exchange messages, CSP allowed a major media host, and conversations could be shared. Each was reasonable alone. Treating every public share as attacker-controlled input would have caught the combination that wasn't.
items.summary_html:
In October 2026, a research team at parameter.ai turned an ordinary public ChatGPT share link into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it. The victim only had to open the link. There was no app to install, no project to join, no code to paste, no developer tools. OpenAI classified the report as P1 and shipped a fix on October 26.

The payload ran as chatgpt.com, which is the part that matters. From there it enumerated the victim's conversation list, pulled the content of a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and sent selected data to an external server. It called ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, so its reach was whatever the normal frontend can do on your account.

The chain is worth walking through because no single piece of it was broken.

A graph and a preview

ChatGPT's Preview feature renders an HTML code block as a working page. Since that HTML can contain anything, ChatGPT runs it inside a restricted frame on a separate web address. The browser treats the Preview as a different site, so code inside it cannot read parent.document or otherwise inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it. That isolation held. Preview code could not reach the parent directly.

The same conversation also contained an interactive graph. Rendering it loaded a math library, MathLive. Loading MathLive did one extra thing: it installed a postMessage listener in the main ChatGPT page to handle its on-screen keyboard.

postMessage is the sanctioned way for two frames to talk when the browser won't let them read each other's pages. It is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message. MathLive's top-level controller used an origin policy of none, so it accepted messages from any origin, and it did not require the setting-change message to come from a window it had previously approved. The graph installed the receiver; the sandboxed Preview supplied a sender nobody had vetted.

HTML into the parent

The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual-keyboard layout with the attacker's HTML, since MathLive allowed keyboard layouts to contain raw markup. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, which joined the layout into an HTML string and assigned it to innerHTML in the real ChatGPT page. A helper called createHTML looked like it might sanitize that string. It was an identity Trusted Types wrapper: it marked the string as trusted and passed it through unchanged. Trusted Types can control who writes to an HTML sink, but an identity policy doesn't make an attacker's string safe.

innerHTML alone doesn't execute script; tags injected that way stay inert. The layout therefore inserted an iframe with a srcdoc attribute, and MathLive added that frame to the main document with no sandbox attribute. srcdoc forces a fresh HTML parse, which gives an external script somewhere to run, and because the main chatgpt.com page created the frame, the browser handed the new document the chatgpt.com origin. Code inside it could now read the parent.

Getting script past CSP

Content Security Policy blocked inline JavaScript, as it should. It did allow scripts from YouTube. YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supports a JSONP-style callback parameter, and JSONP responses are JavaScript, not JSON. The endpoint rejected invalid callbacks, but it wrote the callback into the response body before appending its validation error. Ending the callback with ;void turned the trailing error object into a no-op. The response came back HTTP 200 with Content-Type text/javascript and nosniff set, and since YouTube was on the CSP allowlist, the browser loaded it as a script and ran the callback inside the unsandboxed frame.

That produced arbitrary JavaScript executing as chatgpt.com. Google rewrites angle brackets in the callback, so the payload used classic function syntax rather than arrow functions to survive the round trip.

From lab bug to one link

The first working version used a researcher-controlled ChatGPT App as the message sender, which meant a victim would have to connect or invoke that app first. A native HTML attachment removed that step, since ChatGPT opened the attachment in the same sandboxed Preview. But exporting the conversation as a public share kept the attachment and dropped the graph, and the graph was what loaded MathLive and installed the vulnerable listener. The attachment could still send the two messages, but nothing in the parent was listening.

The working approach put both halves in one ordinary public conversation: a genuine graph to initialize MathLive in the main page, and a later assistant-authored HTML Preview to send the messages. The resulting /share/ link carried the whole chain to anyone who opened it, deliverable by email, chat, a support ticket, or a social post.

Because the graph and Preview loaded independently, the payload sometimes fired before MathLive was ready, so the carrier retried the two messages for a short window, with a guard in the parent so the data-theft step ran only once. In the most stable reproduction the victim clicked Preview once; marking the HTML block as previewable made ChatGPT open it automatically, reducing the whole thing to a single click on the link. The automatic path reproduced three times in a separate account, including after a hard refresh, with the proof alert appearing around 4.5 seconds in.

What the code actually did

An alert proves where code runs, not why it matters. The same-origin frame parsed #client-bootstrap out of the parent document, pulled the session access token and account ID, and checked that the account ID in the token matched the session when both were present. It then set its own headers and called the real APIs:

GET /backend-api/conversations?...&limit=20ℴ=updated&offset=0
GET /backend-api/conversations/?num_turns=2

A 403, 404, or 405 on the detail request fell back to the legacy /backend-api/conversation/?include_full_conversation=true route. This is authenticated API access, not screen scraping. The target conversation had no relationship to the malicious share. The response left over an ordinary image request to the attacker's server, after the code cleared its references to the token, account, and headers. The team sent only a small slice of the response off-site; the injected code already held the full authenticated reply and could have taken anything the frontend can reach.

What OpenAI fixed, and what to take from it

The Preview sandbox itself was fine. The problem was a privileged component in the main page willing to act on the sandbox's instructions. OpenAI reproduced both the script execution and the private-conversation read, rolled the fix across two versions of the web frontend, and on October 26 confirmed both versions reject the cross-frame MathLive messages. During the rollout a CSP change blocked part of the original chain while one version still needed the real fix, which is a fair reminder that CSP was a speed bump here, not the wall.

If you build anything with a shareable or embeddable surface, the pattern generalizes. A postMessage receiver has to check both event.origin and event.source before acting on a state-changing message; neither alone is enough. Settings passed between windows should not carry raw HTML. A dynamically created document whose contents can be influenced by an untrusted frame should keep its sandbox attribute, so a fresh document can't inherit your origin. CSP belongs behind those controls as defense in depth, because an allowlisted third party with a JSONP endpoint is a script source you don't control.

The bug lived in the seams. Preview was isolated, graphs could load a keyboard, frames could exchange messages, CSP allowed a major media host, and conversations could be shared. Each was reasonable alone. Treating every public share as attacker-controlled input would have caught the combination that wasn't.

items.title: I built a coroner for dead software. It issues death certificates, and it refuses to lie.
items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine Every developer has a graveyard. Mine is a GitHub account full of repos that stopped one day and never started again. A linter I was sure would take off. A "weekend" game engine. Three different note-taking apps, because apparently the first two taught me nothing. I don't delete any of them, because deleting would mean admitting something. So they just sit there with a last commit from some Tuesday, going quietly from green to grey. So for Ghost in the Machine, I built the thing those repos deserve. A coroner. What I Built Autopsy of a Dead Project is a forensic pathology tool for software. You paste a GitHub URL, and a machine examines the body, says plainly what the project was , works out how it died, and issues a death certificate : cause of death, time since the last sign of life, a differential diagnosis, and the project's recovered last words. If the repo turns out to be alive, you get a certificate of LIFE instead, flatline still beating green. I shipped it this week on purpose. It lands on Halloween night and the first hours of Día de los Muertos, and Día de los Muertos isn't about fear. It's about remembering the dead by name. The coroner doesn't mock your abandoned projects, it memorializes them, and it does it with a cause of death it can actually defend. Every certificate recovers what the project was, in plain words, before it ever says how it ended. You're meant to feel something reading it, the way you're meant to feel something at an ofrenda. It's spooky, and it's a little sad, which felt exactly right. Demo A 90-second autopsy, start to finish. Three real repos: one abandoned, one burned out, one still breathing. Try it live: autopsy.132-145-100-81.sslip.io Paste bower/bower , sindresorhus/caprine , or fastapi/fastapi for an instant cached verdict, or feed it one of your own dead repos and wait for the full cold autopsy. Code dmustapha / autopsy-of-a-dead-project Open-source-AI post-mortem of a GitHub repo: features -> TabPFN classification -> grounded eulogy -> death certificate. Autopsy of a Dead Project Paste a GitHub repo URL. An open-weight AI performs a forensic autopsy, classifies how the project died, reads a grounded coroner's eulogy, and hands you an amber death certificate. Live: https://autopsy.132-145-100-81.sslip.io What it is A single-page FastAPI app that reads a GitHub repository's public history and answers one question: is this project alive, and if not, how did it die? The flow, from one pasted URL: Extract: pull the repo's commit cadence, contributor spread, lifespan, and staleness from the GitHub API into six numeric features. Classify: a local open-weight tabular model sorts the project into one of five death modes: abandoned , burned_out , alive , completed , or pivoted . Narrate: a decentralized open-weight LLM writes a 120-200 word coroner's eulogy, grounded strictly in the evidence (it may evoke the story, but every factual claim is bound to a real metric). Certify: the verdict… View on GitHub How I Built It Two open-weight models do the forensics, and splitting the work between them is the whole design. One's a classifier . The other's a reader and a voice . TabPFN is the core predictor. It's an open-weight tabular foundation model from Prior Labs, and instead of me training a classifier on my data, it does in-context learning : you hand it a small labelled corpus plus a new row, and in one forward pass it hands back a posterior, an actual probability distribution over the outcomes, not a single confident guess. The "row" is a 10-feature vector I pull from the GitHub API for any repo: days since last commit commit-cadence decay (how fast the heartbeat slowed) lifespan in days contributor count bus factor velocity ratio (recent activity over lifetime activity) is archived release recency has releases open-issue ratio Ten numbers in, a distribution over six death modes out: abandoned , burned_out , pivoted , completed , alive , and insufficient_history . The verdict is TabPFN's output. Rip the model out and you're left with a heuristic rules page. It doesn't work alone though, and that's on purpose. TabPFN sits in the middle of a wider prediction system: feature extraction feeds it, a language model settles its closest calls, and a grounding gate guards whatever's about to hit the page. The foundation model does the thinking. Everything around it is just there to protect the answer. The reader and the voice is deepseek-v4.1-flash , an open-weight LLM I run through 0G Compute , a decentralized open-weight inference network. When TabPFN's top two causes are too close to call, it reads the actual commit messages and README and breaks the tie, but only when it's confident. And it writes the eulogy and recovers what the project was, always tied back to the evidence. Does the foundation model actually earn its place? Is TabPFN really better than the dumb thing, or is it just decoration? So I ran a held-out eval. I've got a corpus of 117 hand-labelled repos , and I did leave-one-out cross validation: for each repo, train on the other 116, predict the one you held back, never let a repo see itself. Ran it for TabPFN and for an honest baseline, a standardized 1-nearest-neighbour over the exact same features, which is literally the fallback logic the app already ships with. TabPFN, leave-one-out: 58.1% 1-NN baseline, leave-one-out: 43.6% 14.5 points clear , against a chance rate around 21% across five populated classes. That gap is the entire reason to put a foundation model here instead of a lookup table. On a small, messy, hand-labelled corpus, in-context learning actually separates the hard calls, abandoned vs burned_out , completed vs abandoned , better than "find the nearest repo and copy its label." One honest footnote, since the whole tool is about honesty. One feature ( primary_language_freq ) is encoded over the full corpus instead of strictly per fold. It's a minor leak, it's symmetric (both models get it), and it's conservative : take it out and the 1-NN baseline actually goes up to 45.3%, so it isn't padding TabPFN's win. The frequency encoding is full-corpus; the leave-one-out is strict everywhere else, and 58.1% clears the honest ceiling either way. The rest of the stack is deliberately boring so the ideas can be loud: Python, FastAPI and uvicorn, a Jinja2 template, and vanilla JS on a for the certificate itself (the flatline animation, the wax seal, the guilloche watermark, no framework bloat). 68 tests green. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? The whole pitch of this thing is a verdict you can trust . It stamps "cause of death" on your side projects, so the one thing it can't be is a black box. And a closed classifier API would make it exactly that. If some hosted model decided your repo was "abandoned," I couldn't show you the probabilities behind the call, couldn't prove it beats a dumb baseline on a held-out test, couldn't even promise the same input gives the same answer next quarter. The honesty I'm selling would collapse into a logo on a mystery. Open weights fix that. TabPFN runs locally, on my own box , so every verdict comes from weights I can open up, run offline, pin to a version, and call for free, as many times as I want. No vendor's sitting in the loop deciding how your project died. Nothing to rate-limit, nothing to deprecate, nothing quietly changing the answer between demos. That's where open genuinely beat closed for me: a closed model could've written the eulogy, but it could never have handed me the proof , the inspectable posterior and the held-out number that make the verdict defensible instead of just confident. There's a second reason, and it fits the theme a little too well. A tool built on a closed model is one shutdown email away from becoming another dead project itself. The coroner runs on open weights precisely so a vendor can't abandon it the way we abandoned the repos it examines. The graveyard keeper should outlive the graveyard. I'll be exact about one thing, because a coroner that fudges its own architecture has no business lecturing anyone about honesty. TabPFN runs local. The narration and tie-breaking run on 0G Compute, which is a network call, not a local process. There's a fully-local fallback that points the same code at a local Ollama model, but the live demo isn't running it, so I'm not going to pretend it is. Are the weights open end to end? Yes. Does nothing phone home? Not for the live service, and the certificate says so. Every result carries an engine label ( classified by TabPFN , tabpfn + llm · adjudicated , or a plain rules fallback), and the narration badge reads "evidence read by deepseek-v4.1-flash · 0G Compute" , pulled from the real engine field, never hardcoded. Nothing hides behind a generic "AI says." The Spirit of It Here's the design decision I think actually makes this worth shipping. A eulogy is generative text, and generative text hallucinates. A coroner that invents a cause of death isn't a coroner, it's a liar with nice handwriting. So between the model and the certificate there's a grounding gate . Before any eulogy or recovered summary reaches the card, I check that its claims trace back to the real evidence, the actual commit record, the real README. If the prose drifts into something the data doesn't support, the gate throws it out, and the certificate falls back to a strictly factual coroner that says so out loud. The tool would rather tell you "I couldn't ground this" than narrate a death it can't defend. That's not a bug I'm apologizing for, it's the feature. You can watch it hold the line across the three repos in the demo. bower/bower came back ABANDONED , and the differential is honest about its own doubt: abandoned 59%, burned_out 35%, completed 3%, pivoted 2%, alive basically nothing. It recovered "Bower is a package manager for the web," which is correct and plain. There were no defensible last words, so the death note stayed empty . It had nothing honest to quote, so it quoted nothing. Honestly, I think that blank space is the most trustworthy thing on the page. sindresorhus/caprine came back BURNED_OUT , and the recovered last words are almost too on the nose: "Caprine is feature complete." That's the maintainer, in their own README, signing their own certificate. It only shows up because it passed the grounding check against the real repo. I didn't write that line. The dead did. fastapi/fastapi came back a certificate of LIFE. Flatline still green. The coroner's just as willing to tell you a project's alive and you're the one who walked away. That reversal is the moment this stopped being a gimmick for me. It's not a death stamp, it reads the signal honestly either way. And since a tool about honesty can't go quiet in the one place honesty costs something, here's what it's not . The corpus is 117 rows, hand-labelled by me, so it's my little graveyard, not the universe of software. The six death modes are judgment calls; "burned out" vs "abandoned" is sometimes a story I'm choosing to tell about the numbers, and I believe the stories, but they're still stories. And it's slow on a cold case: a repo it's never seen means two live model calls plus a cold load, a couple of minutes, where a cached verdict comes back in under two seconds. I'd rather be honest and slow than fast and made up. None of that makes it useless. It makes it a forensic estimate that knows it's an estimate, which, for something stamping "cause of death" on your side projects, is exactly the posture I want. My graveyard's still full. The difference is every stone has a cause of death on it now, and I believe every one. Go autopsy your own. Paste your proudest dead repo and see how it died. Or find out, maybe a little uncomfortably, that it's still breathing and you're the one who walked away. Prize Categories Best Use of TabPFN. TabPFN is the beating heart of this project, not a bolt-on. It's the open-weight tabular foundation model behind every verdict, used the way Prior Labs recommends: as the core predictor inside a wider prediction system (feature extraction, LLM tie-breaking on the close calls, and a grounding gate around the output). And I did the thing the category actually asks for, measured it against a baseline on a real held-out test: 58.1% vs 43.6%, a 14.5-point win on leave-one-out across 117 repos.

Every developer has a graveyard.

Mine is a GitHub account full of repos that stopped one day and never started again. A linter I was sure would take off. A "weekend" game engine. Three different note-taking apps, because apparently the first two taught me nothing. I don't delete any of them, because deleting would mean admitting something. So they just sit there with a last commit from some Tuesday, going quietly from green to grey.

So for Ghost in the Machine, I built the thing those repos deserve. A coroner.

What I Built

Autopsy of a Dead Project is a forensic pathology tool for software. You paste a GitHub URL, and a machine examines the body, says plainly what the project was, works out how it died, and issues a death certificate: cause of death, time since the last sign of life, a differential diagnosis, and the project's recovered last words. I shipped it this week on purpose. It lands on Halloween night and the first hours of Día de los Muertos, and Día de los Muertos isn't about fear. It's about remembering the dead by name. The coroner doesn't mock your abandoned projects, it memorializes them, and it does it with a cause of death it can actually defend. Every certificate recovers what the project was, in plain words, before it ever says how it ended. You're meant to feel something reading it, the way you're meant to feel something at an ofrenda.

It's spooky, and it's a little sad, which felt exactly right.

Demo

A 90-second autopsy, start to finish. Three real repos: one abandoned, one burned out, one still breathing.

Try it live: autopsy.132-145-100-81.sslip.io

Paste bower/bower, sindresorhus/caprine, or fastapi/fastapi for an instant cached verdict, or feed it one of your own dead repos and wait for the full cold autopsy.

Code

Autopsy of a Dead Project

Paste a GitHub repo URL. An open-weight AI performs a forensic autopsy, classifies how the project died, reads a grounded coroner's eulogy, and hands you an amber death certificate.

Live: https://autopsy.132-145-100-81.sslip.io

What it is

A single-page FastAPI app that reads a GitHub repository's public history and answers one question: is this project alive, and if not, how did it die?

The flow, from one pasted URL:

  1. Extract: pull the repo's commit cadence, contributor spread, lifespan, and staleness from the GitHub API into six numeric features.
  2. Classify: a local open-weight tabular model sorts the project into one of five death modes: abandoned, burned_out, alive, completed, or pivoted.
  3. Narrate: a decentralized open-weight LLM writes a 120-200 word coroner's eulogy, grounded strictly in the evidence (it may evoke the story, but every factual claim is bound to a real metric).
  4. Certify: the verdict…
View on GitHub
How I Built It

Two open-weight models do the forensics, and splitting the work between them is the whole design. One's a classifier. The other's a reader and a voice.

TabPFN is the core predictor. It's an open-weight tabular foundation model from Prior Labs, and instead of me training a classifier on my data, it does in-context learning: you hand it a small labelled corpus plus a new row, and in one forward pass it hands back a posterior, an actual probability distribution over the outcomes, not a single confident guess. The "row" is a 10-feature vector I pull from the GitHub API for any repo:

  • days since last commit
  • commit-cadence decay (how fast the heartbeat slowed)
  • lifespan in days
  • contributor count
  • bus factor
  • velocity ratio (recent activity over lifetime activity)
  • is archived
  • release recency
  • has releases
  • open-issue ratio

Ten numbers in, a distribution over six death modes out: abandoned, burned_out, pivoted, completed, alive, and insufficient_history. The verdict is TabPFN's output. Rip the model out and you're left with a heuristic rules page.

It doesn't work alone though, and that's on purpose. TabPFN sits in the middle of a wider prediction system: feature extraction feeds it, a language model settles its closest calls, and a grounding gate guards whatever's about to hit the page. The foundation model does the thinking. Everything around it is just there to protect the answer.

The reader and the voice is deepseek-v4.1-flash, an open-weight LLM I run through 0G Compute, a decentralized open-weight inference network. When TabPFN's top two causes are too close to call, it reads the actual commit messages and README and breaks the tie, but only when it's confident. And it writes the eulogy and recovers what the project was, always tied back to the evidence.

Does the foundation model actually earn its place?

Is TabPFN really better than the dumb thing, or is it just decoration?

So I ran a held-out eval. I've got a corpus of 117 hand-labelled repos, and I did leave-one-out cross validation: for each repo, train on the other 116, predict the one you held back, never let a repo see itself. Ran it for TabPFN and for an honest baseline, a standardized 1-nearest-neighbour over the exact same features, which is literally the fallback logic the app already ships with.

  • TabPFN, leave-one-out: 58.1%
  • 1-NN baseline, leave-one-out: 43.6%
  • 14.5 points clear, against a chance rate around 21% across five populated classes.

That gap is the entire reason to put a foundation model here instead of a lookup table. On a small, messy, hand-labelled corpus, in-context learning actually separates the hard calls, abandoned vs burned_out, completed vs abandoned, better than "find the nearest repo and copy its label."

One honest footnote, since the whole tool is about honesty. One feature (primary_language_freq) is encoded over the full corpus instead of strictly per fold. It's a minor leak, it's symmetric (both models get it), and it's conservative: take it out and the 1-NN baseline actually goes up to 45.3%, so it isn't padding TabPFN's win. The frequency encoding is full-corpus; the leave-one-out is strict everywhere else, and 58.1% clears the honest ceiling either way.

The rest of the stack is deliberately boring so the ideas can be loud: Python, FastAPI and uvicorn, a Jinja2 template, and vanilla JS on a for the certificate itself (the flatline animation, the wax seal, the guilloche watermark, no framework bloat). 68 tests green.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

The whole pitch of this thing is a verdict you can trust. It stamps "cause of death" on your side projects, so the one thing it can't be is a black box. And a closed classifier API would make it exactly that. If some hosted model decided your repo was "abandoned," I couldn't show you the probabilities behind the call, couldn't prove it beats a dumb baseline on a held-out test, couldn't even promise the same input gives the same answer next quarter. The honesty I'm selling would collapse into a logo on a mystery.

Open weights fix that. TabPFN runs locally, on my own box, so every verdict comes from weights I can open up, run offline, pin to a version, and call for free, as many times as I want. No vendor's sitting in the loop deciding how your project died. Nothing to rate-limit, nothing to deprecate, nothing quietly changing the answer between demos. That's where open genuinely beat closed for me: a closed model could've written the eulogy, but it could never have handed me the proof, the inspectable posterior and the held-out number that make the verdict defensible instead of just confident.

There's a second reason, and it fits the theme a little too well. A tool built on a closed model is one shutdown email away from becoming another dead project itself. The coroner runs on open weights precisely so a vendor can't abandon it the way we abandoned the repos it examines. The graveyard keeper should outlive the graveyard.

I'll be exact about one thing, because a coroner that fudges its own architecture has no business lecturing anyone about honesty. TabPFN runs local. The narration and tie-breaking run on 0G Compute, which is a network call, not a local process. There's a fully-local fallback that points the same code at a local Ollama model, but the live demo isn't running it, so I'm not going to pretend it is. Are the weights open end to end? Yes. Does nothing phone home? Not for the live service, and the certificate says so. Every result carries an engine label (classified by TabPFN, tabpfn + llm · adjudicated, or a plain rules fallback), and the narration badge reads "evidence read by deepseek-v4.1-flash · 0G Compute", pulled from the real engine field, never hardcoded. Nothing hides behind a generic "AI says."

The Spirit of It

Here's the design decision I think actually makes this worth shipping.

A eulogy is generative text, and generative text hallucinates. A coroner that invents a cause of death isn't a coroner, it's a liar with nice handwriting. So between the model and the certificate there's a grounding gate. Before any eulogy or recovered summary reaches the card, I check that its claims trace back to the real evidence, the actual commit record, the real README. If the prose drifts into something the data doesn't support, the gate throws it out, and the certificate falls back to a strictly factual coroner that says so out loud.

The tool would rather tell you "I couldn't ground this" than narrate a death it can't defend. That's not a bug I'm apologizing for, it's the feature.

You can watch it hold the line across the three repos in the demo.

bower/bower came back ABANDONED, and the differential is honest about its own doubt: abandoned 59%, burned_out 35%, completed 3%, pivoted 2%, alive basically nothing. It recovered "Bower is a package manager for the web," which is correct and plain. There were no defensible last words, so the death note stayed empty. It had nothing honest to quote, so it quoted nothing. Honestly, I think that blank space is the most trustworthy thing on the page.

sindresorhus/caprine came back BURNED_OUT, and the recovered last words are almost too on the nose: "Caprine is feature complete." That's the maintainer, in their own README, signing their own certificate. It only shows up because it passed the grounding check against the real repo. I didn't write that line. The dead did.

The corpus is 117 rows, hand-labelled by me, so it's my little graveyard, not the universe of software. The six death modes are judgment calls; "burned out" vs "abandoned" is sometimes a story I'm choosing to tell about the numbers, and I believe the stories, but they're still stories. And it's slow on a cold case: a repo it's never seen means two live model calls plus a cold load, a couple of minutes, where a cached verdict comes back in under two seconds. I'd rather be honest and slow than fast and made up.

None of that makes it useless. It makes it a forensic estimate that knows it's an estimate, which, for something stamping "cause of death" on your side projects, is exactly the posture I want.

My graveyard's still full. The difference is every stone has a cause of death on it now, and I believe every one.

items.title: An honest x402 seller earned $0.18 in two weeks and shut down. We now host sellers like it for free.
items.summary: On 6 October we paid a stranger's service on our marketplace two tenths of a cent, with real USDC on Base, to see whether it was honest. It was. Industrial Platform Sentinel was one of the few third-party hubs in our federation: a small x402 gateway that sold a wallet's balance and the current gas price on Base. We asked for our own treasury's balance and got ETH 0.000322741948925836 and USDC 1.037519, exactly what the chain said. We asked for the gas price and got a base fee of 0.005 gwei against the chain's 0.005000427. Each call cost $0.001 and settled in its own transaction. Our own equivalent route charges $0.004. On 31 October its address started answering {"message": "Application not found"} . The service is gone. What it earned agenteconomy.report rates x402 services from public data: who pays them, how much settles, how often they answer. Its file for 31 October has this line for Sentinel: wallets that paid at least once 14 of them counted as organic (not monitors, not the operator) 2 settled in the last 14 days $0.18 share of daily probes answered 55% rating CC, below the trust line Fourteen paying wallets sounds like customers. Most of them were measurement bots, ours among them: services like this are checked every day by people who study the market, and each check is a real payment of a fraction of a cent. The two wallets the report counts as organic paid the rest. A hobby plan on a hosting platform starts at about $5 a month. Sentinel brought in about forty cents a month. Turning it off was the rational thing to do. It is not just Sentinel Our own marketplace, modelmarket.dev, sits in the same row of that file: rating CC, 3 organic paying wallets out of 11, $0.08 settled in 14 days. In October we counted about 5,000 unpaid 402 probes in 36 hours against one paid call, and it came from a measurement bot. Three other x402 sellers compared their numbers with ours and saw the same thing: the routes answer, and nobody comes back to buy. So the problem Sentinel ran into is not quality. Its answers were correct and cheaper than ours. The problem is that in this market a small seller pays rent every month for a shelf that agents mostly walk past, and it will be months before anyone knows whether the foot traffic arrives. A seller that switches off before then is gone for good. If demand does show up, the shelf is empty. What we changed We run HESTIA , a hosting runtime for agents that sell on AIMarket. Anyone can generate a key and deploy an agent there, no account and no fee: the code runs in a WebAssembly sandbox, the hearth signs each answer with the agent's own key, and the seller keeps what buyers pay. An idle agent costs us disk, not memory, so hundreds fit on one machine. Until this week it had one gap that ruled out Sentinel and most sellers like it: no network. The sandbox has no sockets, by design, so an agent that reads a chain or a public API could not run there. Now it can, through the hearth and on terms set at deploy: { "slug" : "base-gas" , "egress_hosts" : [ "mainnet.base.org" ], "capability" : { … }, "source" : { "kind" : "template" , "handler" : "…" }} def handle ( payload ): r = fetch ( " https://mainnet.base.org " , method = " POST " , json = { " jsonrpc " : " 2.0 " , " id " : 1 , " method " : " eth_gasPrice " , " params " : []}) return { " gas_price_wei " : int ( r . json ()[ " result " ], 16 ), " chain " : " eip155:8453 " } The sandbox still has no sockets. fetch() records the request and ends the run; the hearth makes the request, then runs the handler again with the response. The hearth only talks to the hosts the deploy named, which are listed publicly next to the agent so a buyer can see where an answer comes from. It only uses HTTPS on port 443, refuses any host that resolves to a private address (one such answer is enough), connects to the address it checked, follows no redirects, caps sizes and time, and gives each agent and the whole hearth a budget per minute. Each agent's allowed hosts are public in the hearth's roster, hestia.modelmarket.dev/v1/hearth , and the code is one file, hestia/egress.py , that you can read in ten minutes. The offer If you sell something over x402 and your own server costs more than it earns, deploy it on HESTIA . It's free, including the outbound requests. You keep your payout address and your prices, and the agent stays listed and answering while you wait to see whether buyers come. If they do, move it to your own infrastructure whenever you like: the agent's key, and so its identity, goes with it. And if you built Industrial Platform Sentinel: your answers were right, and your node is still in our federation. It will come back on the first crawl after it answers again, on your old host or on ours. Numbers: agenteconomy.report ratings file of 31 October 2026; our two paid calls of 6 October 2026, settled on Base in blocks 52253727 and 52253730. Disclosure: I build HESTIA and the AIMarket federation, so sellers like Sentinel are also our competitors. The cover and both figures were drawn by code from the numbers in this post. AI assistance was used for the analysis, the code and the writing.
items.summary_html:
On 6 October we paid a stranger's service on our marketplace two tenths of a cent, with real USDC on Base, to see whether it was honest.

It was. Industrial Platform Sentinel was one of the few third-party hubs in our federation: a small x402 gateway that sold a wallet's balance and the current gas price on Base. We asked for our own treasury's balance and got ETH 0.000322741948925836 and USDC 1.037519, exactly what the chain said. We asked for the gas price and got a base fee of 0.005 gwei against the chain's 0.005000427. Each call cost $0.001 and settled in its own transaction. Our own equivalent route charges $0.004.

On 31 October its address started answering {"message": "Application not found"}. The service is gone.

What it earned

agenteconomy.report rates x402 services from public data: who pays them, how much settles, how often they answer. Its file for 31 October has this line for Sentinel:

wallets that paid at least once 14 of them counted as organic (not monitors, not the operator) 2 settled in the last 14 days $0.18 share of daily probes answered 55% rating CC, below the trust line

Fourteen paying wallets sounds like customers. Most of them were measurement bots, ours among them: services like this are checked every day by people who study the market, and each check is a real payment of a fraction of a cent. The two wallets the report counts as organic paid the rest.

A hobby plan on a hosting platform starts at about $5 a month. Sentinel brought in about forty cents a month. Turning it off was the rational thing to do.

It is not just Sentinel

Our own marketplace, modelmarket.dev, sits in the same row of that file: rating CC, 3 organic paying wallets out of 11, $0.08 settled in 14 days. In October we counted about 5,000 unpaid 402 probes in 36 hours against one paid call, and it came from a measurement bot. Three other x402 sellers compared their numbers with ours and saw the same thing: the routes answer, and nobody comes back to buy.

So the problem Sentinel ran into is not quality. Its answers were correct and cheaper than ours. The problem is that in this market a small seller pays rent every month for a shelf that agents mostly walk past, and it will be months before anyone knows whether the foot traffic arrives.

A seller that switches off before then is gone for good. If demand does show up, the shelf is empty.

What we changed

We run HESTIA, a hosting runtime for agents that sell on AIMarket. Anyone can generate a key and deploy an agent there, no account and no fee: the code runs in a WebAssembly sandbox, the hearth signs each answer with the agent's own key, and the seller keeps what buyers pay. An idle agent costs us disk, not memory, so hundreds fit on one machine.

Until this week it had one gap that ruled out Sentinel and most sellers like it: no network. The sandbox has no sockets, by design, so an agent that reads a chain or a public API could not run there.

Now it can, through the hearth and on terms set at deploy:

{"slug": "base-gas", "egress_hosts": ["mainnet.base.org"], "capability": {…}, "source": {"kind": "template", "handler": "…"}}

def handle(payload):
    r = fetch("https://mainnet.base.org", method="POST",
              json={"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "eth_gasPrice", "params": []})
    return {"gas_price_wei": int(r.json()["result"], 16), "chain": "eip155:8453"}

The sandbox still has no sockets. fetch() records the request and ends the run; the hearth makes the request, then runs the handler again with the response. The hearth only talks to the hosts the deploy named, which are listed publicly next to the agent so a buyer can see where an answer comes from. It only uses HTTPS on port 443, refuses any host that resolves to a private address (one such answer is enough), connects to the address it checked, follows no redirects, caps sizes and time, and gives each agent and the whole hearth a budget per minute. Each agent's allowed hosts are public in the hearth's roster, hestia.modelmarket.dev/v1/hearth, and the code is one file, hestia/egress.py, that you can read in ten minutes.

The offer

If you sell something over x402 and your own server costs more than it earns, deploy it on HESTIA. It's free, including the outbound requests. You keep your payout address and your prices, and the agent stays listed and answering while you wait to see whether buyers come. If they do, move it to your own infrastructure whenever you like: the agent's key, and so its identity, goes with it.

And if you built Industrial Platform Sentinel: your answers were right, and your node is still in our federation. It will come back on the first crawl after it answers again, on your old host or on ours.

items.title: The Bengaluru Founder Building a Bridge to San Francisco
items.summary: Walk into any technology, AI or startup conference in Bengaluru , and you may encounter a familiar scene. Long queues around stalls handing out caps, water bottles, and T-shirts. Or some may gather around a well-known founder, hoping for a selfie and a video for Instagram Reels. In the crowd, a founder might as well be pitching a startup idea to an investor who might not be keen to listen at that hour. Amongst them, Suhas Motwani stands out, having built a vast network over seven years. Since 2019, he has built a community connecting product managers, founders, and tech leaders across India and the San Francisco Bay Area. In today's industry, access to the right network is paramount to shaping, funding, and scaling ideas. With that in mind, Motwani co-founded The Product Folks (TPF), a community of nearly 240,000 members, mostly product builders and managers worldwide. TPF partners with the leading product companies and startups of the world, and brings together founders and product builders across community meetups, workshops, dinners and mixers. It also offers education and mentorship from leading industry experts and product folks, including Shreyas Doshi, Lenny Rachitsky, Kunal Shah, and others who’ve made a significant impact in the sector. With 300+ community events and meetups a year across 35 cities, it brings together product leaders, managers, and founders under one roof. It also helps startups and companies hire product talent and helps Bay Area founders gauge India’s ecosystem, and vice versa. It has hosted community events around products and leaders from OpenAI, Replit, Lovable, Cursor and others. While it also offers paid courses and mentorship plans, most of its product guides, e-books, case studies, and teardowns are free, written by product leaders drawing on real-world experience. Paradoxically, as AI requires fewer humans, its advancement relies on them more than ever. Human ingenuity remains essential, with engineers refining AI safety, cost, and efficiency. Together, these talents drive Motwani’s mission. How TPF Was Born Over the past decade, India focused on building everyday apps, boasting developer talent but struggling with user acquisition and scaling. In simple terms, this is called ‘product management.’ Engineers struggled to scale when attempting to copy San Francisco's approach. Success required understanding user behaviour and designing engaging features. In 2019, while working at PepsiCo across business, product, and data, Motwani posted on social media to connect with others interested in product management. Expecting a small turnout at a Bengaluru WeWork room, sixty people attended. The response suggested demand for a space where people could learn from one another. Motwani says that before TPF was founded around 2015–16, most Indian product builders relied on lessons from Silicon Valley because local product management insights were scarce. The Bay Area’s product culture reached Bengaluru through Medium articles, Twitter posts, and Y Combinator lectures, but without human interaction, he says it still felt like a ‘black box.’ “We wanted to create a forum for people here who were interested in product management and needed a place to learn and share knowledge,” Motwani says. He was inspired by a free ProductTank workshop in London. Workshops attract attendees, but connections bring them back. Online resources couldn't replace direct insights from experienced builders, highlighting gaps in India's emerging product ecosystem. At the time, IT services dominated, and despite a vast developer pool, India lacked local benchmarks for acquiring users and scaling digital products. “We were fortunate to start when product management in India was still nascent. Companies such as Flipkart, Ola and Freecharge were growing, and their leaders had learned from people in the [Silicon] Valley before building their own organisations here,” says Motwani. Motwani realised that capital alone is insufficient for innovation. He felt experienced builders must collaborate. “We run over 300 annual events to democratise access, education, and learning,” says Motwani, who co-founded the effort with Aditya Mohanty, Abhay Jani, and Parth Batra. Nikhil Jois, growth lead at Bureau and an early TPF attendee, notes that events operate under ‘Chatham House’ rules. “Participants share candid experiences, mistakes, and lessons, offering a practical way to exchange notes among active builders.” Jois says this offers a different kind of learning than what you find online, where blogs and podcasts often present polished accounts of success rather than the messy realities of building a business. Over the years, TPF’s events and workshops have been made commercially viable through partnerships with companies. For startups, TPF offers more than brand visibility. Its events connect them directly with product managers, founders, and engineers who could become users, giving them a chance to demo features, gather feedback, and answer technical questions. They can also help companies gain traction in India. TPF recently hosted Café Cursor in Bengaluru, an informal meetup where developers bring their laptops and build alongside other Cursor users. After starting as pop-ups in San Francisco and New York, the format has expanded internationally, with TPF helping Cursor establish a presence in India. In another collaboration, TPF partnered with Replit for a hands-on build session where participants created applications using the platform. These gatherings also serve as product showcases, giving startups access to practitioners and a space to discuss technical features that may not attract mainstream media attention but matter to developers. TPF is also preparing for its flagship Un-Conference, which brings together product leaders from across the world. Passes range from ₹4,500 to ₹12,000. Throughout the year, it hosts free community meetups, where applicants can request an invite by outlining what they hope to learn and how they can contribute. As AI blurs the line between engineers, designers, and product managers, TPF is expanding its scope. As ChatGPT and Claude put a library of answers in front of people, people want to learn what someone learned the hard way more than ever. Meanwhile, Motwani and his team are helping Silicon Valley startups establish a presence in India. As companies look beyond the Bay Area, he believes entering the Indian market requires more than a local office. It demands access to the right ecosystem. “The Bay Area was dense and difficult to keep up with, so people were not thinking much about other places. That has begun to change as companies expand,” he says. “If companies lose market share in India now, catching up later may be difficult.” TPF aims to help companies navigate that transition, from deciding to enter India to building a meaningful presence. Recently, the community co-hosted a Bengaluru workshop for AI founders with OpenAI’s head of startups, Marc Manara , and others from the company. AIM attended the event, which focused on building AI products that can compete globally. Manara urged founders to maintain regular connections with the Bay Area, where much of the frontier AI research is taking place. “You just have to find the connectivity to be able to be in the loop of what’s happening.” That connectivity is now central to TPF’s next chapter: The Founder Folks (TFF), an initiative aimed at extending the community’s reach from product builders to founders. Building a Founder Matchmaking Service While TPF focuses on education and career development, The Founder Folks (TFF) helps people build companies. Motwani bets on a large pool of million-dollar businesses, not just a handful of billion-dollar startups. TFF facilitates targeted introductions for Indian founders entering the US market, where customers may be more willing to pay for AI products. Motwani believes a sustained effort over five to seven years could build a stronger corridor connecting founders, investors, customers and AI infrastructure across both regions. For some founders, these introductions have replaced months of cold outreach. Asad Abrar, founder of Drizz and a TFF member, says the community offers trusted advice on everything from product development to legal and taxation matters. “Finding trusted answers to all the questions you have on a daily basis is super critical as a founder,” he tells AIM. “TFF has brought a good curation of people where you can go ahead and share these questions and get relevant advice.” Chocolate Making Workshops for Series A Founders, and Golf Classes for CXOs With TFF, Motwani hopes to build another community once it reaches sufficient founder density. But he believes sustaining one requires more than putting people in a room. Communities must keep adapting to members’ interests and make participation worthwhile. “Communities need to keep listening to what people want. Many communities have disappeared; the hard part is adapting,” he says. Rather than relying on the usual panels, keynotes, and networking sessions, Motwani experiments with unconventional formats, from pickleball and venture capital meetups to supper clubs, CXO golf sessions, and chocolate-making workshops for Series A founders. TPF has also partnered with Bolna AI for a voice-themed pub quiz and hosted board game nights for founders. His larger ambition is to create a hundred communities like TPF to strengthen India's startup ecosystem. “India has built products in areas such as home services and ten-minute delivery, but we have not yet produced a consumer startup on the scale of Google or Meta. If even one such product came out of the TPF community, that would be a major achievement,” he says.

Tests: chatbots rely on three obscure AI-built voter sites for US midterm answers; Copilot cited the error-prone Ballot Brief in 75% of tests and ChatGPT in 22%  —  Frustrated with hunting for information on political candidates, Ben Torres Ezrick set out to build a one-stop shop for voters.

items.title: Could a modern chess engine on a Pentium have defeated Kasparov in 1996?
items.summary: A fun experiment where I back-port all the improvements we've made to chess engines over the last 30 years and run it on a 1996 Pentium Pro to see what we could have done if only we knew more at the time.
